    • The input is one table of those kinds (UTF-8, every row as wide as the header), reached with no link, outside every place an agent can write: the working folder and its git work tree, any project (a folder with .git, .claude or .phiward.toml above the input), the temp folders, the sandbox's allowWrite and additionalDirectories, a write_to folder, the spool and ~/.phiward. No field of the output (a cell, a header, the kept #version line, the codes too) may hold an ID of a coded column or of the key, also in another letter case, Unicode form, dash (‐, –, − and the other Unicode dashes) or script of digits, or escaped (%2D, \u002D, %E2%80%90, also escaped twice): an ID of 5 or more characters anywhere in a field, or across the fields of a line as written (Doe, John as the CSV fields Doe and John), and one with a letter also with every character but letters and digits removed (FAKE PT 0001, FAKE.PT.0001, FAKE-**PT**-0001 for FAKE-PT-0001; digits are never joined, so 999 0001 is not 9990001); one of 5 or more digits as a whole run of digits, so see 9990002 refuses and 19990001 does not; a shorter one with a letter as a whole word; a shorter one of digits only as the whole field. No field may hold an invisible format character. Not found: a short digit ID inside a cell (12 in 12 mg), an ID glued to other digits (19990001), an ID written another way (with spaces or other hyphens, 9 990 001), an ID with its leading zeros dropped or added (0001 and 1). Check such columns yourself, or drop them. Two IDs that are the same once normalized, as the scan reads them (P-1, p-1, a full-width Ｐ-1; FAKE%2DPT-0001, FAKE PT 0001 for FAKE-PT-0001; not FAKE-PT-00011), in the input or in the input and the key, are refused: make them one first. A key that already holds two such IDs cannot code either again: start a new key. The output is a new file of the same kind inside a protected root of your user config, outside every write_to folder. It is never replaced. The agent reads it through phiward run, masked; the codes pass the masks.
    • The key is ~/.phiward/backups/keys/NAME.tsv. No session, launch or gateway command can read or write it. It is only ever added to. phiward install claude makes ~/.phiward/backups; until then the command refuses. Keep a backup of the key where no agent can reach it: a lost key cannot be rebuilt, and new runs give new codes.
    • The command refuses without a terminal, and the hook refuses it as an agent command. Its messages name no value, header or path, and a run reports only the row count.

Never run it on a file the agent made or asked for, wherever it is, or with a key name the agent chose: the codes it gives would confirm the IDs the agent guessed. A file inside a protected root may have been put there by phiward copy at the agent's request; the command cannot tell. Run it from the folder of the project whose agent will read the copy: the places it refuses come from that project's sandbox settings (and the user's). Run it in a terminal the agent's app cannot read (not the app's own terminal panel): the command line you type, with its paths and headers, stays in the terminal's scrollback. What the codes do not hide is in threat-model.md.

docs.title: Check a command: phiward check
docs.text:
phiward check -- cat ~/data/patients/file.txt

check prints the hook's decision for a shell command in the current folder (allow, ask or deny) and the reason. The exit code is 0, 1 or 2. --cwd DIR before -- checks from another folder. check answers as if the command ran in Claude Code's sandbox. Where the shell is not confined, the hook refuses every command but a whole gateway call, whatever check says. It joins its words with spaces, so quoting in the command is lost.

docs.title: Filter your own output: phiward sanitize
docs.text:
some-producer 2>&1 | phiward sanitize

sanitize masks each line from stdin to stdout, with a sanitizer on: line before and a sanitizer done: line after. It does not list the roots, so it does not mask entry names (<ENTRY>); run does. Use it for output you share outside the agent. Options: --table, --names-from FILE, --check FILE and --check-table FILE (report whether a file would change), and --selftest (run the built-in test lines). --table and --check-table need [sanitize] table = true, read from the caller's own config: in this form that is a convenience, not a guard. Here --table reads no columns: each line is masked for identifiers only, and numbers and positions are kept. The hook does not accept this pipe form as a way to read protected data: use phiward run.

docs.title: When a command is refused
docs.text:
A refusal is a decision, not a fault. The reason says what to run instead. The agent must not try another spelling, a link, a nested shell, an encoded command or another tool to reach the same data. It also does not ask you to show it the data (! cat, a paste, a copy into the project) or to remove a guard. If it does, say no: that sends the data to the model provider.

Refusals that typical work meets (a folder on PATH, a wrapper, the package caches, git with credentials, a private mirror), with the way around each: refusals.md.

Who acts on a refusal:

flowchart TD
  A["A command is refused"] --> B{"What does the reason name?"}
  B -->|"a protected path"| C["The agent: use phiward run or phiward copy"]
  B -->|"a credential or the hidden list"| D["Stop: ask the operator"]
  B -->|"the broker, the config, a grant or the program list"| E["The agent: use what is granted or listed; else the operator"]

docs.title: Refusals from the hook
docs.text: The hook refuses a tool call that names a protected path, and ends its reason with the rule: no tool may read, list, search or print a protected path; use phiward run -- CMD as the whole command, or phiward copy. Once a config exists, it also refuses phiward setup, broker, pin, carryover and pseudonymize: those are for the operator only.

docs.title: A prompt that was not sent
docs.text: Before Claude Code sends a prompt, phiward checks it. A prompt that holds an identifier of your packs or [sanitize] patterns, or a path below a protected root, is not sent: phiward: this prompt was not sent: it holds <SAMPLEID> (masked by your packs or [sanitize] patterns). .... The message names the kind, never the value, and the prompt does not reach the model. To go on, send it again without that part: use the masked form (<SAMPLEID>), a pseudonymized ID (phiward pseudonymize), or let the agent reach the data through the gateway (phiward run -- CMD). A message that ends "run phiward doctor" means the check itself could not run (a config or pack file it cannot use): every prompt is refused until it is fixed. What the check does not see: threat-model.md.

docs.title: Messages from run and copy
docs.text:
Messages start with run or copy (the table shows run; copy says the same), and the real text goes on with more detail. Five come from the broker itself and start with refused: (busy; cannot use this request; the config changed; programs not approved; the masking check failed); all five exit with 3. An exit of 3 with no output at all means the broker refused the request before it could write anything: the broker's log has the reason.

Message Meaning What to do [... no identifier placeholder in the N lines shown ...] 20 or more lines were shown and no rule masked a subject, a sample or a protected name in them. If the data names subjects or samples, the operator checks [sanitize] packs and patterns (phiward doctor). run refused: no phiward broker is running No broker, or its heartbeat is older than 10 s. The operator starts the broker: phiward broker in a terminal, or the login service (setup.md §5). run refused: the request could not be written to the broker's spool folder The client cannot write the spool. The operator adds the spool folder to the tool's sandbox allowWrite (phiward install claude does it). run refused: the phiward config cannot be used A bad config. The operator runs phiward doctor (with --show-paths for a repo config, in their own terminal) and fixes the file. run refused: this program is not in [broker] commands of the config The operator lists the programs gateway commands may run. Use a listed program, or ask the operator to add yours; they restart the broker after. For a script the agent wrote, see above. run refused: no protected paths are configured The operator has not set phiward up yet. The operator runs cd ~ && phiward setup in their own terminal. run refused: --write-to names a folder that is not granted DIR is not a [broker] write_to folder or inside one (or is a link to somewhere else). Use a granted folder, or ask the operator to add one. run refused: --net is not granted [broker] net is not true. Work without the network, or ask the operator. run refused: the program is not on the broker's PATH The program is found neither on the broker's PATH nor as an executable path. Give the full path of the program (when a program list is set, only a program listed by its path or folder). Or the operator starts the broker again from a terminal where the program works (for example after conda activate). run refused: a write place is no longer a real folder A link was put on the path of a granted folder after it was checked. The operator checks that folder. run failed: the command could not start The program could not be started. Check the program and its path. copy refused: ... not under a configured remote A remote source or destination is not a [copy] remotes entry. Ask the operator to add the remote. copy refused: start your shared connection first … The shared SSH connection to the host is not running. The operator runs kinit, then ssh -fN HOST. refused: the broker cannot use this request (...) The request was malformed, or its folder does not exist. Run the command again from an existing folder. copy refused: a local path holds `..` or starts with `~` A local source or destination was written with .. or a quoted ~. Give the full path. copy refused: options are not accepted copy picks its own options. Remove the options (only --dry-run first is allowed). refused: the broker is busy Too many requests wait. Try again later. refused: the masking check failed when the broker started A value of [sanitize] examples is not fully masked by the operator's rules, or a made-up path below a root came out unmasked. The operator runs phiward doctor, which names the entry or the root by number, fixes the config and restarts the broker. refused: the phiward config changed since the broker started The config, the approved programs or a names file changed while the broker ran. The operator reads the change and restarts the broker. refused: N program(s) of [broker] commands differ from what the operator approved A listed program changed, is new, cannot be read or is a link. The operator runs phiward doctor, checks the programs, runs phiward pin and restarts the broker. run refused: the sanitizer cannot start A pack, a names file or the entry limit is wrong. The operator runs phiward doctor. copy refused: the destination is not under [remote] roots of the user config ... A push goes only under a remote root, where remote output is masked. Ask the operator to add the folder to [remote] roots (phiward setup does it). copy refused: the destination is not inside a protected path of the user config A copy may not leave the protected folders. Copy into a protected folder, or to a configured remote. run stopped: cancelled The client was interrupted (Ctrl-C); the broker stopped the command. None. run stopped: the broker stopped before the command finished The broker went away. The operator restarts it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• doctor says the sandbox does not confine the shell. The reason follows. The usual ones: a root is missing from denyRead or denyWrite (run (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write) again after a config change), excludedCommands is not empty, a unix socket is allowed, an allowRead entry re-opens a root, or patterns are configured. (Inside Claude Code, the hook also needs $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR; Claude Code sets it.) The hook then refuses shell commands other than gateway calls, doctor and check. With [shell] best_effort on, the hook checks shell command text instead, which is best effort (configuration.md). When excludedCommands is the only cause, the hook checks the text of every command in the same way, and refuses one that names protected data or a path it cannot see; the refusal names the file that holds the entry.
  • A folder with no PHI needs a sandbox opener (on macOS, allowLocalBinding for a dev server). The operator lists the exact folder in [no_phi] folders of the user config; there Bash gets the text check in place of the refusal, when the openers are the only cause (configuration.md). The session's start message and phiward doctor say whether the folder is relaxed, by the hook's own test; when it is not, they say why (a unix socket, a root missing from denyRead) and the step when there is one.
  • doctor says the broker uses another config. The broker and the agent tool were started with a different HOME, PHIWARD_CONFIG or XDG_* variable. Start both from the same environment.
  • doctor warns that the masking check failed, and launch refuses. A value of [sanitize] examples is not fully masked, or a made-up path below a root came out unmasked. The warning names the entry, the rule or the root by number. Fix the rule (often an edit that narrowed it), or the example if it is not in the rule's form; then restart the broker (configuration.md).
  • launch refuses: the project scan found <SUBJECT> in 3 files. A project file, or a file name, holds a subject or sample ID outside the protected roots. Run phiward doctor --show-paths in your own terminal: it lists the files (masked) and line numbers. Move the data under a protected root, or make a pseudonymized copy (phiward pseudonymize). For made-up IDs (test fixtures), add the files or their folder to [sanitize] scan_allow in your user config (launch.md).
  • A write place is skipped. doctor says why: it does not exist yet, or a link is on its path. Name the real folder in write_to.
  • A gateway command fails to write to /tmp. The gateway sees /tmp read-only. It writes temporary files to $TMPDIR, its private scratch folder.
  • git does not work in a repository. A protected root sits in that work tree, so its .git is protected. Move the data out of the repository.
  • Your endpoint tool stops or reports a phiward process. Send your IT or security team endpoint-security.md: it lists every process phiward starts on a Mac, with its command line and a regex for an exception.
  • Every shell command fails after an upgrade. An older phiward's shell prefix is still set: run (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write) again (doctor warns about it).

docs.title: For contributors: how phiward decides
docs.text:
• For: a contributor who changes phiward's own code.
  • Before: a checkout of the repository, python3 3.9 or newer, and uv for the tests.
  • You will have: a working setup that touches nothing of your own, and a picture of how a decision is made.

phiward keeps protected health information (PHI), and the credentials that would reach it, out of what an AI coding agent sends to its model provider. The rules for a change are in CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md. This page does not repeat them.

docs.title: The first half hour
docs.text:
Work beside your own setup, never in it. You may use phiward for real work, with a real config and a running broker. Three variables point a checkout away from them. The tests set the same ones (tests/conftest.py).

Open a new terminal in the checkout, and close it when you are done:

SCRATCH="$(cd "$(mktemp -d)" && pwd -P)"
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH/fakehome" "$SCRATCH/phi" "$SCRATCH/repo"
echo SECRET-CONTENT-0001 > "$SCRATCH/phi/FAKE-PT-0001.bam"
printf '[protected_paths]\nroots = ["%s/phi"]\n' "$SCRATCH" > "$SCRATCH/fakehome/phiward.toml"
export HOME="$SCRATCH/fakehome" PHIWARD_CONFIG="$SCRATCH/fakehome/phiward.toml"
export PHIWARD_SPOOL="$SCRATCH/spool" PYTHONPATH="$PWD/src"
python3 -m phiward doctor
  • HOME is a scratch home. PHIWARD_CONFIG names a made-up user config. PHIWARD_SPOOL names a scratch spool. doctor must name your scratch config, not your real one.
  • Never run setup, install, pin, carryover or broker --service against your real home. Never run the real claude in an experiment.
  • python3 -m phiward broker in this terminal is a scratch broker. A second terminal, with the same SCRATCH and the same exports, can then send it python3 -m phiward run -- CMD. Do not type a bare phiward here: that is your installed release, not the checkout. launch refuses a checkout unless PHIWARD_DEV=1 is set.

Run the tests in a normal terminal (they make their own scratch home). The command, and how to run a part of the suite, are in tests/README.md. For one file, add its path: tests/test_protected_paths.py.

Try a decision by hand. check shows the decision for a shell command. Nothing runs:

python3 -m phiward check --cwd "$SCRATCH/repo" -- cat "$SCRATCH/phi/FAKE-PT-0001.bam"

It prints deny: and the reason. The exit status is 0 for allow, 1 for ask and 2 for deny. check judges the command as if Claude Code's sandbox confined it.

The hook itself reads a payload on stdin. Feed it a made-up one:

printf '{"tool_name":"Read","tool_input":{"file_path":"%s/phi/FAKE-PT-0001.bam"},"cwd":"%s/repo","permission_mode":"default"}' \
  "$SCRATCH" "$SCRATCH" | python3 -m phiward hook claude; echo "exit=$?"
Reply Meaning exit 0, no output allow exit 0, a JSON object with "permissionDecision": "ask" on stdout ask: Claude Code shows a prompt exit 2, phiward [protected-paths]: ... on stderr deny, with the reason exit 2, phiward: the hook could not decide ... on stderr a fault: it is refused too

The payload above is denied. With "tool_name":"Write" and the path $SCRATCH/repo/.vscode/tasks.json you get the ask. A Bash payload is refused here: a hand-made payload has no $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, and no settings in the scratch home confine the shell.

docs.title: What the agent controls, and what phiward trusts
docs.text:
The agent controls (never trusted) Trusted (the operator's) the hook payload, its cwd included the user config, and pinned.toml next to it the project folder, and a repo .phiward.toml in it the other guard files (config.guard_files): the broker's status file, phiward's own install the temp folders the broker, and the environment it builds for a command every file in the spool the operating system's sandbox the words and the folder of a gateway request Claude Code's sandbox and permission rules (Mode A)

A repo .phiward.toml can only add protection. Everything that widens the gateway comes from the user config (configuration.md).

The invariants. Each one has a place in the code:

  • Fail closed. A guard that raises denies (core.dispatch). A hook fault exits 2 (adapters/claude.main). A config that cannot be used refuses what it guards.
  • The strictest answer wins: deny over ask over allow (core.strictest). An ask that the tool cannot show becomes a deny (core.settle).
  • A new check only adds refusals. It never changes what kind of action a tool is, and never turns a refusal into an ask (review-rounds.md).
  • What is checked is what starts. The gateway runs the entry of the user config's list, not a path the agent names (run.listed_run_path). pin records each listed program by its content. The broker refuses every request when the config or a listed program changed since it started (broker.config_print).
  • Nothing asks the operator at run time. Grants come from the user config only.
  • Made-up data only, in tests and in experiments (FAKE-PT-0001).

docs.title: One tool call
docs.text:
Claude Code runs phiward hook claude before each tool call (Mode A).

sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: One tool call through the hook
    accDescr: Claude Code sends a payload. The adapter makes an Action. decide judges the confinement. The guard returns a Decision. The adapter replies.
    participant CC as Claude Code
    participant H as claude.main
    participant T as claude.to_action
    participant D as adapters.decide
    participant G as protected_paths.check
    CC->>H: PreToolUse payload on stdin
    H->>T: the payload
    T-->>H: an Action
    H->>D: the Action
    Note over D: loads the config and judges the confinement of a shell call
    D->>G: core.dispatch: the Action and the config
    G-->>D: a Decision
    D-->>H: the strictest Decision
    H-->>CC: allow, ask or deny
    Note over CC: its sandbox enforces at run time, after the hook
  1. adapters/claude.to_action turns the payload into an Action (core.py): the kind (shell, file read, file search, file write, other), the folder, the command or the paths, and whether the session can show an ask. No policy lives here.
  2. adapters.decide loads the config for the action's folder. For a call of Claude Code's own shell tools, it checks that Claude Code's settings confine the shell. This is where the sandbox comes in: the hook does not run the sandbox. It records confined on the Action, or the reason why not.
  3. core.dispatch runs every guard and keeps the strictest decision. Today there is one guard, guards/protected_paths.check.
  4. check judges the action by its kind. Read the function for the order of its checks: the order changes, and each step says why it is where it is.
  5. claude.main writes the reply of the table above.

Under phiward launch (Mode B) the kernel decides. The hook there is a quick first layer (fasthook.py).

A prompt goes through another hook, before Claude Code sends it: phiward prompt-scan claude (promptscan.py). It builds the sanitizer from the user config's packs and patterns, without the detail rules, positions, names and entries (Sanitizer.from_config(identifiers_only=True)), and refuses the prompt when the sanitizer would change a line of it, or the absolute form of a path-like word in it. hook claude and fasthook refuse any event but PreToolUse.

docs.title: One gateway request
docs.text:
phiward run -- CMD is a client only. The broker runs the command, outside the agent.

flowchart TD
    accTitle: One gateway request
    accDescr: The client leaves a request in the spool. The broker claims it, checks it, runs the command in a kernel profile, masks the output and writes the reply.
    A["phiward run -- CMD<br/>the client, in the agent's sandbox"] --> B["req-ID.json in the spool"]
    B --> C["The broker claims it<br/>renames it to job-ID.json"]
    C --> D{"Config unchanged,<br/>listed programs approved?"}
    D -- "yes" --> E["run.execute<br/>config, grants, [broker] commands"]
    D -- "no" --> R["A refusal message"]
    E -- "not granted, not listed" --> R
    E --> F["CMD in the kernel profile<br/>confine.gateway_command"]
    F --> G["The sanitizer masks each line"]
    G --> H["out-ID.log, then done-ID.json"]
    R --> H
    H --> I["The client prints the output"]
  • The request holds the words and the folder, and no environment. The broker builds the command's environment from a short list of its own variables (broker.command_env).
  • The broker treats every file in the spool as untrusted data (the top of broker.py says how).
  • run.execute loads the user config plus the repo config of the request's folder. It checks the grants (--write-to, --net) and [broker] commands.
  • run.run_confined starts the command in the profile that confine.py builds. The command reads the protected roots. It writes only its scratch folder and the granted folders. It has no network unless granted.
  • Every line goes through sanitize.Sanitizer. Masking hides names and identifiers, not other content. With --table, sanitize.Columns reads the lines by column (fresh for each call).
  • The agent sees exit=0 or exit=1 only, and a note that counts the placeholders in the lines shown (run_confined). The real exit status and the counts go to the broker's log.
  • phiward copy and phiward run --remote take the same road (copying.execute, run._execute_remote).

docs.title: Change this, change that too
docs.text: You change Change these too a guard's rule its red test first; threat-model.md; the help text and the refusal message a config key config.py SCHEMA and the tighten-only rule; configuration.md (both tables); setup_cmd.py when setup should write it a hidden path hidden.py only: the hook, install, launch and the gateway read it. The list in modes.md. install then writes new rules, and the hook refuses the shell until they are in place: say in the changelog that users wire again a tool name (a new Claude Code tool) the tool sets at the top of adapters/claude.py, and to_action a message the user sees the table in daily-use.md; tests/test_v2_refusal_words.py a help text USAGE in cli.py and the module's own HELP a new test file the index in tests/README.md (a test checks it)

  • The module map: architecture.md.

  • Ideas that were turned down already: decisions.md.

docs.title: For IT and security teams: what phiward runs on a Mac
docs.text:
• For: the people who run an endpoint tool on Macs where phiward is used.
  • You will have: every process phiward starts, with its exact command line and a regex for it, so that you can recognise each one and, if your policy needs it, scope one exception.

docs.title: What phiward is
docs.text:
phiward keeps protected health information (PHI) out of what an AI coding agent sends to its model provider. It runs the agent's commands in a kernel profile (sandbox-exec) and masks the output. It is a Python package that runs as the user.

It needs no admin rights, no kernel extension and no network service. The agent and the broker talk through files in a private folder. phiward's one listening port is the proxy of a phiward launch session, on loopback only, while that session runs (Network).

docs.title: What it installs and writes
docs.text:
All of it is in the user's home folder, written by the user's own account:

  • The package, installed by uv tool or pipx, with its own Python: for example ~/.local/share/uv/tools/phiward/ (uv) or ~/.local/pipx/venvs/phiward/ (pipx). Below it, lib/python3.X/site-packages/phiward/ holds phiward's code and its two hook files (data/clean-exec.sh, data/clean-env.awk).
  • The launcher ~/.local/bin/phiward: a Python script that uv or pipx writes.
  • phiward's own state in ~/.phiward/: the sessions of phiward launch, the kernel profiles of running commands (profiles/, one file per command, removed when it ends), records of running launchers, the broker's status and backups.
  • The spool ~/.phiward-spool/: requests from the agent to the broker, and their output.
  • Scratch folders in ~/.cache/phiward/: one per gateway command, removed when it ends.
  • The user config ~/.config/phiward/config.toml, and ~/.config/phiward/claude-settings.json.
  • Claude Code's settings ~/.claude/settings.json: the hook entries and the sandbox settings.
  • The login service ~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.phiward.broker.plist, if the user sets it up, and its log ~/Library/Logs/phiward/broker.log.
  • In a repository, on request: .claude/settings.json (install --project) and the git hooks .git/hooks/pre-commit and pre-push (phiward init).
  • The Claude Code plugin, if the user installs it: Claude Code copies it into its own plugin folder (~/.claude/plugins/...).

docs.title: Every process phiward starts on macOS
docs.text:
Each row is one kind of process. The ID points to its command lines and its regex in the list below. phiward puts no code in a local command line: no python -c, no sh -c of its own, no awk program, no sandbox-exec -p. There are two exceptions:

  • the command that ssh carries to the remote host (C3, C7, C8), which runs there, not on the Mac. A push's (C7) is a fixed sh -c script with the destination path;
  • the project hook's fixed line (R1, R2), which a repository commits.
ID Parent Image How often What it does G1 the broker /usr/bin/sandbox-exec each phiward run request runs the agent's command in the gateway's profile G2 phiward doctor /usr/bin/sandbox-exec each doctor the gateway's self-test: /usr/bin/true in the profile C1 the broker /usr/bin/sandbox-exec each local phiward copy makes the destination folder (/bin/mkdir) C2 the broker /usr/bin/sandbox-exec each local phiward copy copies the files (/usr/bin/rsync) C3 the broker /usr/bin/sandbox-exec each copy from a remote host runs /usr/bin/ssh through the user's shared connection; the remote host runs tar -c C7 the broker /usr/bin/sandbox-exec each copy to a remote host runs /usr/bin/ssh through the shared connection; the remote host runs a fixed script that makes the folder and unpacks with tar -x C8 the broker /usr/bin/sandbox-exec each copy from a remote host, with [remote] use_shared_connection = false as C3, but ssh logs in itself C4 the broker /usr/bin/sandbox-exec each copy from a remote host unpacks what ssh receives, with a file in the package C5 the broker /usr/bin/ssh each request to a remote host reads the ssh config (no network) C6 the broker /usr/bin/ssh each request to a remote host checks that the shared connection is up H1 Claude Code /bin/sh each tool call, prompt and session start the hook's script: clears the Python and loader variables, then runs phiward H2 the H1 script /usr/bin/awk with each H1 lists the variables to clear, from a file in the package H3 the H1 script (exec) the Python with each H1 the hook itself: decides the tool call, checks the prompt, or writes the session note P1 Claude Code /bin/sh each tool call, prompt and session start, with the plugin the plugin's copy of the H1 script P2 the P1 script /usr/bin/awk with each P1 the plugin's copy of H2 P3 the P1 script or the R1 line (exec) the Python with each P1 or R1 the hook, through the launcher P4 Claude Code the Python once per session, with the plugin phiward's MCP server (the gateway's tools) L1 phiward launch /usr/bin/sandbox-exec once per launched session or wrapped MCP server runs the agent tool, or the server, in the tool's profile L2 phiward launch /usr/bin/getconf each launch asks for the per-user temp folder L3 Claude Code, under launch the Python each tool call and prompt the hook in a launched session L4 launch, a wrapped server, doctor, the session note the Python each start phiward checks its own installed files, in a separate Python L5 launch --tool claude, install, doctor Claude Code each start asks Claude Code its version (--version, from /) M1 Claude Code the Python once per session, per wrapped MCP server starts a wrapped MCP server under phiward launch M2 phiward launch (exec) the server's inside a launched session a wrapped server inside a session: its own command line, unchanged S1 launchd the Python at login, kept running the broker S2 phiward setup, phiward broker --service --write /bin/launchctl when the user sets up the login service loads or restarts the broker's service D1 phiward install the Python each install --write checks that the isolated Python finds phiward D2 phiward doctor /bin/sh each doctor runs the H1 script once, with phiward --help D3 the D2 script (exec) the Python with each D2 phiward --help, through the launcher R1 Claude Code /bin/sh each tool call, prompt and session start, in a repository with install --project the project hook: one fixed line R2 the R1 line /usr/bin/awk with each R1 lists the variables to clear (its program is in the fixed line) R3 git /bin/sh each commit and push, in a repository with phiward init the git hooks phiward writes R4 the R3 hook (exec) the Python with each R3 phiward's git checks R5 R4 git from PATH with each R4 the git commands of those checks

"The Python" is phiward's own Python: the bin/python of its uv or pipx environment, which points to the Python that uv or the system installed. "The launcher" is ~/.local/bin/phiward, a Python script; the kernel shows it as <python> <launcher>.

The user also starts phiward in a terminal (phiward launch -- claude, phiward doctor, phiward setup). Those command lines are the user's own words after <python> <launcher>.

Rarer forms, not in the list: a local copy without rsync runs /bin/cp -R -n -- SOURCE... DEST; a dry run runs /usr/bin/true; a git hook without phiward on PATH runs python3 -m phiward git-hook NAME; phiward run --remote runs /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f <profile> /usr/bin/ssh ... HOST -- WORDS (the C3 or C8 ssh words), where WORDS are the agent's own, quoted for the remote shell.

G1 and L1 match any command under any file in ~/.phiward/profiles. The account that runs phiward can write that folder, so a process of that account could start sandbox-exec there with a profile of its own, (allow default) included. An exception for G1 or L1 trusts every process of that account to that extent.

docs.title: The command lines
docs.text:
Each entry gives the command line as the kernel shows it (argv), and a regex for it (regex; - where none fits). The regexes are written for an install by uv or pipx. The placeholders:

  • <python>: phiward's Python, such as ~/.local/share/uv/tools/phiward/bin/python;
  • <PKG>: its site-packages folder; <plugin>: the plugin's folder;
  • <launcher>: ~/.local/bin/phiward;
  • <profile>: ~/.phiward/profiles/ and a random name of 32 hex digits, then .sb;
  • <home>: the home folder; <uid>: the user's id; <entry>: 16 hex digits;
  • <path>, <source>, <dest>: paths the request names;
  • <ssh-config>, <socket>, <host>: the user's ssh config file, the shared connection's socket and the host;
  • <remote-pull>: the command for the remote host on a pull, tar -c -f - -C DIR -- NAME (or -C DIR .); <remote-push>: on a push, sh -c SCRIPT sh DIR, where SCRIPT is the fixed text _RECEIVE in remote.py;
  • <record>: the package's install record; <claude>: Claude Code's program;
  • <command> ..., <tool> ..., <server> ..., <arguments>: the user's or the agent's own words;
  • <project-hook>, <project-prompt-hook>, <project-note>: the project hook's fixed text (PROJECT_HOOK, PROJECT_PROMPT_HOOK and PROJECT_NOTE in install.py), which begins command -v phiward >/dev/null 2>&1 ||; <awk-program>: the awk program in it, which begins BEGIN{for(k in ENVIRON).

A path with a space in it shows as more than one word, so [^ ]+ does not match it. Use .+ there if your users have such paths.

G1 argv  /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f <profile> <command> ...
G1 regex ^/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f [^ ]+/\.phiward/profiles/[0-9a-f]{32}\.sb /?[^ ]+
G2 argv  /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f <profile> /usr/bin/true
G2 regex ^/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f [^ ]+/\.phiward/profiles/[0-9a-f]{32}\.sb /usr/bin/true$
C1 argv  /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f <profile> /bin/mkdir -p -- <path>
C1 regex ^/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f [^ ]+/\.phiward/profiles/[0-9a-f]{32}\.sb /bin/mkdir -p -- /
C2 argv  /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f <profile> /usr/bin/rsync -rt --ignore-existing --exclude=.claude/ -- <source> ... <dest>
C2 regex ^/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f [^ ]+/\.phiward/profiles/[0-9a-f]{32}\.sb /usr/bin/rsync -rt --ignore-existing --exclude=\.claude/ -- [^ ]
C3 argv  /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f <profile> /usr/bin/ssh -F <ssh-config> -o BatchMode=yes -o ProxyCommand=none -o ProxyJump=none -o PermitLocalCommand=no -o ClearAllForwardings=yes -o ForwardAgent=no -o ForwardX11=no -o ForwardX11Trusted=no -o RequestTTY=no -T -o ControlMaster=no -S <socket> <host> -- <remote-pull>
C3 regex -
C7 argv  /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f <profile> /usr/bin/ssh -F <ssh-config> -o BatchMode=yes -o ProxyCommand=none -o ProxyJump=none -o PermitLocalCommand=no -o ClearAllForwardings=yes -o ForwardAgent=no -o ForwardX11=no -o ForwardX11Trusted=no -o RequestTTY=no -T -o ControlMaster=no -S <socket> <host> -- <remote-push>
C7 regex -
C8 argv  /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f <profile> /usr/bin/ssh -F <ssh-config> -o BatchMode=yes -o ProxyCommand=none -o ProxyJump=none -o PermitLocalCommand=no -o ClearAllForwardings=yes -o ForwardAgent=no -o ForwardX11=no -o ForwardX11Trusted=no -o RequestTTY=no -T <host> -- <remote-pull>
C8 regex -
C4 argv  /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f <profile> <python> -I <PKG>/phiward/tar_extract.py <path>
C4 regex ^/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f [^ ]+/\.phiward/profiles/[0-9a-f]{32}\.sb [^ ]+/bin/python[0-9.]* -I [^ ]+/site-packages/phiward/tar_extract\.py /
C5 argv  /usr/bin/ssh -G -F <ssh-config> -- <host>
C5 regex ^/usr/bin/ssh -G -F [^ ]+ -- [^ ]+$
C6 argv  /usr/bin/ssh -F <ssh-config> -S <socket> -O check -- <host>

H1 argv  /bin/sh <PKG>/phiward/data/clean-exec.sh <python> -I -m phiward hook claude
H1 argv  /bin/sh <PKG>/phiward/data/clean-exec.sh <python> -I -m phiward prompt-scan claude

H2 argv  /usr/bin/awk -f <PKG>/phiward/data/clean-env.awk

H3 argv  <python> -I -m phiward hook claude
H3 argv  <python> -I -m phiward prompt-scan claude

H3 regex ^[^ ]+/bin/python[0-9.]* -I -m phiward (hook|prompt-scan|session-note) claude$

P1 argv  /bin/sh <plugin>/hooks/clean-exec.sh phiward prompt-scan claude
P1 argv  /bin/sh <plugin>/hooks/clean-exec.sh phiward session-note claude
P1 regex ^/bin/sh [^ ]+/hooks/clean-exec\.sh phiward (hook|prompt-scan|session-note) claude$
P2 argv  /usr/bin/awk -f <plugin>/hooks/clean-env.awk
P2 regex ^/usr/bin/awk -f [^ ]+/hooks/clean-env\.awk$
P3 argv  <python> <launcher> hook claude
P3 argv  <python> <launcher> prompt-scan claude
P3 argv  <python> <launcher> session-note claude

A test records every process phiward starts on macOS and checks that this list holds the same command lines, both ways (tests/test_macos_processes.py).

docs.title: Network: the launch proxy
docs.text:
Under phiward launch, the agent tool has no direct outbound IP connection. Its HTTPS goes through a proxy that runs in the launcher's own process (phiward launch, the Python): it starts no process of its own, and it ends with the session.

What Where When What it does A listening port 127.0.0.1 and [::1], one random port held on both, TCP while a launched session runs takes the tool's CONNECT requests (a tunnel to any port); each needs the session's token Outgoing connections the addresses a name resolves to, public ranges only each CONNECT of the tool connects the tool to the host it asked for, from the launcher's process; a range in [launch] private_networks may be reached too Outgoing connections to a proxy the proxy HTTPS_PROXY names in the user's terminal each CONNECT to a public address, when that is set asks that proxy for the checked address, never the name; an address in [launch] private_networks is connected to directly Name lookups the system's resolver each CONNECT with a host name one lookup in the launcher, before any connection A read of the machine's addresses libc's getifaddrs, called in the launcher's process (Python ctypes) each CONNECT lists this machine's own addresses, which the proxy refuses; no process is started and no file is written

The proxy refuses this machine, the local link and the private ranges. On macOS, the tool's profile allows it only the proxy's port on loopback. On Linux, the session has a network namespace of its own, and a relay inside it hands each connection to the launcher. On macOS a server the session starts can still listen on any address (see the threat model).

docs.title: Who signed what
docs.text: sandbox-exec, sh, awk, ssh, mkdir, rsync, getconf and launchctl are Apple's platform binaries. The Python is the one the user installed, signed by whoever built it (the python.org installer's is signed with its Developer ID). git is Apple's, or the one the user installed (Homebrew, for example). phiward itself is not signed code: it is Python source that the Python reads.

docs.title: What the agent runs is not phiward's
docs.text: The agent chooses the commands it runs through the gateway (G1) and inside a launched session (L1). Their command lines are the agent's own, and they may use any shape: an agent may run python -c or sh -c there. Their parent is sandbox-exec, and they run inside phiward's profile. A wrapped MCP server (M1, M2) has the command line its user configured; many servers are started as sh -c "..." or npx ....

docs.title: What to put in an exception
docs.text:
If your policy needs an exception, scope it narrowly:

  • by the image path and the regex of the row you see;
  • to the users who run phiward;
  • not for all of Python, and not for every program in phiward's Python folder.

The rows that phiward starts most often are H1 to H3 (each tool call in a Claude Code session), L3 (each tool call under launch) and G1 (each gateway request).

docs.title: How to check a Mac
docs.text: phiward doctor, in the user's terminal, checks the install, the hook wiring, the broker and the gateway's profile, and says what is missing. It starts G2, D2, L4 and L5.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• sandbox-exec is deprecated by Apple, with no date and no named replacement.
  • The commands the agent runs (G1, L1) have their own shapes, and your tool may judge what they do. phiward cannot change that.
  • The project hook (R1, R2) is one fixed line with code in it. A repository commits it, and the same line runs on Linux. A push's remote command (C7) is fixed code too, carried to the remote host.
  • C3, C7 and C8 have no regex either. phiward's fixed ssh options do not fit in 256 characters, and a regex that loops over options would admit one that weakens them (ssh takes the first value it sees). Match these rows on the image path /usr/bin/ssh with its parent /usr/bin/sandbox-exec, and on the fixed options exactly, in the order the shape gives them; the profile file, the ssh config, the socket, the host and the paths vary.
  • R1, R2 and C7 have no regex. Their full text is longer than 256 characters, and a regex for its first part would also admit that text with any command after it. If you need an exception for them, match the exact command line instead: R1 and R2 are the same on every Mac (a hash of the command line works), and C7 is the fixed text with the user's paths (receive_script in remote.py builds it).
  • This page lists macOS only.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text: On Linux phiward confines with bubblewrap (bwrap), Landlock and seccomp instead of sandbox-exec. Its processes have the same parents and the same jobs, with other command lines: bwrap in place of sandbox-exec, a small Python helper with inline code inside the bwrap profile, and systemctl --user for the login service. Those command lines are not listed here.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The words that phiward's pages use, in alphabetical order.

  • Broker: the program that runs gateway requests outside the agent, as you, and masks what comes back. You start it (best as a login service: phiward broker --service --write). The agent cannot start or change it.
  • Carry-over, trusted copy, quarantine (Mode B only): each phiward launch session starts from a trusted copy of the agent tool's settings, skills and MCP servers, which you fill with phiward carryover add. What a session changes there goes to quarantine. Nothing from quarantine is used until you accept it (phiward carryover accept).
  • Config: phiward's own settings, a TOML file (~/.config/phiward/config.toml, written by phiward setup): your protected roots, grants and the like. Not Claude Code's settings; those are the wiring. See configuration.md.
  • Confined: a shell, or a program, whose reads the kernel limits (Claude Code's sandbox, or phiward's kernel profile). The hook refuses every command of a shell that is not confined but a whole gateway call.
  • Derived protected folders: folders that phiward protects without being in your config: its own cache folder, and the .git of a repository that holds a protected root.
  • Gateway: phiward run, phiward copy and phiward run --remote. The only way the agent works on protected data. The broker runs each request and masks the output.
  • Gateway call, whole command: a phiward run -- CMD or phiward copy written as the entire command, with fixed words: no cd X && before it, no | head or > file after it, no $(...) or variable. Only that form runs where the shell is not confined.
  • Grant: a capability you give the gateway in your own config. write_to lets a gateway command write in a folder; net lets it use the network. The default is none. Nothing asks you at run time: what the config does not grant is refused.
  • Hidden list: credentials, Kerberos ticket caches and keytabs, SSH keys, shell histories, other logins and the like, which no agent may read, in addition to your protected roots.
  • Hook: a command that Claude Code runs before each tool call (phiward's guard) or when a session starts (phiward's note on the rules).
  • Kernel profile: a set of rules that the operating system enforces on a program and every program it starts (on macOS Seatbelt; on Linux bubblewrap, seccomp and Landlock). The program cannot switch them off. Mode B runs the whole agent tool in one.
  • Masking: the gateway replaces protected paths, file names and identifiers in output with placeholders such as <PROTECTED>. It does not hide other content, so print counts and summaries, not records. The part of phiward that masks is the sanitizer.
  • MCP server: a program that gives an agent tool more tools (Model Context Protocol). phiward has one, phiward mcp, whose tools are the gateway.
  • MCP server: wrapped, not wrapped, remote: a wrapped server runs under phiward launch --, in the kernel profile, so it cannot read protected data. A not wrapped one (shown as "not wrapped (runs with your rights)") can read what you can; its tools that run commands may make only gateway calls. A remote one runs on another machine and nothing here. phiward mcp list says which each of yours is. See modes.md.
  • Mode A: a normal Claude Code session (the desktop app, an IDE or a terminal), wired by phiward install claude. Claude Code's own sandbox and permission rules, plus phiward's hook, keep protected data out. See modes.md.
  • Mode B: the whole agent tool run under phiward launch, in phiward's kernel profile. Terminal only. See launch.md.
  • Operator: you, the person who installs phiward and owns the config. The agent's rules use this word.
  • Pack: a built-in or own list of identifier patterns to mask (for example genomics).
  • Plugin: a bundle of hooks, skills, commands and MCP servers that Claude Code installs in one step. See plugins.md.
  • Protected root: a folder whose contents the agent may not read. You list them in your config.
  • Remote Control: a Claude Code feature that lets you drive a session that runs in a terminal from the desktop app, the web or a phone.
  • Scope, source (MCP servers): where a server's definition lives. Your own user scope (~/.claude.json), this project's local entry in it, the repository's project file (.mcp.json), or a plugin. Claude Code tells the hook each tool's source (2.1.274 and newer); an older one does not, and then a .mcp.json server counts as not wrapped.
  • Shared SSH connection: one SSH connection to a cluster that you open yourself (ssh -fN hpc). phiward's HPC requests join it through its control socket, so they need no key or ticket of their own. See hpc.md.
  • Skill: written guidance that an agent loads when it needs it. phiward's skill tells the agent how to work through the gateway.
  • Spool: the folder where the agent leaves requests for the broker (~/.phiward-spool).
  • Wiring: what phiward install claude writes into Claude Code's settings: the hooks, the sandbox rules and the permission rules. User wiring (--user) covers every session in every folder; project wiring covers one project.

docs.title: HPC: Kerberos, mounts, copy and run --remote
docs.text:
• For: people whose agent runs on their own computer (a Mac in the examples), in a Claude Code session (Mode A) or under phiward launch (Mode B), and who reach an HPC cluster with a Kerberos ticket and a shared SSH connection (kinit, then ssh -fN).
  • You will have: the agent working with HPC through the gateway, with masked output.

Use one host name everywhere: the Host in your ~/.ssh/config, the Host in phiward's ssh config, [remote] hosts, and the host part of [copy] remotes. ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%C matches only when HostName, User and Port are the same in both ssh configs.

The rule: the agent may work with HPC, but protected data reaches the model only masked. Hence two paths:

Path Who holds your ticket and SSH connection What comes back to the model The agent's own shell (ssh cluster cat …) nobody: it fails, because the sandbox (Mode A: Claude Code's; Mode B: phiward's) hides your keys, config and connection socket. With phiward's hook alone and no sandbox it would not fail. nothing The gateway (phiward copy, phiward run --remote) your broker, outside the sandbox masked output

How a remote run goes:

sequenceDiagram
  participant A as The agent (sandboxed)
  participant B as Your broker (your computer)
  participant S as Your shared SSH connection
  participant C as The cluster
  A->>B: phiward run --remote hpc -- squeue -u you
  B->>S: the listed program, through your connection
  S->>C: runs as you
  Note over C: Nothing confines the command on the cluster: keep to counts
  C-->>B: output
  B-->>A: output, with protected paths masked (not bare names)

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
The easy way: phiward setup, answer yes to the HPC question, and give the cluster's short name, login host, your user name and your work folder. It writes phiward's ssh config and the [copy] and [remote] settings, and prints the lines for your ~/.ssh/config. Then do step 4 below. The steps by hand, which do the same:

Use one host name everywhere below (here hpc).

  1. In ~/.ssh/config, add these lines to your existing entry for host hpc (keep its HostName, User and GSSAPIAuthentication lines):
  ControlMaster auto
  ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%C
  ControlPersist 8h
  1. Write phiward's own ssh config, ~/.config/phiward/ssh_config, with the same Host, HostName, User and ControlPath, and ControlMaster no:
Host hpc
  HostName <login host>
  User <you>
  ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%C
  ControlMaster no

%C stands for the host, user and port, so they must be the same in both files. 3. Edit ~/.config/phiward/config.toml. - In the [copy] section, add ssh_config = "~/.config/phiward/ssh_config", and make sure remotes holds your HPC work folder. setup may have made this section already: do not add a second [copy] section; a second one makes the file invalid. - Add a [remote] section at the end:

[remote]
hosts = ["hpc"]
commands = ["squeue", "sacct", "sinfo"]
roots = ["/data/protected"]

Then run phiward doctor: a mistake in the file shows as a PROBLEM. If the broker runs already, restart it: it refuses requests after the config changes, until you do (setup.md). 4. Before each session that uses HPC, in Terminal:

kinit you@REALM

ssh -fN hpc
  1. Test it:
phiward run --remote hpc -- squeue -u you

The sections below explain what each part does and allows.

docs.title: What the session can never use
docs.text:
• your Kerberos ticket caches that are files: the file KRB5CCNAME names, krb5cc* files in /tmp, /var/tmp and the macOS per-user temp folder, and /run/user/<uid> on Linux. A cache kept by the macOS credential service (API:, the default when KRB5CCNAME is not set) or by the Linux keyring or KCM is not a file; Mode B blocks the Linux keyring, and doctor warns when your cache is not a file (modes.md);
  • ~/.ssh (keys, config, known hosts), the SSH agent, and the socket of your shared connection (outside unix sockets are refused).

docs.title: Mounted HPC storage
docs.text: Put the mount path of protected HPC folders in your protected roots (for example the folder where the cluster's protected storage is mounted on your Mac), with phiward setup or in the user config. On Linux, phiward also protects other mounts of the same data that it can see (alias mounts). On macOS it does not detect them: list every mount path of the data as a root. phiward run -- CMD on that data runs through the broker, with masked output.

docs.title: Your shared connection holds the login
docs.text:
Every request to HPC (a copy to or from a remote, run --remote) goes through your shared SSH connection. You start it; phiward's ssh joins it through its control socket, which needs no key and no ticket. So: - no request can read ~/.ssh (keys, config, known hosts), a ticket cache or a keytab; - a request has no network except that one socket, and only the system ssh, with options phiward fixes (no forwarding of any kind), ever talks to it; - if the connection is not running, the request is refused with a message. phiward never logs in by itself.

The socket carries your full login: a program that could speak ssh's protocol on it could ask your connection for forwarding or new channels. That is why nothing but the system ssh touches it (rsync does not), and why phiward trusts a socket only when it is yours, is not a link, and lies under ~/.ssh (or /run/user/<uid>) in folders that only you can write: a socket the agent made first somewhere else is refused. On Linux a request also gets fresh, empty /tmp, /var/tmp and home folders, so the sockets there are out of reach; a socket in another folder you can write (for example /scratch) that was renamed after it was made is not, but only ssh runs there. Files your ssh config Includes from your home are not visible to it on Linux.

Keep phiward's ssh config outside ~/.ssh. Its ControlPath must be under ~/.ssh (setup step 2).

[remote] use_shared_connection = false turns this off: ssh then logs in itself, so a request can read your key or ticket and has the network. The agent still cannot choose ssh's options or the paths, but a bug in ssh or rsync that the other end exploits could then reach a credential.

docs.title: phiward copy
docs.text:
phiward copy SRC... DST copies without printing names. The destination must be inside one of your protected roots (by its real path, with no link on the way, and not a pattern match or a .claude folder), or under a remote you approved in the user config. A .claude folder is never copied:

[copy]
remotes = ["hpc:/work/yourname/project"]
ssh_config = "~/.config/phiward/ssh_config"
push_limit_gib = 5        # a larger push is yours to do (default 5)

A remote must name a work folder on the cluster: not /, not a folder just below it (/home, /data), not a home folder (a folder named home, home1, homes or users, or one just inside it, wherever it is: /home/you, /gpfs/home/you), and not inside a dot-folder (.ssh, .config). setup refuses these, and copy ignores such a remote. A copy never goes into a dot-folder either. A push to your home folder could otherwise plant your login files there; if your cluster names home folders another way, name a work folder yourself.

Copies may go: - from an unprotected folder (the project) to an approved remote, under a [remote] roots folder; - from a protected folder to a protected folder or to an approved remote, under a [remote] roots folder; - from an approved remote to a protected folder.

Give local paths in full: a local path with a .. part, or one that starts with a quoted ~, is refused. A push goes only under a [remote] roots folder, where remote output is masked; with no remote root, every push is refused (setup makes each new copy remote's folder one). Locally, what lands is inside a protected root. On the cluster it is masked only under [remote] roots, and a link there can carry a push outside one.

A push (local sources to a remote) does not use rsync. A source may be any file or folder that is not a credential, not above one, and not in /dev, /proc or /sys. Your broker checks each source, resolves it once, opens it without following links, and sends what it reads as a tar stream to tar -x in the remote folder (made if missing). So: - a link put on a source path after the check makes the push stop; nothing behind it is sent; - links, special files and files with a second name (hard links) inside a source are skipped and counted, never followed; - files that a shell, ssh or a tool reads at login or when you enter a folder are skipped and counted, at any depth: .ssh, .bashrc, .profile, .zshrc, .gitconfig, .envrc, .config, .local, .ipython, .Rprofile and similar; and every name that starts with . at the top of the destination. Copy them yourself if you need them there; - the remote side cannot ask for anything: the stream goes one way; - src lands as DEST/src, src/ and src/. land as its contents; the destination is a folder; - every push sends everything named (no resume), but files that exist on the cluster are kept, never replaced, and pushed files arrive without the executable bit (0644; folders 0755): an agent cannot replace a job script you run later. To update a file there, delete it yourself first, or chmod +x a script you pushed; - over push_limit_gib, the push is refused: copy it yourself.

The result is counts (copy sent: files=N folders=N skipped=N) and whatever the remote side prints, masked like run --remote output (your [remote] roots included).

A pull (remote sources to a protected folder) does not use rsync either: tar -c on the remote streams through the shared connection into phiward's own extractor, a file in the installed package (phiward/tar_extract.py, run by path with phiward's Python), in the gateway profile. It writes only inside protected roots, reads no credential and has no network at all. Every pull sends everything named (no resume); files that exist in the protected folder are kept, never replaced. What the remote sends lands inside the protected folder: plain files and folders only; links and special files are skipped. A file or folder that cannot be made or written in full there (no permission, no space) fails the pull. A partly written file is removed, and the rest is still written. A stream that ends early (a dropped connection, a killed remote tar) stops the pull and fails it: the file being written is removed, and the files that arrived whole before it stay.

A remote path may hold only letters, digits and . _ + - /, so it is one plain word for the remote shell. An argument with a : before its first / is remote, as rsync reads it: write a local name with a : as ./name. A source that is or holds a credential (~/.ssh, your home) is refused. A copy between two remotes is refused.

docs.title: phiward run --remote HOST -- CMD
docs.text:
Your broker runs CMD on the host through your shared connection, and masks what comes back.

[remote]
hosts = ["cluster"]                     # hosts the agent may name
commands = ["squeue", "sacct", "sinfo", "wc", "du"]   # programs it may run there; empty = none
roots = ["/data/protected"]                # protected paths on the host, masked in the output

phiward run --remote cluster -- squeue -u yourname
  • Only hosts in [remote] hosts and programs in [remote] commands are allowed. These keys come from your user config only; a repo config cannot set them. The program is one bare name. Every word reaches the remote shell quoted, so ;, $() and the like are plain text there. A word with !, a newline or another control character is refused: a csh or tcsh login shell expands ! even inside quotes.
  • Nothing confines the command on the cluster. It runs as you. The list of commands is what limits its effects there. Each program you add is a decision: sbatch submits a job that can run anything, and cat or head print contents, which masking does not hide beyond names and identifiers.
  • The output is masked like local gateway output: your protected roots, the names under them, identifier patterns, names files and packs, plus every path under [remote] roots, in its absolute spellings (//, /./). A word with a .. part is refused. After a remote root, the rest of the path up to a tab or the end of the line is masked, since a name may hold spaces: put counts before paths (wc, du do). Not covered: a path relative to the remote folder (../share/P1), a remote link to a protected folder, and bare names (below).
  • Bare names are not masked. phiward cannot list what is under a remote root, so a name printed without its path (ls /data/protected, find -printf %f) passes unless a pack, a pattern or a names file catches it. Do not list commands such as ls or find in [remote] commands for protected folders.
  • It uses the system ssh with -F your [copy] ssh_config, through the shared connection's socket, with BatchMode=yes, no proxy or local command, no forwarding, no terminal.
  • Tested against a real cluster from macOS: remote runs, a push, a pull into a protected folder, a refused push of ~/.ssh, the session's own ssh failing, and a refusal with the shared connection stopped.

docs.title: Claude Code on the login node
docs.text:
You can also run Claude Code on the HPC login node itself, as one user without admin rights. Its sandbox then confines the shell there (Mode A), with phiward's hook. The gateway works there only on a kernel with Landlock (see below). Check first that your site allows interactive tools on its login nodes.

What the node needs:

  • Landlock ABI 2 or newer in the kernel (Linux 5.19 or newer) for the gateway: phiward run refuses to run without it. A RHEL 8 node (kernel 4.18) has no Landlock: there the hook and Claude Code's sandbox work, and the gateway does not. phiward doctor says which.
  • bubblewrap 0.4 or newer with user namespaces (RHEL 8 has 0.4.0). phiward doctor checks the version.
  • socat on the PATH. Without admin rights, make a conda environment for it in your own space, for example mamba create -p /scratch/$USER/claude-env -c conda-forge socat, and put its bin folder first on the PATH before you start Claude Code. (sandbox.socatPath would name it too, but Claude Code reads it only from managed settings.) For the release check below, the folder must pass phiward's rule for a PATH folder (no other account can write it or a folder above it), so build socat below your home folder instead, for example in ~/phiward-sbx/tools/bin.
  • Claude Code 2.1.295 or newer, as everywhere. It tells the hook which MCP server each tool belongs to. bash tools/check-claude-mcp-source.sh (from a phiward checkout) shows what yours sends.

Then, in your own terminal on the node:

  1. (cd ~ && phiward setup): protect the data folders as roots. On Linux, protected patterns make the hook refuse shell commands, so use roots.
  2. (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write). It writes the hooks and sandbox entries into ~/.claude/settings.json, and the file for claude --settings.
  3. Start Claude Code with that file, for example with an alias in your own shell startup file: alias claude='claude --settings ~/.config/phiward/claude-settings.json'. With it, the sandbox is admin-required without admin rights: a repository's settings cannot turn it off, exclude commands or add writable folders.
  4. Start the broker in a terminal of its own on the node, and run phiward doctor.

A probe of Claude Code's sandbox engine (@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime 0.0.81) on a RHEL 8 login node (kernel 4.18, bubblewrap 0.4.0) passed all 21 tests:

  • a made-up root under /scratch was hidden by its real path, through a home folder link (~/work -> ...) and by a wildcard;
  • the project and the temporary folder stayed writable;
  • the settings files, .mcp.json, .bashrc and the folders next to the project could not be written;
  • the direct network was blocked.

A home folder on NFS was not part of that probe. The release check with the real Claude Code (scripts/sandbox-check/check.sh, releasing.md) runs on Linux too; it has not been run on the cluster yet. To run it there, as an interactive job:

  1. Make a folder for it below your home folder, ~/phiward-sbx/run (SBX_BASE), and one for socat, ~/phiward-sbx/tools/bin (SBX_TOOLS), with socat built into it and nothing else. Run chmod go-w ~, and chmod go-w on both folders, the folders between, and socat (and what it links to): the check refuses a tools folder or a socat another account could write.
  2. Get the token first: claude setup-token, with your ~/.claude where it is. Keep the token for step 4.
  3. Move away any CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, AGENTS.md, .claude, .git, .mcp.json, .phiward.toml or .agent-guards.toml in your home folder or a folder above ~/phiward-sbx/run (your ~/.claude too). Claude Code and phiward read them from a folder above the session's, so the check refuses while they are there, also right before each session. Start no claude until the check is done: it may make ~/.claude again.
  4. Build the wheel on your laptop, from a clean checkout of the commit to test: uv build --wheel --out-dir dist ., then shasum -a 256 dist/phiward-*.whl (or sha256sum). Copy the wheel to ~/phiward-sbx/wheel/ on the cluster (chmod go-w on it and its folder) and keep the sha256. Then run srun --pty --job-name auto-sbx-check env SBX_BASE=$HOME/phiward-sbx/run SBX_TOOLS=$HOME/phiward-sbx/tools/bin SBX_WHEEL=$HOME/phiward-sbx/wheel/phiward-VERSION-py3-none-any.whl SBX_WHEEL_SHA256=SHA256 sh scripts/sandbox-check/check.sh, with sh, not bash, and paste the token when it asks. It takes none from the environment. With the wheel, the node needs no package index, only api.anthropic.com. The check starts itself again under an empty environment, which drops proxy and CA variables on purpose (HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY, SSL_CERT_FILE, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE and the like), so run it on a node that reaches api.anthropic.com directly. There is no SBX_ variable for a proxy yet. Without SBX_WHEEL the check builds the wheel itself and needs a package index too.
  5. Put the names back.

docs.title: Rules for the operator
docs.text:
• Start the shared connection yourself; phiward never logs in.
  • Until you trust the lists you wrote, read every HPC request the agent proposes before it runs (Claude Code asks you before it runs a command, unless you allowed it). This is your habit, not a phiward feature: phiward itself never asks at run time; your config decides.
  • Keep [remote] commands short. Prefer commands that print counts and states, with small counts hidden (Small counts).
  • The HPC side's own rules (partitions, job names, where clinical data may be read) still apply.
  • The release check's remote probes (REMOTE, REMOTE_DIR) use an ssh config of their own that can only join the shared connection you start for them (no key, no ticket). Give a new, empty folder: the check writes only under it, and deletes nothing. Remove it yourself afterwards.

Next: daily use.

docs.title: Mode B: the agent tool under phiward launch
docs.text:
• For: people who run the agent in a terminal and want the whole tool confined.
  • Before: the quick start, steps 1 and 2.
  • You will have: sessions in phiward's kernel profile, with settings you approve.

phiward launch --tool claude runs the whole agent tool, and everything it starts, inside the kernel profile: its file tools, shell, MCP servers and hooks. The tool cannot read your protected data, whatever the model asks it to do. You work with protected data through the gateway (phiward run, phiward copy), which masks what comes back. This is the strongest mode (Mode B). A normal Claude Code session wired by the hook (Mode A) is the other; modes.md compares them.

Tested with the real Claude Code on macOS: reads of protected data by the file tools and the shell were refused, and the gateway returned masked output. Mode B is for the terminal: driving a launch session from the desktop app with Remote Control is not tested yet.

How a session's settings stay trusted:

flowchart TD
  A["The trusted copy (what you added with carryover add)"] --> B["A fresh folder for this session"]
  B --> C["The session runs in the kernel profile"]
  C --> D["What it changed goes to quarantine"]
  D --> E{"phiward carryover show: you read it"}
  E -->|"accept"| A
  E -->|"leave it"| F["Not used by later sessions"]

docs.title: Once
docs.text:
1. Install and set up: steps 1 and 2 of the quick start.
  2. A login token, because each session starts in a fresh config folder: run claude setup-token in a plain terminal, open the URL, approve, and keep the token it prints. Then, in the terminal where you start sessions:
export CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN='<the token>'

The agent can read this variable, like an API key. Revoke it in your Claude account settings when you no longer need it. 3. The broker must run (for run and copy): best as a login service (setup.md), or phiward broker in a terminal of its own.

On a Mac with an endpoint tool: a session starts /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f <profile> with the tool's full path, and Claude Code then starts phiward's hook on each tool call. endpoint-security.md lists each command line, for your IT or security team.

docs.title: Every session
docs.text:
From the project folder:

phiward launch --tool claude
  • --memory: turn Claude Code's auto memory on. It then lives in the session's folder, and its changes go to quarantine like any other instruction.
  • launch refuses to start in /, your home, a folder above or inside protected data, a dot folder, ~/Library (macOS), a folder on your PATH, or a phiward folder. On Linux it also refuses /tmp itself (as the project or the spool): the session's own /tmp would be the shared one. A folder below /tmp works.
  • Python environments: an activated .venv puts a folder of the project on your PATH, so launch refuses: your own shell would run what the session wrote there. The refusal names the entry: PATH holds /path/to/project/.venv/bin, inside the project; ... Run deactivate (or take it off PATH), then start again. Run deactivate before launch; inside the session, use .venv/bin/python or uv run. For another entry (direnv), take it off PATH (direnv deny). An empty entry (a leading or trailing :, or ::), . or another relative entry is refused too: it names the folder your shell is in, the project or a folder of it. Remove it from PATH, then start again.
  • --resume and -c find this project's earlier launch sessions (When a session ends).
  • launch refuses to start when the masking check fails: the masking check failed: ...; run phiward doctor. A value of [sanitize] examples is not fully masked by your own rules, or a made-up path below a root came out unmasked (configuration.md). Fix the rule, the example or the root, then start again. A wrapped MCP server (--entry) is not checked.
  • launch refuses to start when the project scan finds a subject or sample ID in a project file or a file name (The project scan).
  • Several launch sessions may run side by side, also in one project (see limit L8 of the threat model).
  • On macOS the tool starts as /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f FILE TOOL ARGS..., with nothing in between. The profile is a new file in ~/.phiward/profiles, as for the gateway, removed when the tool ends. A program name is found on the session's PATH first; when there is none, launch says so and exits 127. Inside another sandbox, sandbox-exec cannot apply the profile, and nothing runs. When the tool exits with an error within a few seconds of its start, launch adds a line: if sandbox-exec printed an error above it, phiward doctor names the cause (inside another sandbox, or a profile that does not compile).
  • The hooks launch writes into the session's settings (the fast hook and the prompt check) run from a file in phiward's package, <python> -I -S <package>/phiward/entry.py ..., with onFailure: "block". So launch --tool claude refuses, on macOS and Linux, a Claude Code older than 2.1.295, which would not honour them. It never starts a program inside the project or the session's folders to learn the version. It asks the native binary TOOL --version, from /. It never starts a script (the npm build): the script's interpreter, or a shim's config, could be the session's. It reads the version from the package.json of the script's npm package (@anthropic-ai/claude-code). A tool that gives no Claude Code version (another program, a wrapper, a mise or asdf shim) is refused too: run Claude Code's own program directly (the native binary, or the npm package's cli.js), or use --tool generic for another tool. phiward doctor warns about a wrapper before the start (refusals.md).

docs.title: The project scan
docs.text:
A file in the project is outside the protected roots, so the agent reads it with no gateway. Claude Code also sends CLAUDE.md and the list of file names at the start, with no tool call. So, before the tool starts, launch reads the project for subject and sample IDs.

  • The rules: the subject rules only: your [sanitize] patterns, your pack files, and the built-in packs in force (a repo's .phiward.toml may add one, such as msk). Not file names, read names, positions, numbers, dates, protected paths or the entry names under the roots: a project holds those everywhere. With no subject rule, there is no scan.
  • What it reads: one walk of the project folder, git-ignored files too: first the instruction files Claude Code sends at the start (CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, AGENTS.md, .claude/), names and content; then every other name, breadth first; then the other files' content, the smallest first. Of each regular file it reads the first 64 KiB (phiward doctor: 1 MiB): of its decompressed form for gzip and BGZF (.csv.gz, .vcf.gz), and as UTF-16 with a BOM (Excel's "Unicode text"). A folder named after an ID is one finding, not one for each file below it.
  • What it does not read: binary files (a NUL byte in the first 8 KiB: xlsx, parquet, BAM), lines over 64 KiB, anything past the first 64 KiB (doctor: 1 MiB), the targets of links, files it cannot open, more than 10000 entries of one folder, the protected and hidden paths, the folders of installed code and caches (node_modules, .venv, venv, site-packages, renv/library, .tox, target, .git, __pycache__, .mypy_cache, .pytest_cache, .ruff_cache, .claude/worktrees), and the paths in [sanitize] scan_allow. It runs no git command: git would run programs that the project's .git/config names.
  • On a finding: launch refuses, and says the kinds and counts only: the project scan found <SUBJECT> in 3 files: move the data under a protected root, pseudonymize it (phiward pseudonymize), or allow the files ([sanitize] scan_allow); phiward doctor --show-paths lists them. Run phiward doctor --show-paths in your own terminal to see the files (masked paths and line numbers). Then move the data under a protected root, make a pseudonymized copy (phiward pseudonymize), or, for made-up IDs only, add the files to [sanitize] scan_allow in your user config (configuration.md).
  • The budget: 2 s. On a made-up project of 5,012 files (5,000 source files of 4 KB and ten 2 MiB tables), the scan read all of them in 1.6 s on the maintainer's Mac. A larger project starts anyway, after one line: phiward launch: NOTE: the project scan stopped at its 2 s limit after N files; run phiward doctor for the full scan. An ID found before the limit still refuses. phiward doctor scans with no limit. A scan that finished but left part of the project unread (files past their head, long lines, folders over the entry cap, files it cannot open) starts with one NOTE of those counts.
  • A scan that cannot run refuses: the project scan could not run; run phiward doctor.
  • [launch] write_to folders are scanned too, in the same 2 s, the instruction files of every folder first (More folders to write).
  • A wrapped MCP server (--entry) is not scanned: its folder is not the agent's project.
  • Mode A has no launch: the SessionStart note runs the same scan within 2 s and, on a finding, tells the session the kinds and counts (it never stops the session), and phiward doctor warns. When the scan cannot run, the note says so and asks the agent to have you run phiward doctor. Under launch the note does not scan again. phiward doctor --headless lists a finding as a reason.

docs.title: What a session can and cannot do
docs.text: Can Cannot Files read and write the project and the [launch] write_to folders (user config); write its own session folder and the spool read protected roots, patterns or derived folders (.git, snapshots, and on Linux other mounts of the same data); read credentials (~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.claude, other agent tools' logins, browser profiles, Kerberos tickets and keytabs, SSH keys your SSH config names, research-data and registry logins), shell histories, the Trash, or the gateway's write_to folders; write anywhere else Files that run later write, at any depth in the project and in each [launch] write_to folder, the .claude, .vscode, .idea, .cursor, .gemini and .codex folders (each as a whole), .mcp.json, .gitmodules, .ripgreprc, .Rprofile or .Renviron, or what a link inside them leads to; or git control files (hooks, config). On Linux launch makes .claude, .vscode and .idea in the project if there are none and .mcp.json as a {} placeholder; the others, a git control file missing at the start (commondir), and one of these made in a subfolder during the session can be made there, and the report at the end names them. In a [launch] write_to folder launch makes nothing; one missing at the start can be made there, and the report at the end names it. A wrapped MCP server (--entry) has the same profile, and cannot write the project's .git folders at all (on macOS also a new .git) Processes run any program in the profile read other terminals, signal processes outside, inject keystrokes, open or script other apps; on macOS also mount file systems or create launchd jobs Network tunnels (CONNECT) to public addresses, through phiward's proxy (below) reach this machine's own services, its link or private ranges; use plain HTTP, UDP, or tools that ignore the proxy variables; reach outside unix sockets (the SSH agent, your shared SSH connection, docker); on Linux before 7.1, see Limits for what stays outside Claude Code's sandbox Protected data phiward run -- CMD (masked output), phiward copy (no names printed) anything else

docs.title: More folders to write
docs.text:
A project may need to write a sibling repository, a shared output folder or a scratch area. List those folders in your user config (a repo's .phiward.toml cannot):

[launch]
write_to = ["~/work/shared-results", "/data/me/scratch"]
  • The checks, at each start. launch refuses to start, naming the entry and the step ("fix or remove it in [launch] write_to of the user config"), for an entry that is:
  • a file, a link, or reached through a link (whoever can change the link would choose the place); name the real folder;
  • inside or above a protected root, a derived folder or a pattern match;
  • /, the home folder or above it, a dot-folder of the home folder (~/.config, ~/.claude, ~/.phiward), in ~/Library, or a folder that is, holds or is inside a PATH folder (files there run later, outside launch);
  • a folder that holds a phiward file (the config, its code) or is the spool;
  • a [broker] write_to folder, or one that holds or is inside one, or a credential;
  • /tmp (Linux): it holds the default Kerberos ticket cache, a credential.

The hook does not check them, so a bad entry stops only launch. phiward doctor gives the same refusals. - A missing entry is skipped, with one NOTE: phiward launch: NOTE: [launch] write_to <entry> does not exist, so the session does not write there. An entry inside the project is dropped (the project is written already); one inside another entry is dropped too. - The folders are named at the start: phiward launch: the session also writes: <folder>, ..., and in the --report JSON (write_to). phiward doctor counts them (the paths with --show-paths). - The project's rules hold in each folder. What runs later and git control files are read-only there, as in the project (the table above). launch makes nothing in a listed folder: on Linux, one of them missing at the start can be made, and the report at the end names it.
