A repository made in a listed folder during the session has writable git control files on both platforms, as in the project; the report at the end names its .git/ paths. - The project scan reads each folder with the project's rules and within the same 2 s: first the instruction files of the project and of every listed folder, then the rest of each in turn. A finding in any folder refuses, naming the folder. A listed folder's instruction files not read in 2 s refuse ("run phiward doctor, or make them smaller"); the project's own, and the rest not read, give the NOTE, naming the folders not finished. - --tool claude gets --add-dir D for each folder, after your own arguments (so a -- among them is refused). From an --add-dir folder Claude Code loads its skills (live), its commands and its subagents, enabledPlugins and extraKnownMarketplaces of its settings, and with CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1 (passed on as you set it) its CLAUDE.md and rules. All of them sit under .claude, which is read-only there and scanned before the tool starts. - The trust prompt. Claude Code 2.1.326 and newer asks you to trust each --add-dir folder. Under launch every session starts with a fresh config folder, so it asks again in every session. That is expected: answer it, or remove the entry. - The end report names what the session changed in each folder, under the folder's name. Each folder is walked at the start and at the end, up to 2 million entries: list a folder, not a whole disk. - An abnormal end. SIGHUP (the terminal closes) and SIGTERM still give the end report (one ignored when launch starts, as under nohup, stays ignored). After a signal, a SIGKILL or a crash, the next launch names the folders of the session that did not finish (on macOS the tool may outlive the launcher): read their files that run later and what it changed before you run anything there. - Not [broker] write_to. That one is the gateway's grant to write inside protected roots, which a session cannot read; this one is what the session itself writes. The two may never overlap (configuration.md). - The broker's PATH filter and phiward pseudonymize treat the listed folders as written by the agent: a program there is not run by the broker, and a table there is not an input.

docs.title: The network
docs.text:
The session has no direct outbound network. launch runs a proxy outside the profile, and the tool's HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and ALL_PROXY (and their lowercase forms) name it, with a token for this session only; NO_PROXY is empty. Claude Code, git, pip, npm and curl use it.

  • Only public addresses. The proxy looks the name up once, checks every address it gets back, and connects to the checked addresses in turn (so broken IPv6 falls back to IPv4). It refuses this machine (localhost, 127.0.0.1 in any spelling, [::1], this machine's names and addresses, which it reads again for each connection), the local link (169.254.x, fe80::) and the private ranges (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x, 100.64.x, fc00::/7).
  • Private ranges you need (an HPC web service, an internal Git server): list them in [launch] private_networks in your user config (configuration.md). A project's .phiward.toml cannot.
  • Tunnels only (CONNECT), to any port of a checked address: HTTPS, and whatever else a tool sends through a CONNECT tunnel. Plain HTTP requests through the proxy are refused.
  • A proxy of your own: when the terminal you start launch from sets HTTPS_PROXY (or ALL_PROXY) to an http:// proxy, phiward's proxy goes through it, by the checked address only (CONNECT <address>:443). A name that does not resolve on this machine is refused, not sent on. An address in your [launch] private_networks is connected to directly, not through that proxy (it does not reach your internal network). Any other kind of proxy there (https://, socks5://) stops the start. Unset it for launch, or give an http:// proxy.
  • At most 64 connections at once. One more is refused, not queued.
  • A refusal says why. The proxy answers 403 phiward: <why> in the status line and the body; most tools print only the status line (pip: "Tunnel connection failed: 403 phiward: ..."). For a private address it reads git.example.internal is a private address; the operator lists its range in [launch] private_networks (user config). At exit, launch prints the hosts it refused (the first 20), also into --report: phiward launch: the proxy refused 2 connection(s): git.example.internal (a private address), ...; private ranges go in [launch] private_networks (user config).
  • ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL (--tool claude): checked at the start with the proxy's rules. A URL that is not https://, or whose host is this machine, its link, or a private range you have not listed, stops the start, since the session could not reach its model: for example ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL (http://127.0.0.1:4000) is not an https:// URL; ...: run Claude Code in Mode A. A name that does not resolve at the start is left to the proxy.
  • launch refuses to start when the proxy cannot start.

What this breaks: - MCP servers over HTTP on this machine, IDE integrations (the IDE's WebSocket on localhost), and /login with a localhost callback (use CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, above). Stdio MCP servers the session starts work. - Tools that ignore the proxy variables (raw sockets, ssh to port 22, some Go and Java tools), and all UDP. They fail visibly. - Docker over TCP (DOCKER_HOST=tcp://localhost); the Docker socket is blocked already. - macOS: the session cannot reach a server on this machine, also one it started itself: test suites with local HTTP fixtures, dev servers, Jupyter kernels (ZMQ over TCP by default) and Dask local clusters. Use unix sockets in the project or the session's temp folder, or an IPC transport (jupyter ... --transport ipc). Name lookups still work. A server the session starts can listen on every address, and the LAN can reach it: bind local servers to 127.0.0.1 (python -m http.server --bind 127.0.0.1) (the limit). - Linux: the session has a network of its own, with its own localhost: servers it starts itself work. The proxy variables name a relay on that localhost, which gets each connection to the proxy as a socket pair from launch (no socket file; it works also where the tool cannot make unix sockets). Name lookups inside the session fail (ping, dig, ssh to a name); tools that use the proxy do not need them. launch refuses to start where network namespaces are not available: it says so when user.max_net_namespaces is 0, and bubblewrap stops the start when it cannot make one for another reason. Nothing runs then; phiward doctor checks both.

docs.title: When a session ends
docs.text:
• The session's folder is thrown away. Each session starts from a trusted copy in ~/.phiward/carryover/claude/, which no session can read or write. Only this project's transcripts are shared between sessions: no login, no caches, no other project's history.
  • This project's transcripts are kept, so claude --resume and claude -c work under launch. launch names the session's transcript folder (CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME, the first 16 hex digits of the sha256 of the project's real path). At the end it copies that folder whole into ~/.phiward/carryover/claude/transcripts/<16 hex>/, and at the next start back into the new session's folder. phiward never reads a transcript: their format is Claude Code's own.
  • Only plain files and real folders are kept. Links are dropped with a NOTE. memory/ (auto memory, an instruction) and mcp-tasks/ are never kept, in any letter case.
  • Sessions that end one after the other are merged; a file is replaced only by a newer one.
  • At most 500 MiB and 20,000 entries for each project; past that, the oldest sessions go first. A session larger than that on its own is not kept, and its end says so with a NOTE.
  • A resumed session restores what Claude Code restores (the conversation, the model, the agent, a permission mode other than bypass, an active goal, scheduled tasks), inside the kernel profile and launch's hooks. What an earlier session wrote is read as history (the limit).
  • To delete them: delete ~/.phiward/carryover/claude/transcripts/ (all projects) or one <16 hex>/ folder in it, when no session runs. phiward carryover status --tool claude lists each project's folder and its size. Claude Code's own commands do not reach them (under launch they see only the session's folder).
  • To turn it off: [launch] keep_transcripts = false in your user config (configuration.md). Each session then starts with no history, and --resume or -c gets a NOTE.
  • Instruction changes go to quarantine. These are files Claude Code reads as instructions or settings (CLAUDE.md, rules/, skills/, agents/, commands/, plugins you install, settings.json), and the MCP and permission keys of .claude.json. The exit message lists them:
phiward carryover show --tool claude
phiward carryover accept ID [ITEM...] --tool claude
phiward carryover add PATH [--as NAME] --tool claude   # your own CLAUDE.md, a skill
phiward carryover status --tool claude                 # sizes; what is safe to delete (kept transcripts too)

accept ID settings.json takes the whole settings.json as the session left it; show lists the keys that changed, and for .claude.json the value accept writes, so read it first. Items you do not name stay in quarantine. add ~/.claude.json takes only its MCP servers, trust and allowed-tools keys, never the login or the history; an MCP server's env and header values there are readable by the agent. - The project report. It lists every file the session changed that is read as instructions for models (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .claude/), every file that runs later (git control files of any repository, hooks, build files, .pth, scripts, executables) and every settings file. Other changed files are named when there are 10 or fewer, and otherwise only counted; code under .venv or node_modules is in that count. In a very large project it says so, and past its limit checks only the first three kinds (dot folders such as .claude first); past 2,000,000 entries it checks nothing more. Treat everything in the project as written by the agent, and read it before you run anything outside launch. Each [launch] write_to folder gets a report of its own, under its name. - Anything under ~/.phiward may be deleted at any time (a disk quota, an HPC purge, or you). The next start rebuilds from what is left, and it never trusts a folder a session could write. carryover status says what each deletion costs.

docs.title: HPC
docs.text: See hpc.md: HPC through your Kerberos ticket and mounts, copy to approved remotes, and run --remote for commands on HPC.

docs.title: Linux: the session's view
docs.text:
On Linux the session sees a snapshot of the file system. Every folder above a protected path or a credential (for example /, /home, your home) is rebuilt for the session from the entries it held at the start, without the protected ones. A protected folder replaced at its path, and a pattern match, credential or ticket cache made after the start, are not in the view.

What this costs: - An entry the host adds to one of those folders after the start (a new folder in your home) is seen only by the next session. A file the host replaces there (an editor saving ~/.gitconfig) stays as it was for the session. - The session's view is checked against what was checked before the tool starts. An entry the host removes from one of those folders while the session starts is left out of the view. An entry the host replaces while the session starts stops the start: nothing runs; start again. A short window stays: an entry removed between bubblewrap's own check and its mount stops the start with bwrap: Can't bind mount ...; start again. - A folder that is missing from the view cannot be made: mkdir ~/.ssh fails (read-only). - A folder that can be entered but not listed (mode 711, common on HPC) cannot be rebuilt. It is shown whole, with the protected roots and credentials in it masked; one made in it later is not hidden. - On Linux the view must fit in bwrap's 9000 arguments, about three for each entry it rebuilds. A protected folder below a folder of thousands of entries (a large data folder) would need more, so launch shows such folders whole instead, those that save the most first, and says before the tool starts how many folders it shows whole. In those folders, as in a 711 folder, a protected entry made or replaced after the start is not hidden. A folder shown whole lists its masked entries by name, so the folder that holds a protected root, or where a pattern's * names the protected entries, is never shown whole: if the view cannot fit then, launch refuses, and you protect that folder as a root instead (/data/study rather than /data/study/<name>). launch also counts bwrap's whole command line before it starts and says so when it is too long. A pattern whose * falls on a folder that cannot be listed cannot cover it: launch refuses, and you protect that folder as a root instead. - A pattern follows a linked folder only in its literal part (/data/... through /data -> /gpfs/...), not at a * level: a match reached through a link there is hidden at the link only. Protect the target as a root.

Protection follows the path, on Linux and macOS. A protected folder that you move into a folder the session can see is readable there, during a session or after it.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
It also reports start-up files next to phiward (.pth, sitecustomize in any form) that no install record lists, or that changed since install. One it cannot check: _virtualenv.py, which uv's and virtualenv's environments add and no record lists.

launch checks its own installed files against the installer's record first, in a separate Python that reads no compiled files. A changed file, a compiled file that does not match its source, or a file the record does not list makes it refuse: reinstall. Without a record (a source checkout or an editable install) it refuses unless PHIWARD_DEV=1 is set. It cannot find code that changes the launcher itself so that the check is skipped, and it trusts the installer's record: a process running as you that changes a file and its record line is not found. It is meant to catch what a session without launch left behind by mistake or by a careless agent; when in doubt, reinstall: the step names the command for the tool that installed phiward.

docs.title: Limits in this release
docs.text:
• Not hidden: shell start-up files (~/.zshrc, which may export tokens), ~/.gitconfig (which may hold an http.extraheader), and, on macOS, Keychain items whose access list trusts the security tool (the session can reach the Keychain service). Keep tokens out of start-up files; prefer Mode A's test result for Keychain-backed tokens until Mode B is checked.
  • Files that other tools run later are read-only. Skills, agents, commands, hooks and settings in the project's .claude, and editor and agent-tool settings (.vscode, .idea, .cursor, .gemini, .codex), cannot be written inside launch: edit them in your own terminal, or bring them in with phiward carryover add. Claude Code's --worktree and agent worktrees (isolation: worktree; both write .claude/worktrees/) and /loop durable tasks (.claude/scheduled_tasks.json) do not work inside launch. A folder that a link in them leads to (.claude/skills -> ../.agents/skills) is read-only too; launch refuses to start when such a link leads to a folder that holds the project, to one that does not exist (Linux), or when one of these folders has more entries than it walks for links (50,000 in one tree; it names the folder). Trees of installed code (node_modules, .venv, venv, site-packages, renv/library, .tox, target, .git, __pycache__, .mypy_cache, .pytest_cache, .ruff_cache; SKIP_TREES in wholetool.py) are not walked, and a .vscode or .idea inside them stays writable, so npm install works; nor are the links in .claude/worktrees followed. R: .Rprofile and .Renviron are read-only, so run renv::init() (it writes .Rprofile) once outside launch; renv::restore() and plain R work inside it (they write renv/library, which stays writable).
  • A git pull, checkout or switch that changes a tracked file in a .claude, .vscode or .idea folder (at any depth) fails partway inside launch, since those folders are read-only. Run them in your own terminal.
  • Git control files are read-only for the repositories found at the start, so git remote add, git config, git submodule update --init, git worktree add and git push -u fail inside launch (and git switch to a remote branch, git branch -u, -m and -d cannot record their settings: git switch still prints "set up to track" but does not); run them in your own terminal. A repository the session makes is not read-only, but its control files are listed in the exit report as files that run later.
  • Linux: Claude Code's own sandbox runs inside launch. phiward turns it off only on macOS. On Linux its bubblewrap starts inside phiward's, and where the host refuses a user namespace inside bubblewrap, Claude Code's Bash tool fails (visibly: the command is refused, nothing runs unconfined). The session's settings set sandbox.allowUnsandboxedCommands: false, so a Bash command is not retried outside it. Bash reaches the network through Claude Code's own proxy, which then goes through phiward's; that a given Claude Code version does this is for the real-tool check to confirm.
  • Linux: unix sockets. launch does not mask sockets by name; the kernel limits them.
  • From Linux 7.1 (Landlock ABI 9): the session reaches only the unix sockets it made itself, and the system's name-service sockets (sssd, nscd).
  • Before 7.1, with --tool claude: Claude Code's own sandbox blocks unix sockets for Bash (its seccomp filter, which the native build carries). launch turns that sandbox on with --settings (sandbox.enabled, sandbox.failIfUnavailable, sandbox.allowUnsandboxedCommands false, and env.CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FILE_MENTIONS: the file install writes for claude --settings), passed as the last arguments of whatever --tool claude runs (claude, a versioned binary, a wrapper); a -- among the arguments stops the start (drop the -- and put the prompt last). Claude Code keeps only one --settings, so your own stops the start too, unless its content is just the same (the file install writes, as a shell alias adds it, or the one v0.2.0b1's install wrote, with no env; launch reads the content, not the path). One more key, another value or a file that does not parse stops the start; if it is phiward's file, rerun phiward install claude --user --write. Under launch, Claude Code reads a config folder of its own, not ~/.claude: put other settings in managed settings, or add a settings.json with phiward carryover add FILE --as settings.json --tool claude.
  • What launch checks before the start. A Claude Code command (claude mcp, doctor, logs, ...), also after options (claude --debug mcp list), is not a session: some ignore --settings and run, and some are hidden from the help. launch refuses it: run it outside launch. To tell a command from a prompt, launch asks the program that runs, inside the session: claude WORD --help for the first word that is not an option (which options take a value comes from claude --help). A help other than the root's means a command; so claude -p mcp is refused too. A help that hangs, fails or is empty stops the start. Some options run something other than a session (--chrome-native-host, --preload, --eval-mock-server, --daemon-worker). launch does not refuse them; they run inside the session's confinement, so the guards still hold. Cost: one help run at each start, and one more when there is such a word. Only Claude Code's native build is accepted (npm and the installer give it from 2.1.250; for an older JavaScript build, run claude install). Before the tool starts, launch runs the filter of the program that will run (found on the session's PATH, then run by its real path) as Claude Code does (the native binary with ARGV0=apply-seccomp) and requires socket(AF_UNIX) to fail. So run the Claude Code binary itself: env, npx, node, a JavaScript program or a wrapper that adds arguments does not pass. It refuses to start when the filter does not block unix sockets, when the session can write the program's real file or a folder above it, on a machine other than x86_64 or aarch64, or when settings open the sandbox (excludedCommands, allowAllUnixSockets, allowUnixSockets, enableWeakerNestedSandbox). With a wrapper of your own, the check is of the wrapper itself. Keep the programs the session runs, and what a wrapper runs, outside the project and the folders the session writes.
  • What is not covered. The tests use a made-up native build. Only the sandbox check shows that the real binary's filter works inside launch's bubblewrap, and whether sessions that Claude Code starts in the background (--bg, its background service) get the same sandbox settings. Claude Code also needs socat and bubblewrap. Bash then cannot use any unix socket, so tmux and Python's forkserver fail there. Hooks, MCP servers, the status line and Claude Code itself run outside that sandbox: they can reach sockets outside. You configure them; the session cannot, because the project's .claude is read-only.
  • Before 7.1, with any other tool (--tool generic, a wrapped MCP server): the tool cannot make unix sockets at all, also its own (socketpairs and pipes work).
  • A launch inside a session (a wrapped MCP server, or a launch for another project) runs its command directly, under the session's own profile: not the narrower profile of a server (which keeps more of the project read-only), and not another project's .phiward.toml. Any other launch builds the full profile; where ~/.phiward cannot be written, that launch refuses and nothing runs.

Read threat-model.md (Mode B, limits L1–L10). In short: - The network goes only to public addresses, through phiward's proxy (above). A session cannot read protected data, so it cannot send it. But it can carry out what it can read, to any public host: gateway output (masked), the login token, the project. - macOS: a process that leaves the tool's process tree keeps running after the session (L5). It can no longer change what a later session reads, but it can write the project, and it keeps its session's one allowed port after the proxy is gone. Close the terminal after a session. - macOS: the Keychain and the per-user temp folder are shared with your own tools. - Masking covers names and identifiers, not content. Through the gateway, print counts and summaries, not records, and hide small counts (Small counts) (rule 3 of the agent rules that phiward init adds to AGENTS.md). Dates can be masked with the dates pack. - tmux, script and other tools that open a new terminal do not work yet. - Other tools than Claude Code run under launch -- PROGRAM with the boundary, but without a per-session config folder (no adapter yet).

Next: what Mode B does not cover is in the threat model.

docs.title: Choose a mode: a Claude Code session (Mode A) or phiward launch (Mode B)
docs.text:
For: anyone who chooses between the two modes, or decides whether phiward is enough.

phiward protects protected data in two ways. Both use the same user config, the same broker and the same gateway (phiward run, phiward copy, phiward run --remote), so work on protected data is equally protected in both. What differs is how much of the agent tool itself is confined. Words are explained in the glossary.

What confines what, in Mode A:

flowchart TD
  A["Claude Code session (app, IDE or terminal)"] --> B["Bash commands"]
  A --> C["File tools: Read, Grep, Edit"]
  A --> D["MCP servers and hooks"]
  B --> E["Claude Code's sandbox (kernel)"]
  C --> F["phiward's hook and permission rules"]
  D --> G["your rights (an MCP server: unless it is wrapped)"]

And in Mode B:

flowchart TD
  A["phiward launch"] --> B["the whole agent tool: shell, file tools, MCP servers, hooks"]
  B --> C["phiward's kernel profile"]

In both, work on protected data goes through the gateway.

The hidden list (both modes): credentials (~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.config/gh, other agent tools' and the Claude app's logins, browser profiles), Kerberos ticket caches and keytabs, SSH keys your ssh configs name, shell and REPL histories, the Trash, thumbnails, local IPC sockets. In Mode A, install puts it in Claude Code's sandbox and permission rules, and the hook refuses it; in Mode B the kernel hides it. Gateway commands cannot read it either. In Mode A, Claude Code's own folder (~/.claude: memory, plans, skills, saved tool output) stays usable; only its login files (.credentials.json, ~/.claude.json) are hidden.

Mode A: a Claude Code session Mode B: phiward launch Start open the project as usual: the desktop app, an IDE, or claude in a terminal phiward launch --tool claude in a terminal (terminal only for now: driving it from the app with Remote Control is not tested) Set up phiward setup (it wires your user settings), once; phiward init in each project with protected work launch.md, once Bash commands in Claude Code's own sandbox (the kernel): protected paths and the hidden list cannot be read in phiward's kernel profile File tools (Read, Grep, Glob, Edit) refused by phiward's hook and by Claude Code's permission rules (inside Claude Code, not the kernel) in phiward's kernel profile MCP servers your full rights, unless you wrap each one (below) confined Hooks your full rights confined Your ~/.claude (skills, rules, MCP config) used as it is each session starts from a trusted copy (carryover add); changes go to quarantine Work on protected data the gateway the gateway Prompts checked before they are sent: one with an identifier of your packs or a path below a root is not sent (threat-model.md) the same check, written beside the fast hook in the session's own settings (the session can remove it) How phiward's hooks start from files in phiward's package, no inline code: a script that clears the Python and loader variables, then phiward's own Python (setup.md) from a file in phiward's package (entry.py); Claude Code 2.1.295 or newer, on macOS and Linux Use it for day-to-day work, every protected step through the gateway long sessions close to protected data, or untrusted input (web pages, other people's repositories)

docs.title: What Mode A does not do
docs.text:
• It does not cover a session that skips the settings. claude --bare (often used for scripts and CI) skips every hook, plugin, MCP server and CLAUDE.md, and an Agent SDK app with settingSources: [] loads no settings file. Then neither phiward's hook nor its sandbox and deny rules apply, and nothing says so. In scripts, run claude -p without --bare; in an SDK app, load the user settings (settingSources: ["user", "project", "local"]), pass phiward install claude --json as its settings, or run the whole program under phiward launch. See unattended.md.
  • @path mentions are turned off (CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FILE_MENTIONS=1, written by install --user; Claude Code v2.1.299+): a mention would put a file's text into the prompt without a tool call phiward sees. Now it is a Read, which the hook judges. @ completion no longer inserts contents. The IDE's open-file and selection context is not covered (setup.md).
  • The file tools are refused inside Claude Code, not by the kernel. A path spelling that both the permission rules and the hook miss reads the file. The hook resolves links and spellings, and Claude Code's deny rules also match a link's target, so this needs a gap in both.
  • Hooks and MCP servers that are not wrapped run with your rights: one could read protected data.
  • On Linux, protected patterns cannot be confined by Claude Code's sandbox (roots only): with patterns, the hook refuses Bash commands other than gateway calls. Use roots, or Mode B.
  • A Bash command can rewrite a project's Claude Code settings (for example to set disableAllHooks) unless you ran phiward init in the project: it writes the project settings (phiward install claude --project), whose sandbox entry denies that write. Without it, the hook refuses the plain forms (a redirection, cp, tee, sed -i, git checkout, code that names the file), not a name built from variables or reached after cd .claude. Run phiward init once in each project where you work with protected data (quickstart.md step 3); doctor notes a project without it.
  • The project wiring runs phiward from your PATH. A PATH folder the agent can write (a relative entry, or one inside the project such as node_modules/.bin) could put another program first; keep such entries out of your PATH. User wiring runs phiward by its full path.
  • Credentials that are not files. The macOS Keychain, a Kerberos ticket kept by the macOS credential service (API:) or by the kernel keyring or KCM on Linux (KEYRING:, KCM:), and tokens in your environment cannot be hidden by a file list. Whether a Bash command in Claude Code's sandbox can reach them depends on that sandbox (in the desktop-app test a Keychain-backed GitHub token was not reachable). doctor warns when your tickets are not a file. Mode B blocks the Linux keyring; the macOS Keychain is shared in both modes (launch.md limits).
  • Refusals "above" the hidden list. A Grep or Glob of a folder that holds a hidden path (your home folder, /tmp) is refused, so a session started in the home folder cannot search it; and with a shell that is not sandboxed, ls ~ is refused. Work in a project folder.
  • A session in the home folder. Claude Code's sandbox then lets the shell write your whole home folder, including the places that start programs later (~/.config, ~/.local/bin, ~/Library/LaunchAgents). So phiward counts that shell as not confined: only gateway commands run, and every file-tool write asks you (or is refused where nobody can be asked). The same holds when allowWrite or additionalDirectories names one of those folders. Open Claude Code in a project folder.

That is why Mode B exists. phiward doctor says which mode a session is in and which layers are on.

docs.title: Mode A for a project
docs.text:
The steps are in quickstart.md: each contributor wires Claude Code for every session (phiward setup, or (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write)), and runs phiward init once in the project.

Do not rely on project wiring alone. Claude Code loads a project's settings only for a session opened in that folder. A session opened on the folder above it, on another checkout or on a worktree elsewhere gets none of them. doctor warns when only the project is wired.

How the agent knows the rules. install also adds a start-of-session note (a SessionStart hook, phiward session-note claude): every session, in any folder, starts with the rules: protected data only through phiward run and phiward copy, which are the intended route and not a workaround; aggregates only; HPC through phiward run --remote (with your hosts and programs). It names no protected path. A project's own AGENTS.md can say the same for tools that do not run Claude Code's hooks.

docs.title: Wrap an MCP server (Mode A)
docs.text:
An MCP server is a program Claude Code starts, and it runs outside Claude Code's sandbox, with your rights. Start it under phiward launch -- and it runs in phiward's kernel profile, even in a Mode A session: it cannot read protected data or credentials. In your own terminal:

  1. Close Claude Code (it writes ~/.claude.json too).
  2. See what each server is, one line per entry, with its file:
phiward mcp list
  1. Wrap the servers that list offers to wrap (it shows the change and asks first):
phiward mcp wrap NAME

or every one at once: phiward mcp wrap --all. 4. Start Claude Code again: a running session keeps each server as it started it. 5. Check: phiward doctor names any server that still runs with your rights, and any entry whose program Claude Code would look up on a PATH folder the agent can write.

A wrapped entry reads:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "docs": { "command": "/Users/you/.local/share/uv/tools/phiward/bin/phiward",
              "args": ["launch", "--entry", "3f9c2a7b1d4e6a08", "--",
                       "npx", "-y", "some-mcp-server"] }
  }
}

wrap gives each entry an id of its own (--entry): a launcher vouches only for the entry with its id, and an id that two entries hold (a copy) is trusted for neither, so list calls such an entry copied and wrap gives it a new id. An entry wrapped without an id (an older phiward) counts as not wrapped until you run wrap again. wrap writes the full path of the installed launcher, the file phiward's install record lists, in every file, .mcp.json too. Only that file by that path counts as wrapped: phiward by name does not, since Claude Code looks a name up on its PATH, where a project's .venv/bin or node_modules/.bin could supply another phiward, which it would start with your rights. If you commit .mcp.json, a contributor whose phiward is elsewhere runs phiward mcp wrap again; list names an entry whose launcher is by name or another file, and wrap gives it the path. (A source checkout has no install record: there the launcher is the phiward found in the PATH folders the agent cannot write.) It keeps its backups only in its own folder, ~/.phiward/backups/<file>-<hash>/, which the agent cannot write: original (the file before phiward first changed it, never overwritten) and last (before the latest change). Nothing is written beside the config file. phiward mcp unwrap NAME undoes it.

What list may say about a server, and what to do:

list says means do wrapped runs in the kernel profile nothing remote runs on another machine, nothing here nothing not wrapped (runs with your rights) a local command phiward mcp wrap NAME not wrapped: wrapped, but its entry sets a cwd or an env key that changes what runs remove it from the entry: for cwd, give the server absolute paths; for env PATH, name the command by its full path not wrapped: its entry id is also in another entry a copy: their launchers cannot be told apart phiward mcp wrap NAME (a new id) not wrapped: it was wrapped without an entry id an older phiward wrote it phiward mcp wrap NAME not wrapped: it names phiward without its path a folder on PATH the agent can write could supply another launcher phiward mcp wrap NAME (writes the full path) not wrapped: its phiward is not the installed launcher the entry names another phiward file phiward mcp wrap NAME not wrapped: its phiward launch has no -- and a program the entry is malformed fix the entry not wrapped: it has options before -- that wrapped entries do not take --tool, --memory or --report in a launcher entry phiward mcp wrap NAME (drops them, and says so) not wrapped: it starts phiward through uvx, env, uv run, pipx run or Python with -m phiward in front of the launcher: what their words mean differs, so wrap does not rewrite it edit the entry so its command is the server program itself, then phiward mcp wrap NAME listens on this machine / no command phiward can read phiward cannot wrap it its command tools may make only gateway calls

Know that: - phiward must be installed with an install record (uv tool install), or the server needs PHIWARD_DEV=1; - launch makes .claude, .vscode and .idea if there are none (on macOS only .claude), and keeps the files that other tools run later read-only for the server, as for the tool; - the env keys of the MCP config reach the server only if [launch] pass_env lists them, and that setting passes them to every launch session, the agent's included; - on macOS, when Claude Code stops the server, only the launcher gets the signal: a server that does not stop at the end of its input keeps running; - plugin and managed MCP servers, and the app's own, are not wrapped this way (wrap does not change a plugin's files: an update replaces them); their tools that run commands may make only gateway calls; - under Mode B (the whole session in phiward launch) a wrapped server's launcher runs inside the session's profile, and the hook treats its command tools the same way (the server is confined there anyway).

How the hook tells which tools are confined: configuration.md; how it trusts a wrapped server: threat-model.md.

Next: the quick start for Mode A, or launch.md for Mode B.

docs.title: The Claude Code plugin, and other plugins
docs.text: For: people who use phiward's Claude Code plugin, or other plugins beside it.

docs.title: phiward's plugin
docs.text:
phiward's repository is also a Claude Code plugin marketplace. The plugin gives a session: - phiward's hooks: the guard on every tool call, and the start-of-session note with the rules; - the skill: how to work through the gateway; - three commands: /phiward:setup (the guided first setup), /phiward:doctor (checks the setup and explains each warning) and /phiward:help (how to work with protected data and HPC); - an MCP server, phiward, whose tools are the gateway: phiward_run, phiward_copy, phiward_remote, phiward_check and phiward_doctor. They do the same checks and masking as the commands, with arguments as lists and no shell.

Tested in a desktop-app session on made-up data: the note, the refusals, the commands and normal work.

The plugin does not install the phiward package, and it cannot set Claude Code's sandbox or permission rules. Those come from the quick start (phiward install claude --user), and they are what stops the reads in a normal session. Keep that user wiring even when you use the plugin: a project can turn a plugin off, but not your user wiring.

docs.title: Install it
docs.text:
In Claude Code, two commands:

/plugin marketplace add msk-access/phiward#v0.2.0b1

/plugin install phiward@phiward

#v0.2.0b1 pins the plugin to the release you installed with uv, so their versions agree. In a terminal, the same is claude plugin marketplace add msk-access/phiward#v0.2.0b1, then claude plugin install phiward@phiward.

docs.title: Offer it to every contributor of a project
docs.text:
The project's committed .claude/settings.json can offer it:

{
  "extraKnownMarketplaces": {
    "phiward": { "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "msk-access/phiward",
                             "ref": "v0.2.0b1" } }
  },
  "enabledPlugins": { "phiward@phiward": true }
}

Each contributor then trusts the folder and installs it (/plugin install phiward@phiward, or claude plugin install phiward@phiward --scope project).

docs.title: Know this
docs.text:
• The plugin runs phiward from the app's PATH. If the desktop app does not find it, every tool call is refused, with a message that says phiward is not installed: quit the app and open it again (quickstart.md). A PATH folder the agent can write could put another program first (modes.md). The user wiring uses the full path.
  • A project can turn a plugin off ("phiward@phiward": false in its settings), unless your organization's managed settings force it on. Your user wiring cannot be turned off by a project that way. A project's disableAllHooks can still turn all hooks off; only managed settings stop that. phiward doctor warns when a project turns the plugin off or sets PATH.
  • For an organization, managed settings are the strong form. They can force the plugin on, allow only managed and forced hooks, and set the sandbox and permission rules.
  • The plugin follows the tag you added. With #v0.2.0b1, the marketplace takes the plugin from that release. Without a tag it follows the repository's main branch. The plugin's version must match the installed phiward package (phiward --version). To move to a new release, update both: uv tool install --force phiward==<version>, then add the marketplace again with the new tag.

docs.title: Other plugins (for example ECC)
docs.text: You can use phiward together with other Claude Code plugins, for example ECC. You do not have to choose. Tested: the phiward plugin and ECC 2.2.3 in one desktop-app session on made-up data. phiward's guard refused the reads of the protected folder, and the normal work ran.

docs.title: How they work together
docs.text:
• Claude Code runs every hook that matches a tool call. phiward's guard runs on each call, whatever other plugins also run. If one hook refuses a call, the call does not run.
  • Other plugins' switches do not turn phiward off. For example, ECC's ECC_HOOKS_ENABLED, ECC_HOOK_PROFILE, ECC_DISABLED_HOOKS and ECC_GATEGUARD=off change only ECC's own hooks.
  • Do not put phiward's guard into another plugin's hook list. Keep phiward as its own plugin, or wire it with phiward install claude --user. The switches of the other plugin could then turn the guard off.
  • The hook is not the protection by itself. In a normal session (Mode A), Claude Code's sandbox and permission rules stop the reads. phiward install claude writes them; no plugin can (modes.md). Under phiward launch (Mode B), the kernel profile stops them.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
1. Do the quick start: install phiward, write your config, wire Claude Code and start the broker.
  2. Optional: add the phiward plugin (above).
  3. Install the other plugin as its own instructions tell you.
  4. Run phiward doctor and open a new session.

docs.title: Know this
docs.text:
• In a normal session, other plugins' hooks and MCP servers run as you, outside Claude Code's sandbox. They are not confined by phiward. A hook can read any file that you can read, and it can add text to what Claude Code sends to the model. Install only plugins you trust, and check what their hooks read and keep. Under phiward launch, they run inside the kernel profile, the same as the tool.
  • A hook sees each tool call. A hook that runs before a call sees its input, also when phiward refuses the call: for example a command that names a protected path. A hook that runs after a call also sees its output. Output from phiward run is masked before Claude Code receives it, so a hook sees the masked output.
  • Some plugins stop the agent's first command and ask it questions. For example, ECC's GateGuard asks the agent to state facts before its first shell command, and its message tells the agent how to turn GateGuard off. That is ECC's decision about ECC's own hook. phiward's refusals tell the agent the approved route; they never tell it how to turn a guard off.
  • Under phiward launch, a plugin is not there until you carry it over. Each session starts from a trusted copy of the tool's config (phiward carryover add, see launch.md). A plugin that a session installs or turns on goes to quarantine. Carrying over a plugin such as ECC into launch is not tested yet.

Next: daily use.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
• For: anyone who sets phiward up for the first time.
  • Before: macOS or Linux, and Claude Code 2.1.295 or newer; 2.1.299 or newer for @ mentions off (phiward doctor warns below it).
  • You will have: phiward installed, your protected folders set, Claude Code wired, and a test that shows it works.
Step Where What you type You see 1. Install Terminal uv tool install ... phiward==0.2.0b1 phiward --version prints the version 2. Set up Terminal (or the plugin) cd ~ && phiward setup its questions, then the config it wrote 3. Check the project folder phiward init, then phiward doctor no PROBLEM or WARNING line

phiward keeps protected data (for example patient data) and your credentials out of what an AI coding agent sends to its model provider. The agent works on protected data only through phiward's gateway (phiward run, phiward copy). A broker runs those commands outside the agent and masks their output. Words in bold are explained in the glossary.

What you get with the steps below: Mode A. The wiring in your user settings covers every Claude Code session, in every folder: phiward's hook checks each tool call, and Claude Code's sandbox keeps shell commands out of your protected folders. In each project where you work with protected data, you also run phiward init once (step 3): without it, a shell command in that project could rewrite the project's Claude Code settings. This is the right start for most people. The stronger Mode B (phiward launch) is for the terminal only; see modes.md when you need it.

docs.title: 1. Install phiward
docs.text:
On Linux, first install bubblewrap and socat (phiward's kernel profile and Claude Code's sandbox need them), with your package manager, for example sudo apt install bubblewrap socat. Without admin rights, see hpc.md. On Ubuntu 24.04, AppArmor can block bubblewrap: see setup.md.

In Terminal:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

uv tool install --python-preference only-managed phiward==0.2.0b1

uv tool update-shell

The first command installs uv, a Python installer that needs no admin rights. If you have Homebrew, brew install uv does the same. The second gives phiward a Python of its own, which uv downloads once (not Xcode's, conda's or the system's, which another account or tool can change). The last command puts ~/.local/bin, where phiward now is, on your PATH.

Then open a new Terminal, and quit and reopen the Claude Code desktop app (Cmd-Q on macOS), so that both find phiward. In the new Terminal, phiward --version prints the version.

Do not install phiward into conda or another shared Python environment: phiward protects its own folder from the agent. Setup also makes phiward's own Python writable by you alone (it says which folders it changed); it never changes your home folder. If an older phiward is in conda, remove it there first (pip uninstall phiward).

docs.title: 2. Set it up
docs.text: Choose one way. Both do the same steps.

docs.title: With Claude Code's help
docs.text:
In a Claude Code session, type these two commands:

/plugin marketplace add msk-access/phiward#v0.2.0b1

/plugin install phiward@phiward

Then open a new session and type:

/phiward:setup

The agent walks you through the steps, and Claude Code asks you before each command. It asks you which folders hold protected data; it never looks into your folders to guess.

It recommends that you write the config yourself, with the two commands of "By hand" below, which it gives you. It can also write the first config for you, while none exists. That is quicker, but then you trust the agent, in that session, to write exactly what you say: do it only in a new session that has not read web pages, other people's files or repositories you do not know. After the first config, only you can change it, in your own Terminal (phiward setup).

If the agent wrote the first config, it holds your protected folders (and copy remotes) only: no results folder, no list of programs, no network. The rest is yours, in your own Terminal: cd ~ && phiward setup, and choose 1 (the steps below). It adds the results folder and the program list, wires Claude Code and starts the broker at every login. More about the plugin: plugins.md.

docs.title: By hand
docs.text:
In Terminal, in your home folder (not inside a project), from a Terminal where your tools (for example samtools from conda) are found:

cd ~ && phiward setup

It asks how you will use phiward. Choose 1, real patient data (the default), and it sets safe defaults for you: - your protected folders (you type them); - a results folder inside the first one, where gateway commands write (Enter accepts it); - a list of programs that gateway commands may run on the data (@genomics), plus a folder of your own scripts if you have one; - no network for gateway commands; - shell commands in Claude Code reach only the hosts you list (Enter says yes). git push and pip install from a session fail until you list their hosts, such as github.com; - which rules mask subject and sample IDs inside your files: none (type 1; there is no default), the msk example pack, or your own patterns; - if you use an HPC cluster: its short name, login host, your user name and work folder. setup writes phiward's ssh config and prints the lines to add to your ~/.ssh/config.

At the end it shows the whole config. Nothing is written until you say yes; then it writes the config and records the folders it protects with your roots (phiward pin). Then it asks three more questions:

  1. "Approve these N program(s) as they are now?" It first lists each program of your program list with its path. The broker runs only the programs you approve. On a first run, with nothing marked, Enter says yes. When a program is marked (changed), or a program in your home folder hides a system program of the same name ((shadows /usr/bin/NAME)), the default is No: read those lines first.
  2. Wire Claude Code for every session? One yes: it shows the change to your user settings (a long list: every protected path and credential, twice) and writes it ((cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write)).
  3. Start the broker at every login? (A system without a service manager for your login, such as a container or WSL without systemd, cannot: setup says so, and you run phiward broker yourself in a terminal that stays open.)

Say yes to each. The wiring ends with an alias claude='claude --settings ...' line. Add it to your shell startup file (for example ~/.zshrc) yourself, if you start claude in Terminal: then a repository's settings cannot turn the sandbox off. Without it phiward still works; the hook checks the project's settings itself (setup.md). (Choose 2 to try phiward on made-up data with open defaults, or 3 to choose every setting.)

When you change your config later, run (cd ~ && phiward setup) again: it restarts the broker for you. After a change by hand, restart it yourself: the broker refuses requests after the config changes, and the refusal names the command.

A team can share its settings in a template: phiward setup --from team.toml fills in the program list, packs and HPC hosts; each person adds their own folders.

docs.title: 3. Set up each project, and check it
docs.text:
In Terminal, in each project folder where you work with protected data, run once:

phiward init

It only adds; it changes nothing that is there. It adds the phiward rules for agents to AGENTS.md, a .gitignore line, the project's Claude Code settings (.claude/settings.json and .claude/settings.local.json) and git hooks. The project settings stop a shell command from rewriting them. In a repository that is not yours, do not commit these files: list the new ones in .git/info/exclude (for example AGENTS.md and .claude/). Then, in the same folder:

phiward doctor

When all is well, you see lines such as:

protected roots: 1, patterns: 0
  sandbox confines the shell: yes
broker: running

Fix each WARNING; each one says how. A NOTE is for your information. Before Claude Code is wired, one line gives the next step; phiward doctor --verbose lists every check. Then open a new Claude Code session in that folder and ask the agent to read a file in a protected folder: it must be refused. Then ask it to run phiward run -- wc -l <that file>: you get a line count, with the file name masked. (If you said No to the login service, start the broker first: phiward broker in a Terminal of its own.)

If you chose 2 or 3 and now use real patient data, list the programs that gateway commands may run ([broker] commands, see configuration.md): run (cd ~ && phiward setup) again and choose 1.

Next: daily-use.md tells you how to work with the agent on protected data.

docs.title: A project where every contributor is protected
docs.text:
1. Each contributor does steps 1 to 3 above.
  2. Someone runs, once, in the project folder:
phiward init --root data/protected

--root names the project's own protected folders, if it has any. init only adds; it changes nothing that is there. It adds: - the phiward rules for agents to AGENTS.md; - the protected folders to .phiward.toml; - the project's Claude Code settings: the shared part in .claude/settings.json, the personal part in .claude/settings.local.json; - a .gitignore line for the personal file; - git hooks that refuse commits holding protected names or identifiers. 3. Commit AGENTS.md, .phiward.toml, .gitignore and .claude/settings.json. Never commit .claude/settings.local.json. 4. Each other contributor runs phiward init once too (for the personal file and the git hooks), then phiward doctor.

docs.title: HPC
docs.text: The agent never uses ssh itself. It runs approved programs on the cluster with phiward run --remote, and moves files with phiward copy. Both go through your own shared SSH connection, which you open in Terminal (for example kinit, then ssh -fN hpc). No agent request can read your key or Kerberos ticket. The one-time setup is in hpc.md.

docs.title: If something goes wrong
docs.text: What you see What to do Every tool call is refused with "phiward is not installed or not on PATH" The app does not find phiward. Quit the app (Cmd-Q on macOS) and open it again. If that does not help, check in Terminal that command -v phiward prints ~/.local/bin/phiward, and run uv tool update-shell again. phiward run says no broker is running Start it at every login: (cd ~ && phiward broker --service --write) in Terminal. Or run phiward broker in a Terminal and keep it open. A command the agent needs is refused The refusal says what to run instead. See daily-use.md. phiward doctor shows a PROBLEM Fix it before you use the agent; the line says how. A wrapped MCP server "failed to connect", or doctor says phiward's own files fail its self-check Usually after uv tool upgrade with umask 002: run (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write) again (it makes phiward's own Python writable by you alone), then start Claude Code again. The WARNING names any other step.

docs.title: What is refused, and the way around it
docs.text:
phiward refuses some things that typical work meets. This page lists them: what works, what is refused and why, and the way around each one. Each refusal names its next step in one line, and phiward doctor warns about the ones it can see before you start. The refusals that are the product itself (a read of protected data, a credential, a guard file) are in daily-use.md.

Run phiward doctor in the project folder first. Its section "launch (Mode B)" runs the start checks of phiward launch without starting anything, and its Claude Code section covers Mode A.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
• Edits, builds and tests in the project: pytest, npm run dev, git status, git commit.
  • Package installs into the project (.venv, node_modules), with the caches below.
  • Work with protected data through the gateway: phiward run -- CMD, phiward copy SRC DST.
  • Under phiward launch: HTTPS to public hosts through phiward's proxy, private ranges you list, and --resume and -c (this project's transcripts are kept).

docs.title: phiward launch (Mode B)
docs.text:
No protected paths yet. Launch says: no protected paths are configured: there is nothing to confine; run (cd ~ && phiward setup) first

The folder cannot be the project. Launch refuses /, your home folder or a folder above it, a dot folder in your home, ~/Library on macOS, and a folder that holds a phiward folder. Each of them is writable as a whole in a session, and other programs run what is there later. The message ends: ); start the tool in a project folder

Launch also refuses a folder inside or above a protected path, and doctor warns about it: the session would reach the protected data. The message is: this folder is inside or above a protected path; start the tool in a project folder

A folder on PATH inside the project (an activated .venv, direnv, node_modules/.bin). Your own shell runs what is there after the session, and the session could write there. The message names the entry and the step. For an activated .venv: run deactivate (or take the entry off PATH), then start again; in the session, use .venv/bin/python or uv run. For any other entry: take it off PATH (for direnv, direnv deny), then start again. Doctor names the entry relative to the project (--show-paths names it in full). An empty entry (a leading or trailing :, or ::), . or another relative entry is refused too: it names the folder your shell is in, the project or a folder of it. Remove the empty or relative entry from PATH, then start again.

A settings file or folder that is a link (.claude or .vscode linked to a dotfiles repository). A session's writes would reach a file a later plain run reads. The message ends: in the project is a link; replace it with a real file or folder

A [launch] write_to folder the session may not write (a link, a file, a folder above or inside a protected path, your home or a dot-folder in it, a PATH folder, the spool, a [broker] write_to folder). The message names the entry and why, and ends: ; fix or remove it in [launch] write_to of the user config

An entry that does not exist is skipped with a NOTE. With a listed folder, --tool claude gets --add-dir after your arguments, so a -- among them is refused with the message below, on every platform. Details: launch.md.

A wrapper, a shim or an old Claude Code (module load scripts, asdf, mise, volta, a site claude script). Launch needs Claude Code's own program, at the version whose hooks it writes, and never starts a script to ask. The step: run Claude Code's own program directly (the native binary, or the npm package's cli.js), not a wrapper or a shim, or use --tool generic for another tool

Launch needs Claude Code 2.1.295 or newer. Doctor judges the build from its files and starts nothing; for a native binary it uses the version it read, and when that is unknown it says only launch can tell.

On Linux, the JavaScript (npm) build is refused too: it does not carry Claude Code's seccomp filter. Update to the native build: claude install.

Files that run later are read-only (.claude, .vscode, .idea, .Rprofile, .Renviron, .mcp.json and the like, at any depth). Other tools run them later, outside the session. The operating system refuses the write with "Operation not permitted", which phiward cannot change, so doctor says it before the start: NOTE: in a launch session the files other tools run later are read-only, at any depth: .claude, .vscode, .idea, .Rprofile, .Renviron, .mcp.json and the like (a write gets 'Operation not permitted'). Edit them in a plain terminal, or phiward carryover add for Claude Code's own files; run renv::init() once outside launch.

So skills, agents, hooks, editor settings, Claude Code's --worktree and /loop tasks are not written inside launch.

The network. A session reaches only HTTPS (CONNECT) to public addresses through phiward's proxy. A private address (an internal GitLab, a package mirror) is refused until you list its range in [launch] private_networks of the user config (configuration.md). A plain HTTP request gets: only CONNECT (HTTPS) goes through phiward's proxy; use an https:// URL for the index or mirror

An ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL the proxy would refuse (http://, this machine, a private range not listed) stops the start; doctor warns about it. Use Mode A for a model on this machine, or list the range. Details: launch.md.

A proxy of your own that is not http://. When HTTPS_PROXY (or ALL_PROXY) in your terminal names an https:// or socks5:// proxy, launch cannot chain it and stops. Unset it for launch, or give an http:// proxy.

No confinement backend. Launch, phiward run and phiward copy need macOS sandbox-exec or Linux bubblewrap (bwrap). Without one they refuse. On Linux, install bubblewrap with the system's package manager and have it on the PATH (setup.md).

Linux below Landlock ABI 9 (the inner mode). There Claude Code's own sandbox blocks unix sockets, and launch passes its own --settings, last. So launch refuses your own --settings (put them in managed settings, or in launch's trusted copy with phiward carryover add FILE --as settings.json --tool claude), Claude Code commands such as claude mcp and claude doctor (run them outside launch), and a -- among Claude Code's arguments: launch passes --add-dir (for [launch] write_to) or --settings to Claude Code as the last arguments, so -- cannot be among them: drop the -- and put the prompt last

Doctor names the mode launch would use (Landlock or inner), and checks your settings for the inner mode.

The login. Each session starts with a fresh config folder, so Claude Code asks you to log in every time. To log in once, run claude setup-token and set CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (the agent can read it).

A source checkout. Launch checks phiward's installed files first. A source checkout or an editable install has no install record: install with uv tool or pipx, or set PHIWARD_DEV=1 (developers only).

docs.title: Mode A: Claude Code with the hook and its sandbox
docs.text:
A sandbox opener stops the whole shell. One of network.allowLocalBinding (macOS), allowUnixSockets, allowAllUnixSockets, allowMachLookup, filesystem.disabled, enableWeakerNestedSandbox, allowAppleEvents or allowNestedUserNamespaces in any settings level means the shell is not confined, and the hook refuses every command but a gateway call. Doctor's line "sandbox confines the shell" names the key and the file. Remove the key; run a dev server or docker in your own terminal. Or, for a folder you are sure holds no PHI, list it in [no_phi] folders of your user config: when network.allowLocalBinding (macOS), enableWeakerNestedSandbox, allowAppleEvents or allowNestedUserNamespaces is the only cause, Bash and Monitor there get the text check in place of the refusal (configuration.md). The socket openers (allowUnixSockets, allowAllUnixSockets) and allowMachLookup are not relaxed, nor is filesystem.disabled: the service behind a socket (Docker's daemon) runs outside the sandbox. For Docker, use a sandbox.excludedCommands entry (docker *) instead of the socket. A non-empty sandbox.excludedCommands does not stop the shell: the hook checks the text of every command, and refuses a path it cannot see (setup.md).

Package caches are read-only. Claude Code's sandbox writes only the project and the temp folder. phiward adds no allowWrite for the caches, because a cache a session writes is code a later run executes. Doctor says: NOTE: Claude Code's sandbox keeps the package caches outside the project read-only (pip: ~/.cache/pip, or ~/Library/Caches/pip on macOS; uv: ~/.cache/uv; npm: ~/.npm), so an install that writes its cache fails with 'Operation not permitted'. Use pip install --no-cache-dir, or set PIP_CACHE_DIR, UV_CACHE_DIR and npm_config_cache to folders under $TMPDIR. phiward adds no allowWrite for them: a cache a session writes is code a later run executes.

Under phiward launch the caches are the session's own, so installs work there.

git with credentials. The SSH agent, SSH keys and the keychain are hidden from the session. The session note tells the agent: git push, pull and fetch that need the operator's SSH key or keychain run in the operator's own terminal

@file mentions. phiward install turns them off: a mention would put a file's text into the prompt without a tool call the hook sees. Ask the agent to read the file with the Read tool.

Grep and Glob above a protected root. When a root sits inside the project (./data), a Grep or Glob from the project folder would list it, so it is refused. Give it a subfolder that holds no protected folder (src/). Doctor warns when the folder is above a root.

Your own --settings. Claude Code keeps one --settings. Put your own settings in your user settings (~/.claude/settings.json) or in managed settings, and start Claude Code with the file phiward writes (doctor names it).

Files that run later. A write to .vscode/, .Rprofile, a skill or a hook asks you first. In -p, auto, dontAsk or bypassPermissions mode nobody can be asked, so it is refused: write the file yourself.

docs.title: The gateway: phiward run and phiward copy
docs.text:
A program not on the broker's PATH. The broker keeps the PATH of the terminal that started it. Doctor warns about each listed program it does not find there. Start the broker again from a terminal where the program works (after conda activate), or list the program by its full path.

The config changed. The broker refuses requests after any change to the config, the pins or the listed programs. Restart the broker. Doctor does not compare the config's content with the broker's yet.

A copy out of a root. A copy may not take protected data out of the protected folders: the destination is not inside a protected path of the user config; results leave a root only as phiward run output (counts and summaries)

Linux below Landlock ABI 2. The gateway uses Landlock as a second layer for its writes and runs nothing without it. It needs Linux 5.19 or newer with Landlock turned on (setup.md).

More messages of run and copy: daily-use.md.

docs.title: Releasing phiward
docs.text: For maintainers. A release is a git tag; the release workflow builds the package, checks it, and publishes it to PyPI. No PyPI token is stored anywhere: PyPI trusts the workflow through trusted publishing (OpenID Connect).

docs.title: Once: connect PyPI to the repository
docs.text:
As an owner of the msk-access PyPI account, in a browser: on PyPI, open Your account → Publishing → Add a new pending publisher (for the first release; after that, the project's own Settings → Publishing), and enter: - PyPI project name: phiward - Owner: msk-access - Repository name: phiward - Workflow name: release.yml - Environment name: leave it empty. The publish job runs in no GitHub environment, as in gbcms and krewlyzer: a pushed tag publishes once the tests and checks pass.

A pending publisher does not reserve the name: the first publish creates the project. So publish the first release before the repository is public: until then, anyone could take the name, and the install line in these docs would install their package. Trusted publishing works from a private repository.

docs.title: The first release
docs.text:
1. Create msk-access/phiward as a private repository and push main and develop.
  2. Add the pending publisher (above).
  3. Push the tag (below). The workflow tests, builds and publishes.
  4. Check https://pypi.org/project/phiward/ and the install line.
  5. Only then make the repository public, and turn on GitHub Pages: Settings, Pages, Deploy from a branch, gh-pages, / (root). The docs workflow publishes there with mike: develop as dev, each release tag as its version with the alias stable, which the site opens on.

docs.title: Each release
docs.text:
The repository uses git-flow (gitflow.prefix.versiontag is v): start with git flow release start 0.2.0b2 from develop, make the changes below on that branch, and git flow release finish 0.2.0b2 merges it into main and develop and makes the tag v0.2.0b2. Then push main, develop and the tag.

  1. Set the version. PyPI's form has no v (0.2.0b2); the tag has it (v0.2.0b2).
  2. __version__ in src/phiward/__init__.py (the package and phiward --version take it from there), plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json and .claude-plugin/marketplace.json. A test fails when they disagree.
  3. In README.md, docs/, plugin/commands/setup.md and mkdocs.yml: the install lines (phiward==), the plugin tags (#v), the /blob/v.../ links, the GitHub install (phiward@v in setup.md), the marketplace "ref" (plugins.md), the status lines (README and docs/index.md), and the release notes link (docs/index.md) and nav entry (mkdocs.yml).
  4. Then grep for the old version, and change each line that names it as the current release: git grep -n -F OLD -- ':!CHANGELOG.md' ':!docs/release-notes' ':!tests'. Lines about an older release stay (for example launch.md's "the one v0.2.0b1's install wrote", the first release's tag line in step 4 below, and the agent-guards rename in setup.md, config.py, names.py and pyproject.toml).

The workflow refuses a tag when an install line (phiward==), a /blob/v.../ link, a plugin tag (#v), a GitHub install (phiward@v), a marketplace "ref" or a status line in README.md, CHANGELOG.md, plugin/commands/setup.md or docs/*.md names another version. It does not check the release notes link or the mkdocs.yml nav entry: grep for them. 2. In CHANGELOG.md, replace "unreleased" with the date (UTC), and write the release notes in docs/release-notes/, linked from the CHANGELOG entry. 3. Run the full test suite on macOS (tests/README.md says how) and on Linux (sh scripts/linux-check/check.sh, needs Docker: Python 3.12 and 3.9, two layouts, on a git archive of HEAD), and the quickstart in clean Linux containers (sh scripts/quickstart-check/check.sh, needs Docker; its image is built fresh, and --quick runs four plain runs on the cached one while you work): a new user's steps, with umask 022 and 002, must end with no doctor WARNING and a wrapped MCP server. On macOS, run sh scripts/quickstart-check/mac.sh WHEEL PYTHON with uv's or Homebrew's python3 (a home folder of its own, no login service). Then check that the real Claude Code obeys the settings phiward writes, which the scripts above cannot show. You run it yourself, in a terminal: it asks only for a token from claude setup-token, pasted at its prompt (or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=KEY), and builds the rest in a home folder of its own, with made-up data. It takes no token from the environment. An agent never runs it (it refuses without a terminal); an agent runs only sh scripts/sandbox-check/linux.sh --stub. It starts itself again under an empty environment first: only HOME, TMPDIR, TERM, your PATH (to find uv and claude; then it uses the system folders) and its own variables (SBX_, MODES, KEEP, REMOTE, CLAUDE_BIN) cross. The second start is clean: no variable, option or function of your shell acts on it. The first start is your shell's, and what it was given acts before the first line: under bash-as-sh, an exported SHELLOPTS=xtrace with a PS4 that holds $(...) runs that command. Run it with sh, not bash (bash check.sh reads BASH_ENV). claude and uv, found through your PATH, must pass phiward's rule (selfcheck.safe_path) before the token prompt. Its programs run with its own home as HOME, in its own folder. SBX_WHEEL with SBX_WHEEL_SHA256 installs a wheel you built beforehand instead of a build (see docs/hpc.md). uv's Python is found in ~/.local/share/uv/python; give its path as an argument if yours is elsewhere. - sh scripts/sandbox-check/check.sh on macOS, and on a real Linux machine with SBX_BASE set (Landlock ABI 2 or newer for the gateway). SBX_BASE holds the check's folders; it may not be under /tmp or the temp folder, nor your home folder itself, nor anywhere the settings phiward installs let the session write (the check refuses). A folder below your home folder is fine. The check refuses SBX_BASE when it or any folder above it, your home folder too, holds CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, AGENTS.md, .claude, .git, .mcp.json, .phiward.toml or .agent-guards.toml: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md and .claude/rules from every folder above the session's, and phiward the settings of every .claude or .git above it and its repository config, so your own would be read into the test. It looks again right before each session. Get the token first (claude setup-token may make ~/.claude again), then move them away while the check runs, or choose another folder. On macOS it is /Users/Shared by default; without that folder, set SBX_BASE to another folder outside those (for example one you make for it on a second volume). - SBX_TOOLS names a folder for socat, when the system has none (a cluster). It may hold socat and nothing else, so it cannot stand in for bwrap, git or sh. The check puts it on the session's PATH after its own bin folders, before the system folders. It must be an absolute folder outside SBX_BASE and outside what the session may write, and pass phiward's own rule for a PATH folder: it, its socat (and what a link leads to) and every folder above them (up to your home folder, when they are inside it) are yours or root's, and no group or other account can write them. Else the check refuses, before the build. - On a cluster, the check's folders go below your home folder, the one place no other account can write a folder above it (scratch and group folders are writable by others, so phiward's self-check refuses phiward installed there). The steps are in hpc.md, at its end. - sh scripts/sandbox-check/linux.sh on a machine with Docker: the same check in a Linux container, with the Claude Code version that scripts/sandbox-check/docker/package-lock.json pins (CLAUDE_VERSION=2.1.295 builds the lowest version phiward supports instead, unlocked). - Re-read "Permission mode on resume" in Claude Code's sessions docs. launch keeps transcripts on its word that a resumed bypass session starts in the mode a new one starts in. If a release restores bypass, launch must add --permission-mode default to a resume.

Each runs one claude -p session per mode (MODES, default A B; Mode B runs under phiward launch), and with Mode A one more short session, the bypass probe: started with --permission-mode bypassPermissions, it Reads the protected file, runs cat on it, then env > env.txt. phiward must refuse the Read (also by the deny rules install writes) and the cat. The token must be in neither the output nor the environment, the settings must not change, and no name may change in the data folder. The judge says ok, or BAD with one word (leaked, token, settings, wrote, hook-skipped: FAIL; facts, no-session, no-read, no-cat: INCONCLUSIVE). If it fails, the threat model must say that bypass skips the hook. Each session runs Haiku (or SBX_MODEL=sonnet, when Haiku declines the request) with a spending cap of $1 and a time limit. The session must be refused when it reads the protected file with the Read tool, and when a Bash command reads it, writes the data folder, ~/.phiward or ~/.claude/settings.json; phiward run from the session must mask its output, a commit of a made-up identifier must be refused by the git hook without showing it, the wrapped MCP server must start, and doctor must stay clean. For a write that worked, the report says whether the file reached the host (recorded right after each session). On Linux, in either mode, the sandbox may put an empty, writable view over a target it hides: a write that reaches nothing on the host is a note, not a failure, when the same session shows the target hidden: for the data folder, the read of the protected file found no such file, or not its content (an empty view); for ~/.phiward, a sentinel there is missing; for the settings, they read as empty. Without that, it fails. That evidence shows the target hidden; what stops a real write is the record, right after each session, of whether the probe file is on the host (for the settings, their hash before and after). When phiward run fails in the session for another reason, the report notes one word for why (for example no-broker or refused), its exit code and an error class (for example permission-denied or traceback). When no word fits (other), it also notes the first line of the output, with each word that holds anything but letters (a digit, a path, an ID, a sign) shown as <x>; no other text of the output is kept. In Mode A, Claude Code's own refusal of the Read ("denied by your permission settings": the deny rules install writes) counts as a refusal. The session also reads the environment of every process it can see in /proc, and records only counts and PIDs: a credential variable's name in any of them fails the mode, and the report says how many of those processes are the session's own ancestors. The names are the list in scripts/sandbox-check/token-names.txt, taken from Claude Code's docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars and the authentication page). CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN is not on it: Claude Code gives it to Bash commands on purpose, so the report only notes how many processes hold it. No value passes through the probe's shell or reaches a file, also under sh -x: each environment is read once. A list with a CRLF line or a line that is not a name is refused whole (scan-error). A scan that read no non-empty environment, whose read failed (scan-error), or whose /proc is not the session's own (foreign-proc) is INCONCLUSIVE. So is a probe line that appears twice in the results, and a session that made anything other than exactly one Bash call, sh ./probes.sh. It ends with a verdict per mode and an overall PASS, FAIL or INCONCLUSIVE. With REMOTE=HOST REMOTE_DIR=/abs/new/empty/folder (on a real machine), it also pushes, runs, and pulls through your shared connection, which you start when it asks; it writes only under REMOTE_DIR and deletes nothing there: remove that folder yourself afterwards. --stub (a stand-in claude, no token) checks the plumbing only, and runs only in the container (linux.sh --stub): elsewhere check.sh --stub refuses, as it would plant a git hook and a home folder on your machine. (That refusal looks for the container's marks, /.dockerenv or SBX_IMAGE: a tripwire, not a gate.) Paste the token when the check asks; do not export it. A token exported in your shell is not used (the check starts again without it), and only the claude process gets the pasted one. /proc still keeps the start environment of your shell and of the check's first start, which the session's scan can see: such a run may FAIL for them, and the check warns. The check's home folder and its judge's folder are removed at the end, also after Ctrl-C, SIGTERM or a closed terminal; if one cannot be removed, the check names it and exits non-zero. A kill -9 of check.sh or launch.py skips that: the session may keep running, and the folders stay (remove them yourself). Only the report and, per mode, the stream and the facts are kept, redacted in memory: with KEEP=1 in a folder of their own (phiward-sbx-kept-* next to it), and with linux.sh in its output folder. If the token's value is still in any of them, nothing is kept ("redaction failed: nothing kept"). A process the session starts in a session of its own (setsid) can outlive the check; its folders are removed all the same, so nothing it writes is kept. The stream reaches launch.py through a pipe, and launch.py writes it, after the session is stopped, into the judge's folder: next to the home folder, outside the folders the check gives the session. The check does not prove that the sandbox cannot write there; a process left running in a session of its own could, before the judge reads it. On Linux too the wrapped MCP server must start in Mode B: its launch inside the session runs it directly (the session's seccomp fingerprint). A server that does not start leaves the mode INCONCLUSIVE, as on macOS. What the session writes in its project folder (results.txt, server.out) a model could forge, line by line. The checks made outside the session are harder to forge: a probe's file on the host, the settings file's hash, the marker or the token in the stream, and the transcript's tool calls (with the limit above). Read a PASS with that in mind. Run the real check when phiward's Claude Code wiring (install.py, claude_settings.py, fasthook.py, mcp.py, wholetool.py) or the lowest Claude Code version it supports changed since the last release; otherwise skip it. Read Claude Code's sandboxing page again: phiward counts network.allowLocalBinding as opening the sandbox on macOS only, because the page says it has no effect on Linux (claude_settings.LOCAL_BINDING); and it gives every shell call the text check while excludedCommands is not empty, because the page says Claude Code matches its entries by the call's text. 4. Commit and tag: git flow release finish does both. Then push main, develop and the tag in one push (the workflow refuses a tag that is not on main):

git push origin main develop v0.2.0b2

The first release was tagged by hand on main (git tag -a v0.2.0b1 -m "phiward v0.2.0b1").

  1.
