The release workflow runs the whole test suite (macOS and Linux, Python 3.9 to 3.14), checks that the tag is on main, that it names the version in the three version files, that no install line (phiward==), /blob/v.../ link, plugin tag (#v), GitHub install (phiward@v), marketplace "ref" or status line in README.md, CHANGELOG.md, plugin/commands/setup.md or docs/*.md names another version, and that the newest CHANGELOG entry no longer says unreleased. It builds the wheel and the source archive, checks them (twine check --strict), installs the wheel and runs it. Only then does the publish job start; nothing waits for an approval, so push the tag only when the release is ready. Its actions are pinned by commit; update a pin by its release's commit, not a tag.
  2. After it is published, check the install line from a clean shell:
uv tool install --python-preference only-managed phiward==0.2.0b1
  1. Make the GitHub release from the tag, with the release notes.

A version on PyPI can be yanked but never replaced: a fix is a new version.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
This page says where phiward is going. The goal stays the same: keep protected health information (PHI) and other protected data out of what an AI coding agent sends to its model provider, and keep the agent useful for real research work.

The plan can change. What is built is in the CHANGELOG. What is not protected is in the threat model.

docs.title: How we choose
docs.text:
1. Protect first what typical use reaches.
  2. Remove the friction that makes someone turn a guard off.
  3. Give an institution the evidence it needs to approve agent use.
  4. Keep it small: take a mechanism away before you add one. Use the Python standard library only. When a check cannot decide, refuse.

docs.title: Next: 0.2.0, trust and evidence
docs.text:
• A full review of the threat model. Before 0.2.0, the threat model is reviewed end to end, and each limit is stated with what you can do about it.
  • A local decision log, on by default. It records each refusal and each gateway run: the date, the layer, the decision and the rule. It never records a path or a value, and the agent cannot reach it. If the log cannot be written, no decision changes.
  • A configuration report. phiward doctor writes a report that a machine can read, for an IRB or a security review. It lists the version, the mode, the layers that are on, the packs, the pinned programs, the network limit and the limits that apply.
  • A wider masking check. It also tests what the hook answers for a made-up path, and tests the network limit with one allowed host and one refused host.
  • Check results with each release. The release notes say which sandbox checks passed, and on which platform.
  • Pages for reviewers:
  • a page for IRB and compliance reviewers;
  • a note on what phiward is not (a BAA, an IRB approval or a data use agreement), and why you still need it when you have one;
  • a page on the usual rules HPC centres set for AI agents;
  • a page for your first week.
  • A host allow list for phiward launch. Launch's proxy uses the same [network] limit and allowed_domains as Mode A.
  • Tokens in the environment kept from the sandboxed shell, where Claude Code supports it.
  • The last typical refusals, each with a clear next step:
  • doctor says when the config changed since the broker started;
  • a write to a file that runs later gets a one-line answer;
  • "don't ask again" and similar answers can stay under launch;
  • a linked file that phiward should allow (from a dotfile manager, for example) works, or is refused with a step.
  • Small fixes to stated limits:
  • the hook-only gaps that have small fixes;
  • MODULEPATH and PYTHONPATH under launch;
  • a warning for Claude Code versions that do not protect project settings themselves.
  • Real machines: the full check on a recent Linux kernel, the hook on RHEL 8 clusters, and local macOS checks.

docs.title: Then: 0.3, research workflows
docs.text:
• A shorter loop for reviewed scripts. Today, each edit of an analysis script that runs on protected data takes four steps: read, move, pin and restart the broker. The goal is one reviewed step, with no restart. The review stays.
  • Pipelines and notebooks. phiward names the places where Nextflow and Snakemake write their logs, and the notebooks that keep saved outputs. The git hook checks notebook outputs. One page covers both workflows.
  • Output control:
  • small-count suppression in run --table, opt-in, with a threshold you choose;
  • a Safe Harbor pack, off by default;
  • a starter pack for common ID shapes;
  • flowcell and instrument IDs;
  • a measure of recall on a made-up corpus.
  • Lab rollout: one config for the whole lab, from a managed place, that can only tighten protection.
  • macOS profiles tested on a set of real research workloads.

docs.title: Later, or when asked
docs.text:
• other agent tools: Cursor first, then Codex and Gemini CLI;
  • masking the results of wrapped MCP servers, and a mode that keeps gateway output smaller;
  • an optional local detector that can only mask more, and is never a dependency;
  • network limits beyond the shell in Mode A (WebFetch, MCP servers);
  • a page on using WSL2 on Windows;
  • a new docs theme before MkDocs Material reaches its end of life.

docs.title: Setup reference
docs.text:
For: anyone who wants each setup step, option and limit explained; upgrades; removal.

The quick start is the short way. This page explains each step, its options and its limits, in the same order. Run the steps in your own Terminal. The guided setup (/phiward:setup) lets the agent run the first-time steps for you, but only while no config exists (below).

  1. Check the requirements
  2. Install
  3. Write the user config with phiward setup
  4. Wire the agent tool
  5. Start the broker
  6. Pin the derived folders
  7. Check everything with phiward doctor
  8. Try it on made-up data
  9. Per repository: .phiward.toml and the git hooks

Later: change the setup, upgrade from agent-guards, remove phiward.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.9 or newer.
  • macOS: /usr/bin/sandbox-exec (part of macOS; Apple marks it as deprecated, Claude Code uses it too). On a Mac with an endpoint tool, your IT or security team may want the list of every process phiward starts: endpoint-security.md.
  • Linux:
  • bubblewrap (bwrap) on the PATH;
  • Landlock ABI 2 or newer in the kernel (Linux 5.19 or newer, with Landlock turned on). The gateway uses it as a second layer for its writes and refuses to run without it;
  • for phiward launch --tool claude before Linux 7.1: socat, and Claude Code's native build, which carries its seccomp filter; launch refuses to start without a filter that works (launch.md);
  • on Ubuntu 24.04, AppArmor can block unprivileged user namespaces (kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns). Then bubblewrap cannot start. Change the setting, or add an AppArmor profile for bwrap. doctor says when this is the cause.
  • Native Windows has no confinement. Use WSL 2, which is Linux.
  • For Claude Code: version 2.1.295 or newer (it needs onFailure on hooks); 2.1.299 or newer for @ mentions off (doctor warns below it). On Linux, Claude Code's own sandbox (Mode A) also needs bubblewrap and socat; install sets failIfUnavailable, so without them Claude Code stops at start instead of running commands unsandboxed. doctor checks both.

Without a working confinement backend, the broker refuses to run anything. It fails closed.

docs.title: 2. Install
docs.text:
Install a release from PyPI with uv (to get uv itself: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh, or brew install uv):

uv tool install --python-preference only-managed phiward==0.2.0b1

Or with pipx:

pipx install phiward==0.2.0b1

Name the version: a beta is not chosen without it. The same release from its GitHub tag, without PyPI: uv tool install git+https://github.com/msk-access/phiward@v0.2.0b1. Pin a version or a tag; do not install a branch. Use uv tool or pipx: they give phiward a Python folder of its own. phiward protects the folder of the Python that runs it (the agent may not write there, or it could change what the broker runs), so an install into a shared environment (a conda base, a project's .venv) would make that whole environment read-only for the agent. They also keep the launcher at one path across upgrades (~/.local/share/uv/tools/phiward/bin/phiward, pipx's folder, for example ~/.local/share/pipx/venvs/phiward/bin/phiward), which phiward mcp wrap writes into each entry; an install whose path holds the version (phiward in a Homebrew Python's own site folder) would need wrap again after each upgrade. Check the install:

phiward --help

docs.title: 3. The user config: phiward setup
docs.text:
setup first asks how you will use phiward:

  1. Real patient data (the default): you give your protected folders; it suggests a results folder inside the first one (the one write place, so no --write-to is needed), sets the program list to @genomics plus an optional folder of your own scripts, gives gateway commands no network, asks whether shell commands may reach only hosts you list ([network]; yes is suggested; with yes, git push and pip install fail until you list their hosts), and asks about HPC.
  2. Made-up data: your folders and a results folder; any program may run.

Every profile also asks which rules mask subject and sample identifiers (Question 8). 3. Every setting: the questions below, one by one.

phiward setup --from team.toml starts from a team template (a config file with shared settings); its settings fill in what your config does not have, and lists are joined with yours. A template may set only shared settings: the program list (by name or @ list, not by path), built-in packs, HPC host names and the programs allowed there, cluster folders to mask, patterns, and limits (only lower than the defaults). It may never set a write place, the network, a copy remote, an ssh config, names files, pack files or environment. One kept in a project (a folder with .git, .claude or .phiward.toml above it) is refused. setup shows every setting in it and asks before it uses them. At the end setup writes the file after your yes, makes the results folder and phiward's ssh config, approves the programs, wires Claude Code, and installs or restarts the broker service (each with a yes; see the end of the dialogue).

The user config holds the facts of your machine: which folders are protected, and what gateway commands may do. Once step 4 is done, the agent's shell cannot write it, and the hook refuses the agent's file tools for its usual spelling (not for every spelling: known gap 2). Write it with:

phiward setup

Each answer is checked as phiward checks the file later; a refused answer is asked again, with the reason. Nothing is written until you say yes at the end. It writes ~/.config/phiward/config.toml (or the file that $PHIWARD_CONFIG names; see configuration.md) with mode 0600, and keeps the old file as config.toml.bak (each run replaces the .bak file, so copy it away if you want to keep an older one).

Once a config exists, setup is yours only: it refuses to run without a terminal, and the hook refuses it as an agent command. These two checks are a convenience, not a boundary: a program can fake a terminal. What stops an agent is that Claude Code's sandbox (or launch) denies writes to the config, ~/.phiward and the service file. If an agent shows you phiward setup as a command to approve, refuse it.

docs.title: The guided first run
docs.text:
We recommend that you run phiward setup yourself, as above. The guided setup (/phiward:setup) recommends it too, and gives you the commands.

It can also let the agent write the first config: phiward setup --first-run --root PATH [--root PATH ...] [--remote host:/path ...], with the paths that you type in chat. This works only while no config exists. It writes protected roots and copy remotes only (each remote's folder also as a [remote] root, so a push can land there), never a grant (no write places, no network). It refuses a PHIWARD_CONFIG, PHIWARD_SPOOL or XDG_* override without a terminal.

When to use it, and what you trust. Before your config exists, nothing protects the agent's choices: you trust the agent, in that session, to write exactly what you said, and to install the broker service and the wiring as they should be. Use it only in a new session that has not read web pages, other people's files or repositories you do not know. Then check what it wrote: phiward doctor --show-paths, in your own Terminal, lists the roots. These limits hold on both paths: - a root that is your home folder or above it, in a dot-folder of your home folder, in ~/Library or in a PATH folder stays protected, but gateway commands cannot write in it (your own tools load code from there); - a copy remote must name a work folder: not /, a folder just below it, a home folder, or a dot-folder; - the broker service skips PATH folders inside a project, and folders the agent's sandbox may write (a temp folder, also inside your home folder, the spool, an allowWrite folder of your own or the managed settings).

The agent-run setup takes KRB5CCNAME and the other Kerberos variables from its session, as your own shell names them. If your ticket cache is in a place other than the default ones, run the setup yourself.

docs.title: Question 1: protected roots
docs.text:
Folders that hold protected data. Give each one as an absolute path or with ~/, one per line, and an empty line to end the list.

  • Give the folder that holds the data, not a folder above it. A root cannot be /, your home folder, or a folder above your home folder (the agent could not work at all). setup refuses these; the loader refuses only /, so take care when you edit the file by hand.
  • A root cannot hold a phiward file or folder (for example ~/.config, which holds the user config). setup refuses such a root.
  • Each root must exist; setup refuses a missing one. Claude Code's sandbox hides a root only when it exists as a command starts.
  • Prefer the real path. A root reached through a link is protected, but gateway commands cannot write to it (doctor says so).
  • Keep protected data outside the git repositories that the agent works in. The .git folder of a work tree that holds a root is protected too, so the agent cannot use git there.

docs.title: Question 2: protected patterns (optional)
docs.text: Glob patterns, such as /data/runs/*/panel, for protected places that are spread out. * is the only wildcard, and only printable ASCII is accepted (see configuration.md). Prefer roots: Claude Code's sandbox cannot take patterns, so on Linux its shell does not count as confined while patterns are set, and the hook then refuses shell commands other than gateway calls (see configuration.md). The gateway and phiward launch still enforce patterns.

docs.title: Question 3: write places ([broker] write_to)
docs.text:
Folders where phiward run --write-to DIR may write. DIR must be one of these folders or a folder inside one. Use this for result folders, for example ~/projects/study-a/results.

  • Each folder must exist, and you must give its real path (no link on the way). It must not hold a .claude folder: choose a results folder, not a project folder. (A .claude folder made there later makes phiward skip the entry.) setup shows the real path when you give a link.
  • A write place cannot be /, your home folder or above it, in a dot-folder of your home folder (~/.ssh, ~/.config), in ~/Library or a PATH folder, above a protected root, in a derived protected folder or a pattern match, hold a names or pack file of the config, or hold or be inside a phiward file or folder. It may sit inside a protected root: what is written there stays protected.
  • Gateway commands write only in their own scratch folder and in these places: protected roots are read only for them. So a workflow that writes results next to protected data needs a write place inside that root, for example ~/data/patients/derived.
  • Each write place gives code that the agent chooses a place to put what it read. To keep the gateway as closed as possible, keep this list short.

docs.title: Question 4: programs ([broker] commands)
docs.text: The programs gateway commands may run. Empty means any program: then code the agent writes can run on protected data. For real data, list them: @genomics or @counts (built-in lists), program names, your own scripts by full path, or a folder of your scripts as a path ending in /. Interpreters and shells (python3, bash) run any code: list your scripts instead. Choice 1 sets @genomics and asks for a folder of your own scripts; how a script gets there is in daily-use.md.

docs.title: Question 5: network for gateway commands ([broker] net)
docs.text: With yes, phiward run --net gets the network. Code that reads protected data could then send it anywhere. The default and the recommendation is no. phiward copy to a configured remote gets the network for that copy without this setting.

docs.title: Question 6: copy remotes ([copy] remotes)
docs.text:
Places on other machines that phiward copy may copy to or from, as host:/absolute/prefix (through your shared SSH connection: hpc.md). For example cluster:/data/work/study-a. Leave the list empty if you do not copy to another machine. Each remote is a place where protected data may go.

A remote copy does not read ~/.ssh/config (the agent may be able to write it). It reads phiward's own ssh config ([copy] ssh_config), which the HPC questions below write for you; or write a small one yourself and set [copy] ssh_config by hand (configuration.md).

docs.title: Question 7: network for shell commands ([network])
docs.text: With yes, the shell commands an agent runs in Claude Code reach only the hosts you list (Claude Code's own sandbox enforces it). Commands that need the network fail until their hosts are listed: git push needs github.com (or your git server), pip install needs *.pypi.org and files.pythonhosted.org. Claude Code itself, WebFetch and MCP servers are not limited by it. Each listed host is a way out, so list few. Choice 1 asks this too, with yes suggested.

docs.title: Question 8: subject and sample identifiers ([sanitize])
docs.text:
The gateway masks the names of files and folders under your protected roots, and the genomics pack masks sequence file names, read names and loci. A patient, sample or donor ID inside a file, or in a name outside the roots, is masked only by a rule for its form. Choose:

  1. Your data holds no such IDs beyond the names under the roots: setup records subjects = "none". This is never the default: type 1 each time.
  2. The msk pack: one institution's forms. It is an example; copy it for another institution.
  3. Your own rules, one per line ([sanitize] patterns), each checked as you type it.

Every profile asks this (in choice 3 it is numbered 8). Setup keeps genomics in any pack list it writes, also on a re-run over a list you wrote without it. Until one of these is set, phiward doctor warns.

docs.title: The HPC questions
docs.text: Choices 1 and 3 then ask whether you work with an HPC cluster. With yes, they ask for its short name, its login host, your user name and work folder there, and the cluster folders to mask. setup adds the work folder to the copy remotes, writes phiward's ssh config and prints the lines to add to your own ~/.ssh/config (hpc.md).

docs.title: The end of the dialogue
docs.text:
1. setup shows the whole new file and the difference from the old one, and asks whether to write it.
  2. It pins the derived folders (step 6).
  3. When a program is new or changed, it lists the programs of [broker] commands as they are now, each with its path, and the count ("N found, M not installed here"). Then it asks "Approve these N program(s) as they are now?" The broker runs only approved programs.
  4. The default is Yes on a first run (nothing approved before) with nothing marked.
  5. The default is No when you approved programs before, when a program is marked (changed), or when a program in your home folder shadows a system program of the same name (marked (shadows /usr/bin/NAME)). Read those lines before you say yes.
  6. With No, the broker refuses every gateway request while a listed program is not approved, until you run phiward pin and restart it.
  7. A program not installed here is approved when you run phiward pin from a terminal where it is found.
  8. It asks whether to wire Claude Code for every session (step 4). One yes is enough: it shows the change and writes it.
  9. It asks whether to start the broker at every login, or restart it (step 5).
  10. It prints the next steps: what you did not say yes to, then phiward doctor in a project folder.

setup keeps the other sections of an existing file ([git], unresolved) and the other [sanitize] keys; it writes [sanitize] subjects, packs or patterns from Question 8. It does not keep comments; the .bak file of this run has them. To set those other keys, edit the file by hand; see configuration.md.

docs.title: 4. Wire the agent tool
docs.text:
There are two modes (modes.md). Mode A, a normal Claude Code session (the desktop app, an IDE, a terminal), is what this section wires; it is the usual way for day-to-day work. Mode B, phiward launch --tool claude, runs the whole tool inside phiward's kernel profile and needs no wiring (launch.md).

Wire your user settings, so every session in every folder is protected. Project wiring alone protects only sessions opened in that folder. The Claude Code plugin (plugins.md) can add the skill, the commands and a second check; keep these user hooks with it. --no-hooks writes only the sandbox and permission settings (for a project whose contributors have user wiring).

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
setup offers to do this. To do it yourself, first look at what will change:

(cd ~ && phiward install claude --user)

This prints a few // comment lines and then the JSON block for ~/.claude/settings.json (a long one: it lists every protected path and credential twice, as sandbox entries and as permission rules). It writes nothing. Then merge it:

(cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write)

It shows a diff and asks for your yes. It keeps a backup (settings.json.phiward.bak). --project writes the project's .claude/settings.json with only what is the same for every contributor (it can be committed) and puts the personal part into .claude/settings.local.json (do not commit it).

Notes:

  • Run setup and broker --service from your home folder (cd ~). They take the folder they run in for a project, and leave its PATH folders (a .venv/bin) out of the broker's PATH. install --user reads only your user config, wherever it runs; install --project also reads the project's .phiward.toml.
  • install --user writes settings.json where Claude Code reads it: in $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR when you set that variable, else in ~/.claude (the file doctor reads too).
  • install only adds entries. When you remove a root from the config, remove it from denyRead and denyWrite by hand.
  • Without a terminal, install --write refuses unless --yes is given. The guided first run gives --yes, before your config exists. After that, do not give --yes to an agent: read the diff yourself.

The block has five parts.

  1. One PreToolUse hook entry with the matcher * (every tool). It sets "onFailure": "block": without it, Claude Code lets a tool call go on when the hook fails. The hook runs from files in phiward's package, with no inline code (Claude Code's exec form, command and args): "command": "<package>/phiward/data/clean-exec.sh", "args": ["/path/to/python", "-I", "-m", "phiward", "hook", "claude"]. The script unsets every PYTHON*, LD_* and DYLD_* variable (a project's settings could set them to load other code; the list is clean-env.awk beside it, run by /usr/bin/awk; if awk cannot list them, the hook refuses every call), then phiward's own Python runs isolated (-I: no user site folder). Each failure blocks the call: a script that is not there cannot start (onFailure: "block"), and a Python that is not there, or a start without the arguments (a Claude Code that ignores args), exits 2. Before it writes, install checks that this Python finds phiward with -I (an install in the user site folder is not seen there) and that /usr/bin/awk exists. The plugin runs its own copy of the script with phiward by name; install --project runs phiward by name after the same unset, in one /bin/sh line (a committed file names no path of this machine). A project's env.PATH would choose that phiward, so the hook refuses every call while a project sets it, and you should wire your user settings too. install replaces every earlier form of its own hook entries (.../bin/phiward hook claude, ... -I -m phiward ..., the one /bin/sh line an earlier release wrote) in place.

After an upgrade that moves phiward's Python (uv tool upgrade --python ..., or another Python version), the script's path in the settings is gone, and every tool call is refused until you run (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write) again. doctor names the cause. 2. A SessionStart hook (phiward session-note claude): every session starts with a short note on the rules (the gateway is the intended route). It names no protected path. 3. A UserPromptSubmit hook (phiward prompt-scan claude, "onFailure": "block", the same command form as the first). It checks each prompt before Claude Code sends it. A prompt that the sanitizer would change is not sent: a match of the user config's packs or [sanitize] patterns, or a path below a protected root. The message names the kind, never the value. What it does not see: threat-model.md. 4. permissions.deny: Read(...) and Edit(...) rules for every protected root and every entry of the hidden list (credentials, tickets, histories). They are a second check on the file tools, inside Claude Code. 5. The sandbox block (shortened here; the real one also lists the hidden list):

{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "failIfUnavailable": true,
    "allowUnsandboxedCommands": false,
    "filesystem": {
      "denyRead": ["/data/patients", "/Users/me/.cache/phiward"],
      "denyWrite": ["/data/patients", "/Users/me/.cache/phiward",
                    "/Users/me/.config/phiward/config.toml", "/Users/me/.config/phiward",
                    "/path/to/site-packages/phiward", "/Users/me/.phiward/broker.json",
                    "/Users/me/.local/share/uv/tools/phiward",
                    "/Users/me/.local/bin/phiward",
                    "/Users/me/.local/lib/python3.12/site-packages"],
      "allowWrite": ["/Users/me/.phiward-spool"]
    }
  }
}
Setting Why sandbox.enabled: true Claude Code runs shell commands in its sandbox. failIfUnavailable: true Claude Code does not start when its sandbox cannot (on Linux it needs bubblewrap and socat). Without it, commands would run unsandboxed. allowUnsandboxedCommands: false The model cannot retry a command outside the sandbox. denyRead Every protected root and the derived folders (the cache folder, the .git of a work tree that holds a root). denyWrite The same roots, the phiward config and code, the broker's status file, the Python folder that runs phiward, the phiward launcher, the user site folder, and [copy] ssh_config when set. An agent that can change these can turn the guard off or change what the broker runs. Run install again after you set ssh_config. allowWrite The broker's spool folder: a gateway call is a client in the sandbox that writes its request there.

Patterns ([protected_paths] patterns): with Claude Code 2.1.236 or newer, install --user also adds each pattern and pattern/** to denyRead, and on macOS to denyWrite. On macOS the shell can then count as confined with patterns. On Linux the sandbox cannot deny writes to a wildcard path, so the entries are an extra layer, the shell does not count as confined, and the hook refuses shell commands other than gateway calls. Protect plain folders (roots) on Linux.

The --settings file. install --user --write also writes ~/.config/phiward/claude-settings.json, which sets sandbox.enabled, failIfUnavailable and allowUnsandboxedCommands: false, and turns @ mentions off (below). Start Claude Code with claude --settings ~/.config/phiward/claude-settings.json (an alias in your shell startup file does it): a false given with --settings makes the sandbox admin-required, as managed settings would, so a repository's .claude/settings.json cannot turn the sandbox off, add excluded commands or writable folders, or re-open a folder you deny (Claude Code's sandboxing page, "Repository settings under an admin-required sandbox"). The file and its folder are guard files. doctor checks the file, but cannot tell whether a session was started with it, and the hook does not rely on it: it keeps checking the user and project settings itself.

After an upgrade, run (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write) again. A new phiward can add guard files; until the sandbox's denyWrite covers them, the shell does not count as confined and the hook refuses shell commands (doctor says so).

The shell is pinned to bash. install --user sets env.CLAUDE_CODE_SHELL to /bin/bash: the hook reads commands as bash does. A project's settings that set CLAUDE_CODE_SHELL or CLAUDE_CODE_SHELL_PREFIX make the hook refuse every call (a project's value wins over yours in Claude Code).

@ mentions are turned off. install --user sets env.CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FILE_MENTIONS to 1 (also in the --settings file). Why: with mentions on, @path in a prompt puts the file's text into the prompt without a tool call phiward's hook sees. With them off, Claude Code passes the path and the agent reads the file with Read, which the hook and the deny rules judge like any read. The cost: @ completion of files no longer inserts their contents; the agent reads them with one more tool call. Claude Code ignores the setting in a project's settings, so install --project does not write it, and it needs Claude Code v2.1.299 or later (older ones do not know it). doctor reports a missing or different value, and a Claude Code older than v2.1.299. It does not cover what an IDE adds to the prompt (the open file and the selection): set claudeCode.attachSelection and claudeCode.attachOpenFile to false in the VS Code settings when protected files are open in the editor; doctor cannot see them. A session started by the Desktop app or a runner whose own environment sets the variable takes that value instead.

An older phiward offered --shell-prefix, which ran every shell command through its own kernel profile. It is gone: Claude Code's sandbox confines the shell. If you used it, run (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write) again; it removes the prefix setting (doctor warns while it is there, because every shell command would fail).

--block-outside-reads (optional, --user): sets permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories (Claude Code 2.1.257 or newer: Read, Grep and Glob refuse paths outside the working folders, in every permission mode) and permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting (2.1.319 or newer: a call that would wait on a prompt is refused). Each is written only when claude --version is new enough. They are defence in depth around the project, not a protected-path rule: phiward's own checks are the same with or without them. doctor shows which are on.

Bash stops asking. With the sandbox on, Claude Code runs sandboxed Bash commands without a permission prompt (its sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed, true by default): the sandbox takes the place of the prompt. deny rules and narrow ask rules such as Bash(git push *) still apply. To be asked for each command, set "autoAllowBashIfSandboxed": false in the sandbox block of ~/.claude/settings.json; phiward works the same either way.

The shell counts as confined only when all of these hold:

  • the settings in the table above are in force;
  • excludedCommands is empty. With an entry set, the hook does not refuse the whole shell: it checks the text of every command, as with [shell] best_effort, because Claude Code decides by its own matcher which calls run outside the sandbox. A command that names protected data, or that builds a path the guard cannot see ($(...), a variable it does not know), is refused, and the refusal names the file that holds the entry; the rest run. ls, pytest and git status pass. phiward doctor says so;
  • network.allowAllUnixSockets is not true, and network.allowUnixSockets is empty (a socket such as Docker's reaches a process outside the sandbox);
  • no other project settings file that Claude Code may read turns part of the sandbox off;
  • none of these is set, because each lets a command reach past the sandbox: filesystem.disabled, enableWeakerNestedSandbox, allowAppleEvents, allowNestedUserNamespaces, network.allowMachLookup, and on macOS only network.allowLocalBinding (there a sandboxed command can reach every service on localhost; on Linux the key has no effect, so it is not counted). Run a dev server in your own terminal, or list its folder in [no_phi] folders (below);
  • no allowRead entry re-opens a root;
  • no protected patterns are configured.

No PHI here. For a folder you are sure holds no PHI (a website, a tool's code), list it in your user config:

[no_phi]
folders = ["/Users/me/code/website"]   # exact folders; not their subfolders

A session whose project is that folder then gets the text check of [shell] best_effort for Bash, in place of the refusal, when only sandbox openers leave the shell unconfined (not filesystem.disabled, and not a root missing from denyRead). Protected roots are still denied, and prompts, the project and files that run later are still checked. The session's start message says the folder is relaxed (or why not), and phiward doctor lists the folders. Configuration has the rules, and the threat model the limits.

The hook reads the merged settings: managed settings and their managed-settings.d drop-ins, the project settings, and the user settings in $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR (or ~/.claude). The project settings are .claude/settings.json in $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR and the .claude/settings.local.json that Claude Code reads: at the git repository's root, or a worktree's main checkout (the project folder when there is no repository, the root is your home folder, or the root is not yours). A .git entry counts only as git counts it: an empty .git folder is passed over, and a worktree's .git file must be named back by its worktree entry. Only these files can make the shell count as confined. Every other settings.local.json Claude Code may read, and a project settings file that does not parse as JSON, can only make it count as not confined. Settings passed with --settings cannot be seen. While the shell is confined, the hook relaxes its text check for shell commands: the kernel guards them. The file tools stay guarded by the hook only (see the gaps of the hook alone).

The hook also refuses file-tool writes (Write, Edit) to the phiward config, code and status file, and to any .claude/settings.json, .claude/settings.local.json and the managed settings. The shell sandbox's denyWrite covers the phiward files for shell commands.

The strong form is managed settings. A repository can put "disableAllHooks": true or excludedCommands in its own .claude/settings.json. Managed settings (installed by an administrator; a repository cannot change them) with the same block prevent that. The file is /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json on macOS and /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json on Linux.

docs.title: Other tools
docs.text:
Only the Claude Code hook exists (phiward hook claude). It also reads the payload that GitHub Copilot sends when it runs hooks from .claude/settings.json.

For another tool, run the whole tool under phiward launch (Mode B, launch.md): its shell, file tools and MCP servers then run in phiward's kernel profile.

docs.title: 5. Start the broker
docs.text:
Open a terminal of its own, outside the agent tool, and run:

phiward broker

Keep it open while the agent works. For each request it prints three lines (its id with the subcommand, the command's exit code with its line counts, then the code it reported), never the output. Stop it with Ctrl-C. Only one broker runs at a time.

  • It builds each command's environment from its own variables only: PATH, HOME, USER, LOGNAME, LANG, LC_*, TZ and TERM. The program is found on your PATH, not on the agent's.
  • --max-jobs N sets how many commands run at the same time (default 4). At most 8 requests per job wait; past that, a request is refused as busy.
  • It keeps its spool folder at ~/.phiward-spool (or $PHIWARD_SPOOL), and its status file at ~/.phiward/broker.json. When the broker stops, it removes the status file.
  • It makes the spool folder with mode 0700. It refuses to start when the folder is a link, is not yours, or has another mode, and it stops when the folder is moved.

The broker must run in the same user account as the agent, with the same HOME, PHIWARD_CONFIG and XDG_* variables. doctor warns when they differ.

Or run it as a login service, so you do not keep a terminal open. You still decide that it runs; the agent cannot start, stop or change it (the service file is a guard file):

(cd ~ && phiward broker --service --write)

It writes a LaunchAgent (macOS) or a systemd user service (Linux) that starts the broker at login and again if it stops, with the PHIWARD_* and XDG_* variables of the terminal you run it in. Run in your own terminal, it then loads the service, or restarts it when it runs already (launchctl or systemctl --user); without a terminal it only prints those commands. It also prints the commands that remove it. Its log is in ~/Library/Logs/phiward (macOS) or ~/.local/state/phiward (Linux), which no session can read; phiward doctor shows whether it is running. The gateway is then available whenever you are logged in; every request is still checked against your config.

After an upgrade, restart the broker. A broker that still runs keeps the old code. Its status file names its phiward version. doctor warns when that differs from its own, or is missing (a broker older than this change writes none, and a status it cannot read counts as missing), and doctor --headless gives it as a reason it is not ready. Run (cd ~ && phiward broker --service --write) again, or stop phiward broker and start it again.

docs.title: 6. Pin the derived folders
docs.text:
phiward setup does this each time it writes the config. After the guided first run, or after you edit the config by hand, do it yourself (phiward doctor notes when they are not pinned). In your own terminal:

phiward pin

It records, now, the folders phiward protects without being told (the .git of a work tree that holds a root, snapshot folders next to a root, other mounts of the same data), so a file the agent plants later cannot hide them. It also lists the programs of [broker] commands as they are now, and approves them with the same yes. Then restart the broker, so it uses the new pins; pin ends by printing the command: (cd ~ && phiward broker --service --write).

docs.title: 7. Check with doctor
docs.text:
In the top folder of each project where the agent works (it reads .claude/ there):

phiward doctor

It prints, among others:

  • the config files in use, and the counts of roots, patterns and derived folders;
  • whether the confinement backend works here;
  • whether the sanitizer starts;
  • the grants: the number of write places (and the ones skipped, with why), network yes or no, the number of copy remotes;
  • whether the broker runs, and whether it uses the same config as this shell;
  • keys that a repo config set but may not set (they are ignored);
  • for Claude Code: each settings level, whether phiward is wired with onFailure: "block", and whether the sandbox confines the shell (and if not, why not).

One WARNING says that your user config enables no pack that masks subject or sample identifiers: add one with phiward setup (Question 8), or record [sanitize] subjects = "none". A repo's .phiward.toml cannot clear it.

Fix each line that starts with PROBLEM or WARNING (doctor exits with 0 even when there are WARNING lines). It also warns when the current folder is inside or above a protected path. Its section "launch (Mode B)" runs the start checks of phiward launch here, without starting anything. What each typical refusal means, and the way around it: refusals.md.

doctor shows the protected paths only as counts; add --show-paths to list them. It always names the files it reads, and a PROBLEM line can quote a path from the config. Run it in your own terminal when the paths are sensitive: when an agent runs it, the output reaches the model.

docs.title: 8. Try it on made-up data
docs.text:
Do this once, with a made-up folder, before the agent sees real data. Make a folder with a fake file, for example ~/phiward-trial/FAKE-PT-0001.txt holding FAKE-CONTENT, and add ~/phiward-trial as a root (run (cd ~ && phiward setup) again, and let it wire Claude Code again, so that the sandbox covers the new root). The broker must run (step 5). Then, in a project folder:

phiward run -- ls ~/phiward-trial

This must print <ENTRY> in place of the file name, a note that counts it, then run done: exit=0 ....

phiward run --net -- true

With net not set, this must print run refused: --net is not granted.

Then the real test, in the Claude Code desktop app: open a new session in a project folder, and ask the agent (1) to read ~/phiward-trial/FAKE-PT-0001.txt with its Read tool, (2) to run cat ~/phiward-trial/FAKE-PT-0001.txt, (3) to run phiward run -- wc -l ~/phiward-trial/FAKE-PT-0001.txt. The first two must be refused; the third must print a count with the name masked. Also ask it to edit a file and run a script in the project: those must work. Remove the trial root afterwards, from the config (with setup) and from denyRead and denyWrite in the Claude Code settings (by hand).

docs.title: .phiward.toml
docs.text: A repository can commit .phiward.toml. It can only add protection: more roots and patterns, built-in packs, protected branches, a stricter unresolved, a lower inventory_limit. It cannot grant anything: write_to, net, remotes, sanitize rules and pack files come from the user config only. A repo config or a template cannot set [sanitize] subjects, and a pack a repo config adds masks but does not clear doctor's warning about subject identifiers. A root that only a repo config adds is protected from the agent, but gateway commands cannot write to it. See configuration.md.

docs.title: Git hooks
docs.text:
phiward git-hook install

This writes pre-commit and pre-push hooks in the current repository (it refuses to replace a hook that is not its own, unless you add --force).

  • pre-commit refuses a staged file inside a protected path, and an added line or file name that holds an identifier.
  • pre-push refuses a push to a protected branch. It does nothing until you list branches in [git] protected_branches (by hand; setup does not ask).

They print only sanitized names, line numbers and placeholder words. A human can bypass them with --no-verify; an agent must not.

docs.title: Change the setup
docs.text:
Run (cd ~ && phiward setup) again. It starts from the current file: for each list it shows what is there and asks whether to start that list again. Or edit the file by hand and run phiward doctor. A bad file makes every guarded action refuse until you fix it.

After you add a root, wire the agent tool again ((cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write)), so that its sandbox lists it; doctor says when a root is not covered. After you remove a root, remove it from denyRead and denyWrite by hand (install only adds).

Restart the broker after every change. The broker takes a fingerprint of the config, the pins and the names and pack files the config names when it starts, and refuses requests when their content changes, until you restart it. Saving the same text again changes nothing. So a config that something else changes has no effect until you have read it. On macOS: launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/org.phiward.broker; on Linux: systemctl --user restart phiward-broker.service; or stop phiward broker and start it again.

docs.title: Upgrade from agent-guards 0.1.0
docs.text:
phiward was called agent-guards before 0.2.0b1.

  1. Uninstall agent-guards first (uv tool uninstall agent-guards, or pipx uninstall agent-guards): phiward also installs an agent-guards command, so the installer refuses while the old one is there. Then install phiward (step 2).
  2. Move your config: mv ~/.config/agent-guards ~/.config/phiward. In each repository, rename .agent-guards.toml to .phiward.toml. Until you do, phiward refuses, because the old files may protect paths.
  3. Wire Claude Code again: (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write). This replaces the old hook entries.
  4. Delete ~/.agent-guards (sessions cannot read it).

The command agent-guards stays as an alias of phiward during the beta.

docs.title: Remove phiward
docs.text:
1. Unwrap your MCP servers first: a wrapped entry names phiward's launcher, so it fails to start once phiward is gone. phiward mcp list names them; phiward mcp unwrap NAME for each.
  2. Remove the phiward entries from the agent tool's settings (the backup from install has the old file), and the alias claude='claude --settings ...' line if you added one.
  3. Stop the broker. If it runs as a login service: launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.phiward.broker.plist and remove that file (macOS), or systemctl --user disable --now phiward-broker.service and remove the unit (Linux).
  4. In each project where you ran phiward init: remove the git hooks from .git/hooks, the phiward section of AGENTS.md, and the phiward entries of .claude/settings.json and .claude/settings.local.json.
  5. Uninstall: uv tool uninstall phiward (or pipx uninstall phiward), and the plugin if you added it (/plugin uninstall phiward).
  6. Remove ~/.config/phiward, ~/.phiward, ~/.cache/phiward, ~/.phiward-spool and the broker's log (~/Library/Logs/phiward on macOS, ~/.local/state/phiward on Linux).

docs.title: Status
docs.text: phiward is a beta. This page lists what has been tested, on made-up data, and what has not been tested yet. It lists only results that passed. Each line names its source; the threat model's summary has the detail. Read the threat model before you rely on phiward for real data.

docs.title: Read this first
docs.text:
• On Linux, the real Claude Code has passed only in Docker. The maintainer's sandbox check has passed in Docker since 2026-11-22. No run on a real Linux machine has passed yet (threat model).
  • On RHEL 8 (kernel 4.18) the gateway cannot run. That kernel has no Landlock, and phiward run refuses to run without it. The hook and Claude Code's sandbox are meant to work there, but no run on RHEL 8 has passed yet (hpc.md).

docs.title: What passed
docs.text:
Platform What passed macOS Mode A: the real Claude Code desktop app, wired by install claude: reads of protected data and credentials refused, ssh to HPC failed, normal work unaffected. Mode A with the plugin only, in the desktop app: reads refused by the hook (no sandbox or permission rules without install). Mode B: the real Claude Code under phiward launch. A small stdio MCP server wrapped in phiward launch. HPC through the shared SSH connection, against a real cluster. The full test suite. Linux The maintainer's sandbox check with the real Claude Code, in Docker (since 2026-11-22). The full test suite, with bubblewrap. The published @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem 2.3.0, wrapped in phiward launch: it read ordinary files and could neither read nor list a protected folder.

Source: the threat model, "What was tested".

docs.title: Not tested yet
docs.text:
From the threat model, "Not tested":

  • the real Claude Code on a real Linux machine (it has passed only in Docker);
  • phiward launch driven from the app with Remote Control;
  • a published MCP server under launch on macOS (on Linux it was);
  • a protected folder on a mounted HPC volume;
  • [network] limit in a live Claude Code session (the settings it writes are tested; Claude Code enforces them);
  • other agent tools than Claude Code.

From other pages:

  • Claude Code's real sandbox is not tested by phiward's test suite: the suite never runs the real claude. The release check does, run by the operator. It does not cover MCP tools, WebFetch, IDEs on Linux, remote with use_shared_connection = false, RHEL 8, NFS home folders, sssd or Kerberos; and the first check after your own install is yours (threat model, known limits).
  • A plugin carried over into launch (such as ECC) is not tested yet (plugins.md).
  • Keychain-backed tokens under Mode B are not checked yet: prefer Mode A's test result for them (launch.md).
  • Keystroke injection (TIOCSTI) was confirmed under a profile like phiward's old one, and is not tested under Claude Code's own sandbox (gap 5).

docs.title: Threat model and limits
docs.text:
For: people who decide whether phiward is enough for their data.

This page says what is protected, against whom, and where the limits are.

docs.title: For reviewers: the summary
docs.text:
• What leaves the machine: what the agent tool sends to its model provider: your prompts, the files and output the agent reads, and the masked output of gateway commands. phiward keeps protected files, credentials and unmasked gateway output out of that.
  • The network reaches public hosts in both modes. phiward does not stop the agent from sending what it can read. It stops the agent from reading protected data. In Mode A, [network] limit lets the shell commands reach only listed hosts. Claude Code's own sandbox enforces it. The WebFetch tool, MCP servers and commands a project excludes from the sandbox stay open. In Mode B the tool has no direct outbound network: every connection goes through phiward's proxy, which allows only public addresses (not this machine, its link or private ranges, unless the user config lists a private range). Each host that can be reached is itself a way out (a push, a gist, a host behind a shared CDN).
  • Trusted: the operator, the operator's terminal, the user config, the broker, the operating system and its sandbox (Seatbelt on macOS; bubblewrap, seccomp and Landlock on Linux), and Claude Code's own sandbox and permission rules in Mode A.
  • Not trusted: the agent, everything it writes, and the code it runs.
  • Who it is built against: an honest user, and an agent that text it reads (prompt injection) can turn against the user. phiward is not built to stop a determined attacker who already runs code on the machine with the user's rights. Some routes such an attacker could use are stated as limits below.
  • Masking hides names and identifiers, not other content. Gateway commands should print counts and summaries, not records, and hide small counts (Small counts).
  • What stops what. The kernel is the strongest guard:
What the agent tries Mode A stops it with Mode B stops it with The main limit A shell command reads protected data or the hidden list the kernel: Claude Code's sandbox the kernel: phiward's profile other hard links and other mounts (the shell sandbox) A file tool (Read, Grep, Glob, Edit) reads them the hook and Claude Code's permission rules, not the kernel the kernel a spelling that both miss (Mode A) An MCP server or a hook of the tool reads them nothing, unless the server is wrapped in phiward launch -- the kernel not wrapped, they run with your rights (gaps of the hook alone) A gateway command prints protected data masking of names and identifiers the same other content, and a command written to leak (the gateway) It sends out what it can read nothing by default; [network] limit for shell commands only its proxy: public addresses only, not this machine's services each host that can be reached is itself a way out It uses credentials that are not files (the Keychain, tokens in the environment) nothing: a file list does not hide them Linux: the kernel keyrings are blocked; macOS: the Keychain stays reachable. Only a short list of environment variables is passed Mode A, Mode B
  • What was tested, on made-up data:
What Where Result Mode A: the real Claude Code desktop app, wired by install claude macOS reads of protected data and credentials refused (Read tool, cat, Monitor), ssh to HPC failed, normal work unaffected Mode A with the plugin only macOS, desktop app session note given, reads refused by the hook; no sandbox or permission rules without install Mode B: the real Claude Code under phiward launch macOS file tools and shell refused protected data; gateway output masked; skills and an MCP server carried over An MCP server wrapped in phiward launch: a small stdio server driven the way Claude Code drives one, and on Linux the published @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem 2.3.0 macOS, Linux works; refused protected data and credentials. Wrapped, the published server read ordinary files and could neither read nor list a protected folder; unwrapped, it read both HPC through the shared SSH connection macOS to a real cluster remote runs, push, pull, refused push of ~/.ssh, refusal without the connection A typical session replayed through phiward's own entry points (the session note, the prompt scan, the hook, the gateway, phiward mcp), with made-up values planted under a root, in the project and in pasted prompts; Mode A with a full and a default config, and under phiward launch (what it does not cover) macOS, Linux (launch: Linux) under the root: refused or masked (only placeholders left; --table keeps numbers outside identifier columns); in prompts: your identifiers blocked, entry names, file and read names and positions sent; in the project: sent in Mode A (the session note warns), refused at the start under phiward launch (the project scan). A pack file weakened, a pattern edited or a root removed in the config is found The maintainer's sandbox check with the real Claude Code (scripts/sandbox-check/linux.sh) Linux, in Docker passed, since 2026-11-22 The full test suite (over 1,000 tests) macOS; Linux (bubblewrap) passes
  • Not tested:
  • the real Claude Code on a real Linux machine (it has passed only in Docker);
  • phiward launch driven from the app with Remote Control;
  • a published MCP server under launch on macOS (on Linux it was);
  • a protected folder on a mounted HPC volume;
  • [network] limit in a live Claude Code session (the settings it writes are tested; Claude Code enforces them);
  • other agent tools than Claude Code;
  • the real Claude Code under launch with its network through phiward's proxy (the test suite checks the proxy and the profiles with made-up servers; the sandbox check with the real tool is the operator's).
  • Independent reviews: each part had adversarial reviews before this release, and each finding was fixed or is listed on this page as a limit.

docs.title: What is protected
docs.text: The asset is protected data (for example patient data, sample identifiers, file names under a protected folder). The leak path is tool output: everything an agent's tools print goes to the model provider. phiward keeps protected data out of that output. Its git hooks also keep protected files and identifiers out of commits, and pushes off protected branches. They work against a careless agent: a deliberate commit with --no-verify (or a changed core.hooksPath) skips them.

docs.title: Against whom: read this first
docs.text:
This release has two modes (modes.md), and they protect against different agents:

  • Mode B (phiward launch) is meant as a boundary against a hijacked agent, for what is on this machine. A hijacked agent is one under prompt injection that tries on purpose to get the data out. The whole tool, its file tools, MCP servers and hooks included, cannot read protected data or the hidden list. Its limits are in Mode B below.
  • Mode A (a Claude Code session wired by the hook) confines Bash with Claude Code's own sandbox. It refuses protected data and the hidden list to the file tools inside Claude Code (the hook and permission rules, not the kernel). It stops a careless agent and makes a deliberate one work hard. It is not a kernel boundary for the file tools, and hooks and MCP servers that are not wrapped run with your rights. See Mode A.
  • The hook alone (without Claude Code's sandbox or launch) guards against a careless agent only: the gaps of the hook alone.

In every mode, the agent works on protected data only through the gateway, and the gateway's masking hides names and identifiers, not other content.

The operator, the operator's terminal and the user config are trusted. The agent can run any command it likes in its own shell, write any file it can write, and choose what it asks the gateway to run.

docs.title: The shell sandbox: the strongest layer
docs.text:
The kernel confines the agent's shell. In Mode A it is Claude Code's sandbox, with the entries (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write) writes. In Mode B (phiward launch) it is phiward's own profile, for the whole tool. An agent shell command cannot read or write anything in a protected root (or, on macOS, a pattern match), the hidden list, or the phiward config, code or status file. Claude Code's sandbox also keeps its own settings files, .mcp.json, the project's .git/config and hooks, the working folder's own .vscode and .idea, and the shell startup files from being written. A nested .vscode or .idea (sub/.vscode/tasks.json) is not in that list: VS Code and JetBrains read one only when you open that subfolder as a workspace or project, and a rule for every depth would deny npm install and git pull in every project. The hook asks before a file tool writes one; a shell command can. Git's other control files are a known limit (see "Git's control files" below). Links, letter case, nested shells and child processes are covered for ASCII paths, because the kernel does the check. Exceptions (gaps 8, 9): other hard links to a protected file, other mounts of the same file system, and a root spelled /System/Volumes/Data/.... phiward does not confine the shell itself in Mode A. It checks that Claude Code's settings confine it (doctor), and the hook refuses shell commands when they do not.

It does not cover everything: the agent tool's own file tools (Read, Grep, Glob, Edit), its MCP servers and its hooks run outside the kernel profile, and a few path spellings and pattern forms are not enforced by the kernel. See the gaps of the hook alone.

docs.title: The gateway: a controlled opening
docs.text:
The gateway (phiward run, phiward copy) runs the command the agent asks for, with read access to the roots. What it can do besides is fixed by the user config:

Channel Default Opened by Output to the agent always, sanitized — Writes its private scratch folder only (protected roots are read only) [broker] write_to + --write-to (may sit inside a root); a copy's own destination Network none [broker] net = true + --net; a copy to a [copy] remotes entry Other processes none (see below) macOS: net = true also allows name lookups; unix sockets stay blocked Its environment the broker's allow list only —

The program runs from the broker's PATH, which keeps only folders the agent cannot write. A folder is dropped when it is relative, writable by others, inside a project, or a folder the agent's sandbox may write. Those are a temp folder (inside your home folder too), the spool, and the allowWrite and additionalDirectories folders of your own and the managed settings. The broker does not know a project's own settings. So a project whose settings open a PATH folder of yours to writes (allowWrite ~/bin) lets the agent put a program there, and a gateway call may run it (still confined, with its output sanitized). Keep tools out of folders a project opens.

On macOS the broker writes each request's profile to a new file in ~/.phiward/profiles (a random name, made only if no file has that name, mode 0600, read back before use) and runs /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f on it; the file is removed when the command ends. phiward launch writes the tool's profile there the same way and runs /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f FILE TOOL, with no program in between; the file is removed when the tool ends. No session can write that folder (Claude Code's sandbox denies ~/.phiward; under launch it is not a write place), and the hidden list keeps the session's shell, its file tools and every gateway command from reading it; under launch the tool's own profile denies reading it. A request is refused when ~/.phiward is a link, another account's, or writable by other accounts, or when profiles is a link or another account's; profiles is made 0700.

On macOS phiward puts no code in a local command line: no python -c, no sh -c of its own, no awk program and no sandbox-exec -p. Its hooks run files of the package (exec form), and the pull's extractor is a file too. Two exceptions: the command that ssh carries to the remote host, which runs there (a push's is a fixed sh -c script), and the project hook's fixed line (install --project). Words that the agent or the user chose (a gateway command, a wrapped server's command) keep their own shape. endpoint-security.md lists every process and its command line; tests/test_macos_processes.py records them and checks the list.

"Other processes" means: no clipboard, notifications, unix sockets, signals or views of other processes. macOS denies Mach services, and both macOS profiles also deny mounting file systems and creating launchd jobs; Linux uses seccomp, Landlock and new IPC and PID namespaces. For the agent tool under launch on Linux, unix sockets are limited as below says.

The sanitizer masks protected paths, entry names under the roots, and identifiers from the packs. Out of the box, only file names, read names and loci are masked inside file contents; phiward doctor warns until a pack or rule for subject identifiers is on, or subjects = "none" is recorded. This stops accidental leaks from ordinary tools (ls, find, error messages, tracebacks). It also covers a name that a tool writes with escapes: git's octal quoting (\303\274), JSON's and Python's \u00fc and \xfc, and a URL's %C3%BC. A line whose decoded form holds a name is withheld. It does not stop a command that is written to leak: base64, HTML entities, splitting a name into parts, or printing content that is not an identifier all get past it.

docs.title: Grants and the safe setting
docs.text:
A grant gives code that the agent chooses that capability. With a write place, that code can put what it read where something else may pick it up. With the network, it can send what it read anywhere. A copy remote is a place where protected data may go.

Protected roots are read only for the gateway. It writes only in its scratch folder, in the write_to folders you grant (which may sit inside a root), and at a copy's destination. A grant is refused where your own tools load code later (the home folder or above it, its dot-folders, ~/Library, PATH folders) and where it would hold a names or pack file. A copy remote must name a work folder. A copy never goes into a dot-folder. A push refuses a destination that is your home folder on the cluster or above it (checked there, by real path). A push never sends files that run at login (.bashrc, .ssh, .gitconfig, .envrc) or any dot-name at the top of its destination.

The broker takes the config it started with. It records a fingerprint of the user config, the pins, and the names and pack files the config names at start, and refuses every request after their content changes, until the operator restarts it. So a change that the agent manages to make does not take effect unseen. The repository config (.phiward.toml) is not part of it: it can only add protection. A request that starts just as the config changes may still use the new one.

Terminal checks are a convenience. setup, pin, pseudonymize and carryover add|accept|reset refuse to run without a terminal, but a program can fake one. What stops an agent from changing them is that Claude Code's sandbox (Mode A) or the kernel profile (Mode B) denies writes to the config, ~/.phiward and the service file, and hides ~/.phiward/backups (the pseudonymize keys) from every session and gateway command. A plugin-only session, with no sandbox, has only the hook.

To make the gateway itself as tight as it can be, set write_to empty, net false, remotes empty. Then the only way out of the gateway is its sanitized output, and the only leak through it is a command written to encode data on purpose. This does not make the hook alone safe against a hijacked agent: the file tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside the kernel profile (gaps 1–6).

docs.title: Why nothing asks at run time
docs.text: Earlier versions asked the operator to approve grants, first on the broker's terminal, then in a native dialog. Reviews showed that both are in reach of the agent's code. It runs in the same user session, so it can write to the terminal, draw a window over the dialog, or (on X11, or with Accessibility permission on macOS) send it input. Approving a command's words does not approve the code it loads (its scripts, .git/config), which the agent can write. So grants are now decided ahead of time, in the user config. The agent's shell cannot write it; the agent's file tools are refused by the hook for its usual spelling only (gap 2). phiward setup is a dialogue, but a first-time one, in the operator's own terminal. Its result is a file the operator reads before it is written.

docs.title: The hook: a first layer
docs.text:
The hook guards the file tools, which a shell sandbox does not cover, and checks shell command text. Where the shell is kernel-confined, the text check is relaxed for shell commands; that relaxation trusts Claude Code settings files that phiward does not itself deny (gap 17). For the file tools, the hook is the only guard, and it checks paths as text: that is enough for a careless agent, not for one that tries (see gaps 1 and 2 below).

Without the kernel, shell commands are refused; the text check is best effort. Where no kernel confines the shell (Claude Code's sandbox off or not there), the hook refuses its commands by default (configuration.md). Only with [shell] best_effort on does it check their text instead. Shell text cannot be read completely, so that check is a first layer: for real data, use the sandbox or phiward launch, where the kernel decides. What the text check does:

  • It refuses (by unresolved, deny by default) every word it cannot read whole:
  • a path built from $(...), backticks, a special parameter ($1, $_, ${1:-x}, $((...)), $[...]) or variables the command sets, joined to other text (ph$(echo i), X=../ph; Y=i/f; cat $X$Y);
  • a variable whose value is made over several steps (X+=, printf -v, read, mapfile, two assignments);
  • any $'...', and a ${NAME...} with a modifier (${HOME:-x});
  • cd -, popd, a cd to a folder built from variables, find -execdir, a cd word it does not read as a command, and $PWD after a cd in the line;
  • a .. after a folder that does not exist yet and, in a line that runs ln, any path through a name that does not exist yet (the line may make it a link);
  • a zsh or extglob group outside quotes, comments and heredocs, and text it cannot parse.
  • It follows the folder a command runs in: cd and pushd after a keyword or in a group or function (then cd d, { cd d; }), cd with no folder (~), and the folder options of git -C, make -C/--directory, tar -C and env -C/--chdir. A line of plain steps (;, &&) reads each step from the folder the steps before it left (cd build && cmake ..); any other line reads every step from every folder it names.
  • It reads shell code passed as text: the string after sh -c (and bash, zsh, dash, ksh), the words of eval, and the heredocs a shell reads.
  • It counts a dot glob (.*, .?) as .. too: bash before 5.2 expands it so.
  • It lets through, as ordinary text: $(...) and variables in the words of an echo or printf at the top of a line that defines no function and does not pipe their output on, $(pwd) and $PWD when the line does not change folder, and a cd to exactly one $(...). A for loop's variable is like any other variable the line sets.
  • It accepts, and only the sandbox stops: a path printed by a command (cat $(printf ...), cd "$(cmd)") or built by an interpreter (python -c, awk); a word that is exactly one $(...) is judged by the command inside it.
  • Not yet covered, so only the sandbox or launch stops them: commands run through another program (a wrapper in front of sh -c or ln), some ways of changing the folder a command runs in, recursive commands that follow links, names made by moving or copying, and shell code given on standard input. Closing them is planned.

In the sandbox all of these are the kernel's to stop. A path whose written form passes through a protected folder (../phi/x/../../repo) is refused in every mode, whether or not the names on the way exist.

A wildcard gets one verdict, whatever a protected folder holds. Who stops a read decides what the hook does with a glob:

  • A shell in Claude Code's sandbox: the kernel stops a read of a protected path or a credential, so the hook decides from the pattern alone, against your roots and patterns, and never lists the disk. cat /data/p*/G* and cat /data/p*/F* are both refused; cat lea* (a link the agent made to protected data) is allowed by the hook and refused by the kernel.
  • A shell without the sandbox, and the file tools: the hook is the guard. It decides from the pattern against your roots, patterns and the hidden list (* names dot entries too), then walks where the glob can go and checks every link a glob part matches: its target, then the rest of the glob from there. A link to a folder is followed, as the shell follows it. A literal part is looked up by name (a folder that cannot be listed hides nothing); names are compared in every case and Unicode form; a file or folder that is a root under another name (a mount, a hard link) counts. No folder that is, or can lead the glob into, a protected path is listed. Under **, a link into a protected folder refuses the glob (the shell would walk into it only if it is a folder, and only the protected folder knows that). More than 200 000 names listed (each folder counted once) and entries looked at, or .. after a wildcard, are refused with their own reason; nothing is cut short. In the sandbox, .. after a wildcard is read as text over the whole path (repo/*/../../phi is phi). Bracket classes and ? count as any text (a superset); . parts are dropped as the shell drops them. A file tool's glob is also read with its braces expanded, backslashes dropped and extglob groups (@(a), !(a), (a|b), nested ones too) as *; a group that spans folders ((a/b|c)) is refused.

A project's settings can run code before phiward starts. Claude Code applies a project's env to hooks, and starts a hook's command with sh -c. A project's settings can add hooks of their own, and its env can make that shell run code (SHELLOPTS=xtrace with a PS4 that holds $(...)), before phiward runs. So phiward cannot guard against project settings it did not write. The guard keeps the agent from writing them (.claude/settings*.json and .mcp.json, by the hook outside the sandbox and by the sandbox inside it). You trust the project settings you bring in (gap 17).

What Claude Code runs as code, and where the file tools write (Mode A). The hook sees every tool (its matcher is *; about 85 ms per call). Claude Code's built-in tools that only carry text (Agent, Task, TodoWrite, AskUserQuestion, plan mode, SendMessage, ToolSearch) are not text-checked: a subagent's own tool calls reach the hook. For a write, in this order: 1. Refused in every mode, by every writer the hook sees: phiward's own files, the shell's start-up files, every Claude Code settings file and .mcp.json, anything inside a .git folder and any file named .git, ~/.gitconfig and ~/.config/git/, and a phiward in any PATH folder. Why .git: git runs what its config, hooks and commondir name, and Claude Code runs git outside its sandbox. A writer the hook sees is a file tool, or an MCP server's tool that names the file itself. The hook does not see a bare server's tool that moves a whole folder above one. A bare server runs with your rights anyway: wrap it. 2. Asked or refused: what Claude Code runs as code, and what an editor or a tool runs. Claude Code's code is skills, subagents, commands, hooks, workflows, plugins, routines, launch.json and scheduled_tasks.json, under any .claude folder but its worktrees, and under the user config folder. An editor's or a tool's is any .vscode, .idea, .cursor, .gemini or .codex folder, .gitmodules, .ripgreprc, .Rprofile, .Renviron. The hook asks you in the modes known to prompt (default, acceptEdits, plan). It refuses in every other (bypassPermissions, dontAsk, auto, a missing mode). A skill or subagent may hold hooks that run with your rights: allow it only after reading it. 3. A file tool's write outside the folders the sandbox lets the shell write (the project, the temp folder, allowWrite, additionalDirectories) and Claude Code's memory and plans folders: asked or refused, as in 2. To stop the prompts for a folder, add it to permissions.additionalDirectories in your user settings.

The app's own tools that start the project's code are asked or refused as in 2. They are the preview, the simulator's build and its launch action, and changing the session's folder. The preview's preview_start runs the command .claude/launch.json names. In a check in the desktop app it ran outside the sandbox, although the project turned the sandbox on. Tools that name a folder by a path field and are not MCP tools (Copilot's list_dir, file_search), and the app's browsers with a file: URL, are also judged as a search: a folder above protected data is refused. Not covered: a script the browser runs in a page (javascript_tool, execute_javascript). It can open a file: URL it builds itself; its text is checked only. The app's browser reads with your rights: keep it out of protected work.

A shell command in the sandbox meets Claude Code's own rules: from version 2.1.318 its sandbox denies writes to the working folder's settings, skills and hooks and the user folder's code folders. Not covered: a .claude folder below the working folder, folders added with /add-dir, and older versions. A script that a settings file names (a hook, statusLine, apiKeyHelper) runs too: keep it in your user folder's hooks/ (~/.claude/hooks/), which no session in a project writes; phiward doctor names one that a session can write.

A Claude config folder is known by what it is. It is the .claude of every folder above the file written and above the project, where it really leads (a link, also one whose target is not made yet). Its settings and code places count where they really lead (skills -> ../shared/skills, a stow-managed ~/.claude). From those code folders one list of code roots is built for each call. The file tools and MCP tools meet it, and doctor. The list holds: - every link inside the code folders, followed until nothing new turns up (a skill, an agent or a command linked in one at a time, and links inside those); - the plugin folders that CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR and CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR name. In plugins, links are followed only to where an install is (marketplaces/NAME, cache/MARKETPLACE/PLUGIN/VERSION): a link deeper in a plugin is its own, in a folder the agent cannot write; - a linked tree past 50,000 entries as a whole; its deep links are not followed (doctor names it); - no link to / or to a folder that holds your home folder (it would hold every write). doctor names it too.

A write in a root or below it is asked or refused (as 2 above). The shell is not held by this list: Claude Code's sandbox denies the real path of its own code folders only. So a skill linked in from a folder a session can write (the project, the temp folder) can be changed by that session's shell. doctor names each such link with its one step (replace the link with a copy). Not seen: a .claude link below the working folder that is off the path to the file written, a folder added with --plugin-dir, and a directory marketplace's own folder (Claude Code copies from it into its cache). A file tool's write to a file with another name (a hard link, nlink > 1) is asked or refused, since that name may be a code file. This check is for the built-in file tools only: an MCP server's tool is not checked for it.

What phiward does with a project's env:

  • Its hooks start a shell script from phiward's package (the user wiring and the plugin, in exec form: no inline code), or /bin/sh by absolute path (install --project). They unset the variables that make Python or a library load other code or read a file they name. These are: every PYTHON*, LD_*, DYLD_*, OPENSSL_*, MALLOC_* and macOS Malloc* variable; __PYVENV_LAUNCHER__ (macOS framework, conda and Homebrew Pythons read it even with -I); GCONV_PATH, LOCPATH, NLSPATH, GLIBC_TUNABLES, HOSTALIASES, LOCALDOMAIN, RES_OPTIONS, RESOLV_HOST_CONF, NIS_PATH, TZDIR and GETCONF_DIR; and a TZ that names a file (/..., :/...; a zone name stays). /bin/sh and awk read the loader's and allocator's variables and GCONV_PATH/LOCPATH before they are unset; doctor notes a project that sets them. A phiward whose Python needs PYTHONPATH or LD_LIBRARY_PATH cannot start after the clean-up, so every call is refused; doctor says so. The variables are listed by /usr/bin/awk (by absolute path). When awk cannot run, the hook refuses every call (exit 2) instead of running with them. This is a list of known names, not an allow list: the hook itself reads XDG_*, CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, KRB5* and the variables an SSH setup uses. The user wiring then runs phiward's Python isolated (-I).
  • The plugin's and install --project's hooks run phiward by name. A project env.PATH could make them run another program called phiward, which may allow every call: the refusal of PATH below comes from phiward, which then never starts. For real data, wire your user settings ((cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write): absolute paths, -I); doctor --headless requires that wiring.
  • LD_* and DYLD_* reach the shell and awk before they are unset: a project that sets them can load code there. They are not refused (projects set LD_LIBRARY_PATH for their builds); doctor notes them.
  • The hook refuses every tool call, and names the file, when a project's settings set one of the variables below, or when a project settings file does not parse (an empty one is {}). doctor names them too. The refusal comes after such a shell has run: it tells you, it does not undo.
  • PHIWARD_*, KRB5*, USER, LOGNAME, CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR;
  • PATH (it chooses the phiward the plugin's and project hooks start);
  • CLAUDE_CODE_SHELL_PREFIX and CLAUDE_CODE_SHELL (a project's would win over yours);
  • a variable that makes the shell run code (SHELLOPTS, BASHOPTS, PS4, BASH_ENV, ENV, PROMPT_COMMAND, IFS, CDPATH, GLOBIGNORE, BASH_FUNC_*).
  • The hook reads the settings of every project a call may belong to: $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, and every folder at or above the call's own folder that holds .claude or .git (not the home folder). So a submodule or a folder with its own .claude cannot hide the project's settings. A redirect in any of them refuses every call.
