L3 .claude/settings.local.json is read-only, but a plain run outside launch still reads whatever was in it before the session. Read it once before the first launch. L4 macOS: the per-user temp folder is writable, and it is also your own TMPDIR. A file planted there can be used by a later plain run. A session can also read /private/tmp (except Kerberos caches) and the per-user temp folder, where your own tools leave files (R's RtmpXXXX, Python temp files, other Claude Code sessions' scratch). Do not run tools that load code from TMPDIR; keep protected data out of temp folders. L5 macOS: a process that leaves the tool's process tree (a new session, a double fork) keeps running after the tool exits; launch never ends a process. Its session folder is moved to trash/ and thrown away, and a later session's folder is new, so nothing it writes there reaches a later session. It can still write the project (after the report, not reported), the spool and the per-user temp folder, and can make a folder again at its old run path (never read). Its profile still allows its session's one proxy port on loopback, which the launcher no longer holds: a process that binds that port later (by chance or on purpose) can talk to it. The port is random for each launch, and a later session has its own port and token. Close the terminal after a session; a separate macOS user for the agent (not part of this release). L6 Carry-over (stateless): each session runs in a config folder built from a trusted copy that no session can read or write, and thrown away after it. Nothing in the tool folder is shared between sessions but this project's transcripts (open-transcripts): no login, no caches. On macOS two things outside it still are: the Keychain (Claude Code keeps its login there, so a session may add or change login items, including the one your plain claude uses) and the per-user temp folder, which your own tools also use. Instruction files a session changes, and the MCP and permission keys of .claude.json, go to quarantine; only what you accept (phiward carryover accept) or add yourself (phiward carryover add PATH) is trusted. A session cannot read another session's folder. Everything phiward keeps for this may be deleted at any time; you lose only what it costs to rebuild (launch.md). Login: a fresh folder means a new login each time, unless you set CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (from claude setup-token) or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, which the agent can read. Project memory (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .claude/rules/ in the project) is reported, not put back. Read the quarantine and the project report before you accept or run anything. L7 Names that a gateway command makes while it runs are not in that run's inventory, so they are not masked in its own output. The next call sees them. Print aggregates, not names (rule 3 of the agent rules in a project's AGENTS.md). L9 claude --bare and an Agent SDK app with settingSources: [] load none of phiward's wiring (hook, sandbox block, deny rules), and nothing says so. Do not use --bare on protected work; load the user settings in an SDK app or pass phiward install claude --json as its settings, or run it under phiward launch (unattended.md). L10 Linux: a folder of thousands of entries above a protected folder makes launch show that folder whole, with its protected entries masked (the view must fit in bwrap's 9000 arguments). There, a protected entry made or replaced after the start is not hidden. launch says how many folders it shows whole, and refuses when the folder that holds a protected root would have to be shown whole (it would list the root's name). Protect large data folders as roots, not one entry each among many; keep new protected data in folders that exist before the session. L8 Two sessions in one project share its write places: one can plant files that the other runs. Not confirmed in a test. Several sessions may run side by side; prefer one per project when one of them reads untrusted input.

docs.title: Agents with nobody watching: headless, the Agent SDK, scheduled runs, CI
docs.text:
• For: you, the operator, when an agent runs with no person at each step.
  • Before: the quick start is done.
  • You will have: guarded unattended runs, and a list of what holds and what does not.

An agentic workflow is a script that calls claude -p, an app built on the Claude Agent SDK, a scheduled or long-running agent, or several agents working together. phiward fits these well where it runs on your own machine, because nothing in it asks at run time. The grants are set ahead of time in your user config, and what they do not allow is refused. The limits of each mode are in modes.md and threat-model.md.

docs.title: Before every unattended run
docs.text:
phiward doctor --headless

It exits with 0 when a Claude Code session in this folder would be guarded, and with 1 and the reasons when not. Put it first in the script. A NOTE line (for example, that no rule masks subject identifiers) does not change the exit status. It checks that:

  • your user (or managed) settings run phiward's isolated hook on every tool. That is the /bin/sh -c '...; exec <python> -I -m phiward hook claude' that phiward install claude --user --write writes. The plugin's and project hooks alone are not enough here, because a project's env.PATH can replace them;
  • the program the hook names is there, every entry blocks on failure and has no async or if, and every tool is covered (the matcher *);
  • no settings file Claude Code may read turns hooks off (disableAllHooks, managed allowManagedHooksOnly) and the project's settings set no env that changes the hook;
  • the permission deny rules for protected and hidden paths are there;
  • Claude Code's sandbox confines the shell (on Linux, bubblewrap and socat are installed);
  • the broker is running, with the same phiward version as doctor (restart it after an upgrade).

With protected patterns, the shell counts as confined only on macOS (Claude Code 2.1.236 or newer, after install claude --user --write). Otherwise --headless reports it as not ready, because the hook then refuses shell commands other than gateway calls.

docs.title: What fits
docs.text: Workflow Set it up like this What holds claude -p in a script, cron job or LaunchAgent, on your machine (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write) and the broker service, as for interactive use. Never --bare. The same as an interactive session (Mode A). A refusal holds in every permission mode, bypassPermissions and dontAsk included. An Agent SDK app (Python, TypeScript) on your machine Leave settingSources at its default, or pass settings from phiward install claude --json (below). Add the callback below as a second check. Mode A, as above. The agent reads untrusted input (web pages, other people's files) Run it under Mode B: phiward launch --tool claude --report ~/phiward-runs/run.json -- claude -p "...". Read the report. The whole tool in phiward's kernel profile. Subagents, an orchestrator with workers Nothing extra. Hooks, the sandbox and deny rules apply to a subagent's tool calls too. As for the session that started them. A scheduled agent that uses HPC The shared SSH connection must be open, and your Kerberos ticket valid, when it runs. run --remote is refused (fails closed) when they have expired.

docs.title: What does not fit
docs.text:
• claude --bare, or an SDK app with settingSources: [] and nothing in its place. They load none of phiward's wiring: no hook, no sandbox block, no deny rules. Nothing says so. Claude Code's docs recommend --bare for scripts; do not use it for work beside protected data.
  • CI runners and containers that hold the data. The broker must run outside the agent, as you; in CI every other step runs as the same user, can read the data and can change your config. A broker inside a container usually cannot start its confinement, and refuses.
  • A repository you have not read. claude -p shows no trust prompt: a cloned repository's project settings (hooks, env, permission rules) apply at once. Run phiward doctor --headless in that folder first; the hook refuses every call when the project's env would change it, and the checks above name the rest.
  • GitHub-hosted runners, cloud sessions, SLURM jobs. There is no operator side there. Keep protected data away from them. Only the identifier check works without data: phiward sanitize --check FILE.

docs.title: An Agent SDK app
docs.text:
Two layers, use both.

1. The wiring as settings. An app that loads no settings file still gets phiward's hook, sandbox block and deny rules from one JSON file:

phiward install claude --json > ~/.config/phiward/sdk-settings.json

Run it in your own terminal (it prints every protected path, so it refuses without one). Put the file next to your user config: that folder is protected from agent writes (with PHIWARD_CONFIG somewhere else, beside that file). Pass it as the settings option (Python ClaudeAgentOptions(settings=...), TypeScript options.settings). Write it again after you change your phiward config.

2. A PreToolUse callback. It runs phiward's own hook on each tool call, so the decision is the same as in a Claude Code session. It judges the shell as not sandboxed (the hook is strictest then), because it cannot know which settings your app loaded. It refuses everything when phiward is missing. Copy it into your app; do not install phiward into the app's own environment (the agent may be able to change files there).

import asyncio
import json
import shutil

# your `uv tool install`, outside this app; give its full path if the app's PATH holds folders
# the agent can write (a project's .venv/bin)
PHIWARD = shutil.which("phiward")


def _deny(why):
    return {"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
                                   "permissionDecision": "deny",
                                   "permissionDecisionReason": why}}


async def phiward_guard(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    """PreToolUse callback: phiward's hook decides. Every failure refuses the call."""
    if PHIWARD is None:
        return _deny("phiward is not installed, so every tool call is refused")
    proc = None
    try:
        payload = dict(input_data)
        payload.pop("permission_mode", None)  # judge the shell as not sandboxed
        proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(
            PHIWARD, "hook", "claude", stdin=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
            stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE, stderr=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE)
        out, err = await asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(json.dumps(payload).encode()), 30)
        if proc.returncode != 0:
            return _deny(err.decode("utf-8", "replace").strip() or "phiward refused the call")
        reply = json.loads(out) if out.strip() else {}
        decision = reply.get("hookSpecificOutput", {}).get("permissionDecision")
        if decision == "ask":
            return _deny(reply["hookSpecificOutput"].get("permissionDecisionReason",
                                                         "phiward would ask") + " (nobody to ask)")
        return reply if decision in (None, "deny") else _deny("phiward's reply was not understood")
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 - every failure refuses the call
        if proc is not None and proc.returncode is None:
            proc.kill()
        return _deny(f"phiward's hook did not answer ({type(exc).__name__})")

Register it for every tool:

from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgentOptions, HookMatcher

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    settings="/Users/me/.config/phiward/sdk-settings.json",
    hooks={"PreToolUse": [HookMatcher(matcher=".*", hooks=[phiward_guard], on_failure="block")]},
)

In TypeScript, the same callback:

import { spawn, execFileSync } from "node:child_process";

// phiward from your `uv tool install`, found once, outside this app
let PHIWARD = null;
try { PHIWARD = execFileSync("sh", ["-c", "command -v phiward"]).toString().trim() || null; } catch { PHIWARD = null; }

const deny = (why) => ({ hookSpecificOutput: { hookEventName: "PreToolUse",
  permissionDecision: "deny", permissionDecisionReason: why } });

export async function phiwardGuard(input) {
  if (!PHIWARD) return deny("phiward is not installed, so every tool call is refused");
  const payload = { ...input };
  delete payload.permission_mode; // judge the shell as not sandboxed
  return await new Promise((resolve) => {
    let out = "", err = "";
    const p = spawn(PHIWARD, ["hook", "claude"], { stdio: ["pipe", "pipe", "pipe"] });
    p.stdin.on("error", () => {}); // the hook may exit before it reads; its exit decides
    const timer = setTimeout(() => { p.kill(); resolve(deny("phiward's hook did not answer")); }, 30000);
    p.on("error", () => { clearTimeout(timer); resolve(deny("phiward is not installed, so every tool call is refused")); });
    p.stdout.on("data", (d) => { out += d; });
    p.stderr.on("data", (d) => { err += d; });
    p.on("close", (code) => {
      clearTimeout(timer);
      if (code !== 0) return resolve(deny(err.trim() || "phiward refused the call"));
      let reply = {};
      try { reply = out.trim() ? JSON.parse(out) : {}; } catch { return resolve(deny("phiward's reply could not be read")); }
      const decision = reply.hookSpecificOutput?.permissionDecision;
      if (decision === "ask") {
        return resolve(deny((reply.hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecisionReason || "phiward would ask") + " (nobody to ask)"));
      }
      resolve(decision === undefined || decision === "deny" ? reply : deny("phiward's reply was not understood"));
    });
    p.stdin.end(JSON.stringify(payload));
  });
}

Register it with hooks: { PreToolUse: [{ matcher: ".*", hooks: [phiwardGuard], onFailure: "block" }] }.

The app's own code, and the tools you write into it, run as you and are not guarded by phiward: keep protected data out of them, or reach it through the gateway (phiward run).

docs.title: Mode B with nobody watching
docs.text:
phiward launch --tool claude --report ~/phiward-runs/run.json -- claude -p "count the reads per sample"

launch passes the arguments after -- to the tool and needs no terminal. Give the tool its login in CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (the agent can read it).

--report writes a JSON file whenever launch ends, also when nothing could run. A report that says needs_review: true is written before the tool starts, so a crash or a signal leaves one too. Give a file path outside every place the session can write (the project, the spool, the temp folder, ~/.phiward, in any spelling). It must not be a file that controls the guards (phiward's config or code, Claude Code's settings, a hidden credential). Otherwise nothing runs. The file is written new and moved into place, so nothing the session left at that path is opened. When the place is refused, nothing is written. For launch inside launch it is written with exit: null before the tool takes over the process (the outer launch reports the run). It holds:

  • exit: the tool's exit status;
  • ran: whether the tool started;
  • needs_review: true when the tool did not run, or the session changed instructions (they wait in quarantine), files that run later (build files, git hooks, CI workflows), settings, or git control files, or the project had more entries than launch compares. Other changed files are counted, not flagged;
  • project_changed: the changed project files by kind (instructions, runs_later, settings, other);
  • carryover: the lines about the session's instructions and quarantine;
  • git_control_changed: the git control files that changed (Linux);
  • notes: every line launch printed at the end.

A script should stop, and a person should read the notes, when needs_review is true. Accept nothing from quarantine without reading it (phiward carryover show).

docs.title: Risks that grow when nobody watches
docs.text:
• Rules that match nothing. A scheduled run whose identifier rules match none of its data looks like clean data. After it, read the broker log: no placeholder shown on a run over named data means a pack or a pattern is missing.
  • Prompt injection. A page or file the agent reads can tell it what to do, and nobody sees it happen. phiward still keeps it from reading protected data, but what it can read it can send: the network is open by default. In Mode A, [network] limit keeps shell commands to the hosts you list (configuration.md); the WebFetch tool and MCP servers stay open. In Mode B, phiward launch's proxy refuses this machine and private addresses; public hosts stay open.
  • Masked output is still content. Gateway output hides names and identifiers, not other content. Write the gateway commands an agent may run so that they print counts and summaries, and limit them with [broker] commands.
  • Long runs add up. Each gateway call returns up to [broker] max_output_lines lines; many calls return many lines. Set a lower limit for unattended runs, and cap the run itself (claude -p --max-turns N, the SDK's max_budget_usd).
  • Several agents share one broker and one spool. Requests carry no agent identity, and an agent can change another agent's reply in the spool (it is the same user). One agent's masked output passed to another is ordinary text to phiward.
  • Secrets in the environment. Mode A hides credential files, not environment variables. Do not put tokens an agent should not have into the environment of the run.

docs.title: Why phiward: what exists, and the gap it fills
docs.text: For: anyone who decides whether phiward is needed, beside sandboxes, containers and PII tools.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
An AI coding agent sends what its tools print to a model provider: file contents, command output, file names. In research on patient data, that output can hold protected health information (PHI), sample identifiers or file names that are identifiers themselves. Often there is no agreement with the provider that allows this.

People who work beside such data still want the agent's help: to write and run analyses, to check results, to submit jobs to an HPC cluster. So the question is not only "how do I keep the agent away from the data?", but also "how does the agent still work on the data, without seeing it?".

docs.title: What exists
docs.text:
This list is from each project's own documentation, read in November 2026. Check them again before you choose; they change fast.

Kind Examples What it gives What it does not give for this problem The agent tool's own sandbox and permission rules Claude Code's sandbox, permission deny rules and managed settings Bash in a kernel sandbox; file tools refused listed paths; an organization can force settings You write every path and credential by hand, per tool. No way to work on protected data with masked results. Nothing for HPC. Sandboxes around a whole command Anthropic's sandbox-runtime, nono, landrun A kernel profile (Seatbelt, bubblewrap, Landlock) around any program; network proxies A general sandbox: no model of protected data inside a readable project, no masked way back to the data, nothing for HPC. Containers and VMs Docker Sandboxes, dev containers, Apptainer Strong isolation; a session that is thrown away The data must stay outside. Docker does not run on most HPC systems. Work on the data itself is not possible from inside. Code-only PHI guards phi-guard A container that holds only the committed code; an egress firewall; masking by a cloud service Made for work away from PHI, by design. No masked way to run analyses on it. Nothing for HPC or mounted data. PII detection and redaction Presidio, LLM Guard, MCP PII proxies Finds and masks personal data in text, often with language models Sees only the text it is given. The agent's shell and file tools go around an MCP proxy. Nothing stops the agent from reading the data first. Secret scanners gitleaks and similar Find credentials in commits Not about tool output or PHI.

docs.title: The gap phiward fills
docs.text:
phiward is for work beside protected data: the agent helps with the analysis, and the data does not reach the model provider.

It is built for an honest user, and for an agent that is honest but can be misled by text it reads (prompt injection). It is not built to stop a determined attacker who already runs code on the machine (threat model).

  1. Protected data by folder, for the whole tool. You name the folders that hold protected data once. phiward writes that into Claude Code's sandbox and permission rules (Mode A), or runs the whole tool in its own kernel profile (Mode B), together with a list of credential files that no agent may read.
  2. A masked way to work on the data. The agent does not read protected data; it asks the gateway (phiward run, phiward copy). Your broker runs the command outside the agent, as you, and masks the output: protected paths, the names of files under them, and identifier patterns become placeholders. Ask for counts and summaries: masking hides names and identifiers, not other content, and not small counts (Small counts).
  3. HPC without giving the agent your login. phiward run --remote and phiward copy go through your own shared SSH connection. No request reads your key or Kerberos ticket, and only the hosts and programs you list are allowed.
  4. Easy for a team. One setup command, a guided setup inside Claude Code (/phiward:setup), phiward init for a project, and a check (phiward doctor) that says what is missing.
  5. Local and deterministic. No cloud service, no language model in the masking, no network. Python's standard library only.

docs.title: What phiward reuses, and what it does not do
docs.text:
• It reuses the operating system's sandboxes (Seatbelt on macOS; bubblewrap, seccomp and Landlock on Linux), Claude Code's own sandbox and permission rules, and the system ssh, tar and rsync.
  • It filters the network in two places. With [network] limit, the shell commands of a Mode A session reach only the hosts you list; the WebFetch tool and MCP servers stay open. In Mode B, phiward launch sends the tool's network through a loopback proxy of its own, which refuses this machine and private addresses. Public hosts stay open in both: an agent can still send what it can read there.
  • Masking hides names and identifiers, not other content in a record. Gateway commands should print counts and summaries.

All limits are in threat-model.md.

  • phi-guard: https://github.com/matthewevans/phi-guard
  • Presidio: https://github.com/microsoft/presidio
  • LLM Guard: https://github.com/protectai/llm-guard
  • gitleaks: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks

Next: the two modes, then the threat model.

docs.title: phiward v0.2.0b1 (beta)
docs.text:
The first public release of phiward. It keeps protected data (for example patient data) and your credentials out of what an AI coding agent sends to its model provider.

Start with docs/quickstart.md: install phiward, set it up (with Claude Code's help through /phiward:setup, or by hand), and check it.

uv tool install --python-preference only-managed phiward==0.2.0b1

Or from the GitHub tag: uv tool install git+https://github.com/msk-access/phiward@v0.2.0b1.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Mode A, the default: every normal Claude Code session (the desktop app, an IDE, a terminal) is wired by phiward install claude --user. Bash runs in Claude Code's sandbox, the file tools are refused protected data and credentials, and every session starts with a note on the rules.
  • Mode B, the stronger one: phiward launch --tool claude runs the whole tool (file tools, shell, MCP servers, hooks) in phiward's kernel profile. Terminal only for now.
  • The gateway: the agent works on protected data only through phiward run and phiward copy. The broker runs them outside the agent and masks the output.
  • HPC through your own shared SSH connection: phiward run --remote and phiward copy. No request reads your key or Kerberos ticket (hpc.md).
  • Easy onboarding: a Claude Code plugin with /phiward:setup, /phiward:doctor and /phiward:help; phiward init for a project; phiward mcp, the gateway as MCP tools (plugins.md).
  • The broker as a login service: phiward broker --service --write.

A summary of this release is in the CHANGELOG.

docs.title: Tested, on made-up data
docs.text:
• Mode A in the Claude Code desktop app on macOS: reads of protected data and of a credential by the Read tool, cat and Monitor were refused; ssh to HPC failed; normal work was unaffected.
  • The plugin in a desktop-app session: the session note, the refusals, the commands, normal work; and beside another plugin (ECC).
  • Mode B with the real Claude Code on macOS: the file tools and the shell were refused protected data; the gateway returned masked output; a skill and an MCP server carried over.
  • HPC against a real cluster: remote runs, a push, a pull into a protected folder, and the refusals.
  • An MCP server wrapped in phiward launch, on macOS and Linux.
  • The full test suite on macOS and Linux; fuzz tests; several adversarial reviews.

docs.title: Not tested yet
docs.text:
• The real Claude Code on Linux (the test suite runs there).
  • phiward launch driven from the desktop app with Remote Control.
  • A published MCP server wrapped in phiward launch on macOS (on Linux it was).
  • A protected folder on a mounted HPC volume.
  • [network] limit in a live Claude Code session (the settings it writes are tested; Claude Code enforces them).
  • Other agent tools than Claude Code.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
All limits are in docs/threat-model.md, with a summary for reviewers at the top. The main ones:

  • Identifiers inside files need a pack or patterns. Out of the box, masking inside file contents covers only sequence and alignment file names, read names and loci (the genomics pack). Subject and sample identifiers inside files are masked only with a pack that has them (the msk example), your own [sanitize] patterns or names_from. The gateway masks entry names under the protected roots (4 characters or longer). Planned for 0.2.0b2: setup asks, doctor warns, and the output says what was masked (#3, #5).
  • The network is open by default. [network] limit (asked by setup) limits the shell commands of a Mode A session to listed hosts; WebFetch, MCP servers and Mode B stay open. The agent cannot read protected data, but it can send what it can read.
  • Masking covers names and identifiers, not content. Print counts and summaries through the gateway.
  • In Mode A, the file tools are refused inside Claude Code, not by the kernel, and hooks and MCP servers that are not wrapped run with your rights.
  • run --remote is not confined on the cluster. [remote] commands is what limits it.
  • macOS: the Keychain and the per-user temp folder are shared with your own tools.

docs.title: Upgrade from agent-guards
docs.text: phiward was called agent-guards before this release. See setup.md.

docs.title: phiward v0.2.0b2 (beta)
docs.text: The second beta. It keeps protected data (for example patient data) and your credentials out of what an AI coding agent sends to its model provider.

docs.title: In short
docs.text: This release checks more of what reaches the provider, and refuses more by default. Prompts are checked before Claude Code sends them. @ mentions are off (Claude Code 2.1.299 or newer), so a mention no longer puts a file's text into the prompt without a tool call the hook sees; the IDE's open-file and selection context is not covered. phiward launch checks the project's own files for subject and sample IDs, and sends the tool's network through a proxy that refuses this machine and private addresses. A masking check tests your rules with made-up values at each start. phiward pseudonymize makes coded copies of tables, VCF, JSON and Markdown files for the agent. run --table reads tables by column. Two new options give back what the stricter defaults take: [no_phi] folders and [launch] write_to. Upgrading from 0.2.0b1 needs a few steps in your own terminal: install, restart the broker, re-run the wiring, and the others in the checklist next. Every change is in the CHANGELOG.

docs.title: Upgrade checklist (from 0.2.0b1)
docs.text:
In your own terminal, in this order:

  • [ ] uv tool install --force --python-preference only-managed phiward==0.2.0b2
  • [ ] (cd ~ && phiward broker --service --write) (restarts the broker; without the login service, stop phiward broker and start it again)
  • [ ] With [network] limit on: move any host you added to Claude Code's settings by hand into [network] allowed_domains
  • [ ] (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write) (required)
  • [ ] In each project you wired with install claude --project --write: run that command again
  • [ ] Plugin users, in Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add msk-access/phiward#v0.2.0b2
  • [ ] Claude Code 2.1.299 or newer (2.1.295 is the minimum; doctor warns below 2.1.299)
  • [ ] phiward doctor in each project: fix each WARNING

docs.title: What changes for you
docs.text:
Do these once, in your own terminal, in this order.

  1. Install the new version: uv tool install --force --python-preference only-managed phiward==0.2.0b2.
  2. Restart the broker. A broker that runs keeps the old code until it restarts. Run (cd ~ && phiward broker --service --write); it restarts the login service. Without the service, stop phiward broker and start it again. phiward doctor now warns while the running broker's version differs from its own, and doctor --headless is not ready.
  3. Re-run (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write). It is required.
    • It adds the prompt check (a UserPromptSubmit hook), the setting that turns @ mentions off, and ~/.phiward/profiles to the hidden list. It rewrites the hooks in the new form.
    • Until you run it, doctor warns, and doctor --headless is not ready (no prompt check).
    • On macOS, until you run it, the hook refuses every shell command but a gateway call once the broker has run: the sandbox does not hide the new ~/.phiward/profiles.
    • Hosts you added by hand. With [network] limit on, install now sets sandbox.network.allowedDomains to exactly your [network] allowed_domains. It prints each host it removes. Move each host you added to the settings by hand into [network] allowed_domains first, or git push and pip install to it fail.
    • Run it again after any upgrade that moves phiward's Python. Until then every tool call is refused, and doctor names the cause.
  4. A project you wired with phiward install claude --project --write: run that command again in the project. Its committed hooks have no prompt check, so doctor --headless reports the project as not ready. Projects set up with phiward init only are not affected.
  5. Plugin users: add the marketplace again with the new tag, /plugin marketplace add msk-access/phiward#v0.2.0b2 (plugins.md). The plugin stays at the tag you added, with that release's hooks.
  6. Run phiward doctor and fix each WARNING. Each one names its step. doctor does not check the plugin's version: plugin users check step 5 by hand, in /plugin in Claude Code. The plugin's version must match phiward --version.

Claude Code: 2.1.295 or newer, as before. 2.1.299 or newer turns @ mentions off; doctor warns below it.

Refusals you may meet now. Each refusal names its fix.

  • A [remote] roots entry that is not absolute (~/data, data) makes the config unusable. Then every guarded action refuses: the hook, the gateway and launch. Write the remote's absolute path.
  • A push with no [remote] roots. phiward copy to a remote now writes only under [remote] roots; with none, every push is refused. Run (cd ~ && phiward setup), which makes each copy remote's folder a remote root, or add each remote's folder to [remote] roots. doctor warns about a copy remote without one.
  • An empty or relative PATH entry (a leading or trailing :, ::, ., bin) stops launch, and every MCP server wrapped by phiward mcp wrap: such a server then "failed to connect". phiward doctor names the entry. Remove it from PATH (often a trailing : in your shell startup file).
  • launch --tool claude and the program it runs. On macOS and Linux it refuses a Claude Code older than 2.1.295, a tool that gives no Claude Code version, a shim or wrapper (npx, env, a script), and an npm build without its package.json. Run Claude Code's own binary, or use --tool generic.
  • launch --tool claude and your own --settings (Linux below 7.1). launch passes its own --settings, and Claude Code keeps only one. Yours is dropped when its content is the same as the file install writes, from this release or the earlier one. Any other --settings stops the start. If it is phiward's file, run (cd ~ && phiward install claude --user --write).
  • hook claude answers PreToolUse only. A hook claude entry you wired by hand under another event (PostToolUse, ...) now exits 2 there, with a refusal that names phiward doctor. What Claude Code does with exit 2 depends on the event. Remove the entry; phiward's hooks go under PreToolUse and, for the prompt check, UserPromptSubmit.
  • The masking check. launch refuses to start, and the broker refuses every request, when a root, a protected pattern, a [remote] roots entry or a [sanitize] examples value does not come out fully masked. Run phiward doctor: it names the entry, the rule or the root by number.
  • The project scan. launch refuses a project whose files or file names hold subject or sample IDs. Run phiward doctor --show-paths to see the files. Move the data under a protected root, or list made-up files in [sanitize] scan_allow.
  • launch network. The tool reaches the network only through phiward's proxy, which refuses this machine and private addresses. List the private ranges you need in [launch] private_networks. On Linux, launch needs network namespaces.
  • Linux: launch refuses /tmp itself as the project or the spool. A folder below /tmp works.
  • Files that run later are read-only under launch. In Mode A the hook now asks before a file tool writes .cursor, .gemini, .codex, .Rprofile or .Renviron, and refuses where it cannot ask.
  • Copies: a local path with .., a quoted ~ or an empty one is refused. Give the full path.
  • Doctor warns until your user config masks subject IDs (a pack, patterns or names_from) or records [sanitize] subjects = "none". phiward setup asks.

Changed defaults and new options (user config only):

  • [launch] keep_transcripts is on by default. launch --tool claude now keeps each project's transcripts in ~/.phiward/carryover/claude/transcripts/, so --resume and -c work. To keep nothing, set it to false.
  • [no_phi] folders: exact folders you are sure hold no PHI. There, in Mode A, a shell that only a sandbox opener such as allowLocalBinding (macOS) leaves unconfined gets the text check, not the refusal. Nothing to do unless you need it.
  • [launch] write_to: more folders a launch session may write, besides the project. launch checks each one at its start. Nothing to do unless you need it.
  • Also new: [launch] private_networks, [sanitize] examples, scan_allow and id_columns.
